true_positives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated for every request and crashes when member is None

Line 71 unconditionally dereferences `organization_context.member`, regardless of whether `optimized_pagination` was requested. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is optional (`RpcOrganizationMemberSummary | None`) and is None whenever the caller is not an organization member — e.g. org auth tokens, API keys, or a superuser acting on an org they don't belong to. Those requests now raise `AttributeError` and return a 500 for a previously working endpoint. Additionally, `has_global_access` is not a field on `RpcOrganizationMemberSummary` (global access is exposed on the request's `Access` object, i.e. `request.access.has_global_access`), so this attribute lookup will fail even when `member` is populated. Move the check behind the `use_optimized` flag and use a real, existing access API.

false_positives.candidate:
Comment claims negative offsets are supported, contradicting the paginators

The added comment states that negative offsets are allowed as a "performance optimization ... enables efficient reverse pagination", but no code changed here and every paginator in `sentry/api/paginator.py` (`OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, `CombinedQuerysetPaginator`, `CallbackPaginator`) explicitly rejects negative offsets with `BadPaginationError`. Leaving this comment in `Cursor.__init__` will mislead future readers into assuming negative offsets are a supported contract of the cursor type.

New OptimizedCursorPaginator has no tests

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` duplicates ~70 lines of `BasePaginator.get_result` and adds a new `enable_advanced_features` code path, yet no tests were added in this PR for the class or for the modified offset handling in `BasePaginator.get_result`. Given the class is already broken for datetime keys and forwards negative offsets to the ORM, tests covering normal paging, prev cursors, and rejection of negative offsets are required before this can be relied on by an endpoint.

No test covers the new insert-time eviction or score ordering

The buffer tests were only mechanically updated to pass the new required `end_timestamp_precise` field. The core behaviour this PR introduces — zset-based storage, the 1000-span cap with `zpopmin` eviction of the oldest spans, and the removal of the old "skip too large segment" path — is completely untested. A regression in the Lua eviction arithmetic (e.g. popping too many spans, or evicting the root span) or in the zunionstore score aggregation would not be caught. Add a test that inserts more than the cap into one segment and asserts which spans survive, plus one asserting eviction keeps the highest `end_timestamp_precise` members.

Redirect-resolution loop bound silently reduced from 10000 to 1000

The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000` and the explanatory comment ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. This is an unrelated, undocumented behaviour change: traces whose redirect chains are deeper than 1000 will stop resolving to their real root, so those segments get split into multiple partial segments and are emitted as if complete, with no error or metric to signal it. Either keep the previous bound or document/justify the reduction and add observability for hitting the cap.

Silent offset clamping in BasePaginator yields incorrect pagination instead of a clear error

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes behaviour for every paginator derived from `BasePaginator`. For forward cursors a negative offset is now silently clamped to 0, but the raw negative `offset` is still used to build the next/prev cursors in `build_cursor` (e.g. `_build_next_values` computes `next_offset = offset + limit`), so a client passing a negative offset gets page-0 rows together with cursors that skip or repeat rows rather than a deterministic error. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still passed unclamped to the queryset slice, which raises `ValueError` from Django. Also note the subsequent check at line 192 (`len(results) == offset + limit + extra`) still uses the unclamped `offset`, so it no longer matches the number of rows actually fetched.

Span eviction limit is hardcoded to 1000 and drops spans with no metric or log

`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)` silently discards spans. Two problems: (1) the limit is hardcoded in Lua while `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` (default 1001) is the configured knob — that parameter is now dead code and operators cannot tune the limit, and the two values disagree by one; (2) the previous behaviour logged an error and emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` when a segment was too large, whereas the new path emits nothing, so oversized segments are now published as silently truncated segments that downstream consumers cannot distinguish from complete ones. Pass the limit in as an ARGV from `max_segment_spans` and emit a metric/return value when eviction occurs.

Unguarded `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` can crash the consumer on messages lacking the field

`end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` raises `KeyError` for any ingest-spans message that omits the field; the `cast(SpanEvent, ...)` on line 134 is a type-checker-only assertion and performs no validation, so a single malformed/older-format payload aborts batch processing and stalls the partition. Previously no span field beyond trace/span/project ids was mandatory. Consider defaulting (e.g. to the message/produce timestamp) or explicitly dropping such messages with a metric.

`max_segment_spans` is now unused dead configuration

The span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` was removed, so `self.max_segment_spans` (set from the constructor parameter on line 158) is no longer read anywhere; the span limit now lives as a hardcoded `1000` in `add-buffer.lua`. Anyone constructing `SpansBuffer(max_segment_spans=...)` will have their setting silently ignored. Either wire the value through to the Lua script's ARGV or remove the parameter.

zunionstore uses the default SUM aggregate, corrupting end-timestamp scores on duplicate payloads

`zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the same call for `parent_key` on line 53) uses Redis' default `AGGREGATE SUM`. Scores here are `end_timestamp_precise` values, and merges happen repeatedly as spans arrive. If the identical span payload is present in both merged keys — which happens with Kafka at-least-once redelivery or when a span is written under a parent key and later re-resolved — the resulting score becomes the sum of two epoch timestamps (~3.4e9), making that member permanently "newest". Since the new eviction logic (`zpopmin`) relies on these scores to drop the oldest spans, inflated scores cause the wrong spans to be evicted. Pass `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) so the score keeps timestamp semantics.

true_positives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sample-rate extraction silently swallows all errors and drops a 0 rate

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` wraps both the context lookup and the `float()` conversion in bare `except Exception: pass`, and gates on `if client_sample_rate:` (falsy), so a malformed or zero `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` results in no `sample_rate` on the event with no signal at all. A test that intends to store an upsampled event but passes a slightly wrong value will instead silently assert against raw counts, making failures hard to diagnose. Narrow the exception handling (e.g. `(TypeError, ValueError)`) and check `is not None` rather than truthiness.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility uses the outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`

`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` as its first argument (the dataset actually queried), but the eligibility check passes the enclosing `dataset` variable: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)`. In the dashboard-widget-split code path, `_get_event_stats` is intentionally invoked with a different dataset (`discover`, or the widget's split dataset) while the outer `dataset` is the metrics/discover dataset selected from the request. As a result the `count()` -> `upsampled_count()` decision is made for a dataset that is not the one being queried: upsampling can be skipped for an errors query that should be upsampled, or (when the outer dataset is errors-like and the scoped dataset is not) `upsampled_count()` can be sent to a dataset that has no `sample_weight` column, producing a Snuba error or wrong numbers. The check should use `scoped_dataset`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental git submodule (gitlink) `sentry-repo` committed without a .gitmodules entry

This PR adds a gitlink entry `sentry-repo` pointing at `a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a` (the base commit of this very repository) with no corresponding `.gitmodules` mapping. Git will report "no submodule mapping found in .gitmodules for path 'sentry-repo'" and `git submodule update`/`clone --recurse-submodules` will fail, and the self-referential pointer serves no purpose. This looks like a local working-directory artifact and should be removed from the commit.

Cache key uses `hash()` of the project tuple, so distinct project sets can collide

The cache key embeds `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))` rather than the project ids themselves. Two different project sets within the same organization that hash to the same value will share a cached eligibility verdict, which means a non-allowlisted project set can be treated as upsampled (counts multiplied by the sample weight) or vice versa. Serializing the ids (e.g. `"-".join(map(str, sorted(ids)))`, or a cryptographic digest if length matters) removes this failure mode at no cost.

Caching allowlist eligibility for 60s can serve 10x-wrong counts and cannot be invalidated

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` stores the result of the allowlist check in the shared cache under `error_upsampling_eligible:{org}:{hash(project_ids)}` for 60 seconds. The underlying value comes from `options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist")`, which is already cached by the options store, so there is no meaningful performance gain; what it does add is up to a minute of stale behavior. After an operator removes a project from the allowlist (e.g. to stop bad data or roll back the feature), charts keep returning `sum(sample_weight)` values that are inflated by the inverse sample rate (10x in the tests here) — and conversely, newly allowlisted projects keep returning raw counts. Because the cache key is per (org, exact project-id set), there is no practical way to purge all affected entries. Additionally, if the cache backend (redis/memcached) outlives a database reset in CI or local dev, project ids can be reused and a stale `True`/`False` will be applied to an unrelated project set. Consider removing the cache entirely or keying it on the option value/version.

Docstring claims the allowlist is read fresh on every call, which the caller's cache contradicts

`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`'s docstring states: "This function reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time... This is intentional to ensure we always have the latest configuration state." Its only caller, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, caches the result for 60 seconds, so the system does not always see the latest configuration. The comment in the caller ("This is safe because allowlist changes are infrequent and eventual consistency is acceptable") asserts the opposite guarantee. A future maintainer reading either docstring will reason incorrectly about staleness; the two must be reconciled.

Misleading comments on upsampled count assertions

In `test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` the assertions `assert data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10` / `== 10` are annotated "# First bucket has 1 event" / "# Second bucket has 1 event". The value 10 is the upsampled count derived from `client_sample_rate: 0.1`, not an event count; the comments make the expected values look like a bug to anyone reading the test. Reword to state that one stored event at a 0.1 sample rate is expected to be upsampled to 10.

No test covers the public entry point, its cache, or the errors-dataset path

The unit tests only exercise the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) and the column transform. The public function `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` — which contains the new cache key construction, the `cache.get`/`cache.set` logic, and the combination of eligibility with the dataset check — is never called in any test, so the cache-hit path, cache-staleness behavior, and the empty-`project_ids` case are unverified. Separately, no test issues a request with `dataset=errors`, even though `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns `True` unconditionally for that dataset and `upsampled_count` was only registered in the Discover dataset's `function_converter`; if the errors dataset config does not inherit that function, the primary intended path raises an invalid-function error and nothing here would catch it.

Top-events path upsamples only the series, not the top-N selection or orderby

In the `top_events > 0` branch only `timeseries_columns`/`y_axes` are rewritten to `upsampled_count()`; `selected_columns=self.get_field_list(...)` and `orderby=self.get_orderby(request)` keep the raw `count()`. The top-N groups are therefore selected and ordered by un-upsampled counts while the plotted series are upsampled. When the per-event sample rates differ across groups/projects, the chosen top groups and their ordering do not match the magnitudes shown in the chart.

Trailing whitespace and an over-length line will fail the repo's formatting checks

Several added lines contain trailing whitespace (e.g. the blank-but-indented lines inside the docstrings and between statements in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, and similar lines added in `organization_events_stats.py` around the `upsampling_enabled`/`final_columns` blocks), and the `cache_key = f"error_upsampling_eligible:..."` assignment exceeds the 100-character limit configured for black in `pyproject.toml`. The pre-commit/lint CI job will reject the branch until these are reformatted.

`default_result_type="number"` conflicts with the integer result it replaces

`upsampled_count` is declared with `default_result_type="number"` even though the aggregate is wrapped in `toInt64` and it is substituted for `count()`, which declares `"integer"`. Because the rewrite aliases the result back to `count`, clients receive meta `fieldType`/`type` of `number` for a field they previously got `integer` for, which changes formatting/axis handling in the UI for the same logical series. Use `"integer"` for consistency.

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is dead code and cannot invalidate in practice

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is not called from anywhere in this PR, and by construction it can only delete the single key for one exact (organization, project-id set) combination. Eligibility is cached per distinct project-id set, so a single allowlist option change would require enumerating every combination of project ids that has ever been queried. Shipping it gives the false impression that the cache is invalidated on configuration changes; either wire up a real invalidation (option-value-based cache key / option update hook) or drop the function.

`upsampled_count` has no fallback when `sample_weight` is missing/NULL

The new aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` with a comment asserting the schema guarantees `sample_weight` exists for all events in allowlisted projects. That guarantee does not hold for data stored before a project was allowlisted or before the SDK started sending `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` (the test factory change in this PR only sets `sample_rate` when that context is present). For such rows `sample_weight` is NULL/0, so `sum` silently drops them and a chart over a time range that spans the rollout collapses to zero or badly undercounts — with no error surfaced to the user. Wrapping the column, e.g. `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))`, makes unweighted events count as 1.

`upsampled_count` is registered as a public function, exposing it to arbitrary user queries

Unlike the neighbouring internal aggregates, the new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is not marked `private=True`, so any user can put `upsampled_count()` in a Discover/dashboard field or yAxis. This (a) lets users obtain sample-weight-scaled counts for projects that are not on the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`, bypassing the gating this PR builds, and (b) will fail at the Snuba layer (500 / SnubaError) for datasets or storages where the `sample_weight` column does not exist, since nothing validates dataset or project eligibility at resolution time. Mark it private, as this is an implementation detail of the server-side column rewrite.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes nodestore preserves input ordering

`fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids`, calls `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` (which returns a dict keyed by node id), and then pairs them positionally with `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. This relies on the backend returning values in exactly the same order as the requested ids and on never omitting missing keys. Some backends (e.g. Bigtable, which returns rows sorted by row key) do not guarantee that, and any omitted/missing entry shifts the pairing. The result is `ErrorEvent.id` being attached to the wrong error's title/message/timestamp, so the summary sent to Seer references incorrect event ids. Iterate `node_ids` and look up `events.get(node_id)` per id instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feature-flagged table widget path renders hardcoded empty data

In `tableResultComponent`, when `organization.features.includes('use-table-widget-visualization')` is true the component renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` instead of passing `result`/`fields`/`result.meta`. Because `columns` is an empty array (not nullish), `TableWidgetVisualization`'s fallback to derive columns from `tableData.meta.fields` is also bypassed. The consequence is that every table widget on a dashboard renders completely blank (no headers, no rows) for any organization that has this flag enabled, silently hiding real widget data. Either wire the real data through or keep the new component behind code that is not reachable from a user-facing flag.

true_positives.golden_comment: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
age/timestamp mutual-exclusion checks use truthiness instead of presence

`validate_timestamp` checks `self.initial_data.get("age")` and `validate_age` checks `self.initial_data.get("timestamp")`. Since both use truthiness, a value of `0` counts as absent: a report containing both `timestamp: 0` and `age: 0` passes both validators even though the stated rule is that exactly one of the two fields may be present, and a report with `timestamp: <valid>` plus `age: 0` produces an error only on the `age` field. Use `"age" in self.initial_data` / `"timestamp" in self.initial_data` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Analytics event recorded before the feature check and request validation

`analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` is the first statement in `post()`, so it fires even when the organization lacks `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` (404 response) or when the body fails schema validation (400 response). The resulting metric therefore counts rejected calls as assemble attempts. Move the `analytics.record` call after the feature/validation gates (or after the task is queued) so it reflects actual assembles.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

false_positives.candidate:
60s processing deadline is likely too short for a 100-identity chunk

`check_auth_identities` is scheduled by `check_auth` with `chunk_size=100` and sequentially calls `check_single_auth_identity` for each id; each call does a DB read, an RPC membership check and `provider.refresh_identity()`, which performs an external IdP request. A 60s `processing_deadline_duration` gives ~0.6s per identity. If the deadline is hit, the task is killed mid-chunk and (a) the remaining identities were already stamped with `last_synced=now` in `check_auth`, so they will not be re-selected for roughly another AUTH_CHECK_INTERVAL, and (b) the trailing `check_auth.apply_async(...)` that chains the next chunk never runs, stalling the whole sweep. Either raise the deadline substantially or reduce the chunk size.

Both saved-search conversion migrations turned into no-ops pointing at a migration not in this change

`0917_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views` and `0920_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_revised` both have their `RunPython` bodies replaced with `return` and a comment saying "See 0921_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_rerevised.py for the correct migration". No such migration is added in this PR, and the only test covering the conversion (`tests/sentry/migrations/test_0917_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views.py`) is deleted. If 0921 does not exist, organization-visibility `SavedSearch` rows are never converted into `GroupSearchView` rows anywhere, and the codebase is left with two dead migrations whose comments reference a nonexistent file plus zero test coverage for the conversion logic.

Custom cell renderers returning falsy React nodes are silently overridden

Both `renderDefaultHeadCell` and `renderDefaultBodyCell` do `const cell = render...(...); if (cell) return cell;`. The documented contract (see tableWidgetVisualization.stories.tsx and the prop JSDoc) is that only `undefined` falls through to the default renderer, but `null`, `''` and `0` are valid React nodes meaning "render this" and will instead be replaced by the default rendering. Check `cell !== undefined` so a custom renderer can intentionally render nothing.

Dead _handle_regex_match helper left in parametrize_w_experiments

After removing `ParameterizationRegexExperiment`, the experiment loop always calls `experiment.run(content, _incr_counter)`, but the inner `_handle_regex_match` closure (lines 335-343) is still defined and is now unreachable dead code duplicating the helper in `parametrize_w_regex`. Remove it to avoid confusion about which callback experiments use.

Error/breadcrumb merge compares timestamps in different units

`gen_request_data` interleaves errors and replay events with `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)`. Error timestamps come from the nodestore event payload and are epoch *seconds* (e.g. 1718900000.0), while rrweb replay event `timestamp` values are epoch *milliseconds* (e.g. 1718900000000). With real data every error timestamp is ~1000x smaller than every breadcrumb timestamp, so all errors are emitted before all breadcrumbs regardless of when they actually occurred, defeating the purpose of the chronological merge (and the log text prints raw, mismatched numbers). Normalise both to the same unit before comparing. The new unit test passes only because it uses hand-written second-scale event timestamps.

Issue titles are interpolated into a markdown link without escaping

`MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE = "* \u203c\ufe0f [**{title}**]({url}){environment}\n"` now puts the (truncated) issue title inside markdown link text, whereas the previous template only bolded it. Issue titles frequently contain `[` / `]` (e.g. `KeyError: 'items[0]'`), which terminates the link text early and renders a broken link/raw brackets in the PR comment. Escape `[`, `]` (and backslashes) in the title before formatting.

One invalid report rejects the entire browser report batch

The loop validates each report and returns `422` for the whole request as soon as any single report fails validation, so all other valid reports in the same batch are dropped. Browsers send Reporting API payloads as batches and will retry the whole batch, meaning a single persistently malformed/unsupported report (e.g. a `type` not in `BROWSER_REPORT_TYPES`, or a `url` the `URLField` regex rejects) permanently blocks metrics for every other report delivered with it. Prefer skipping/counting the invalid entries (with a metric or log) and returning 200 for the rest.

React Query key no longer includes the organization

The hook was switched from `useApiQuery([path, options])` (where `path` contained `/organizations/${organization.slug}/...`) to `useQuery({queryKey: ['use-trace-item-attribute-keys', queryOptions]})`, and `makeTraceItemAttributeKeysQueryOptions` only contains itemType, attributeType, project ids and the datetime range. When the project selection is "all projects" (`projects: []`), two different organizations produce an identical cache key, so attribute keys fetched for one org can be served from cache to another org. Add the organization slug (and ideally the endpoint path) to the query key.

get_environment_info issues a per-issue recommended-event lookup while building PR comments

`get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` for every issue included in a merged-PR comment. That helper runs a search/Snuba query plus a nodestore fetch per group, so building one comment now performs up to 5 extra event lookups (per PR, for both GitHub and GitLab comment workflows) purely to render an environment name. Consider resolving environments with a single cheap query (e.g. GroupEnvironment) instead of fetching recommended events, and note that the broad `except Exception` silently degrades to no environment on any failure.

true_positives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-code component is exported under the name TwoFactor

The new component in `BackupCode.tsx` is declared as `export default function TwoFactor({ center = true })`. The copy-pasted name makes React DevTools, error stacks and future greps report this backup-code input as "TwoFactor", which is confusing next to the real `TwoFactor` component it is rendered alongside in login.tsx and DisableTwoFactorModal.tsx. Rename it to `BackupCode`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write, allowing reuse

The backup-code login path decrypts the whole `backupCodes` JSON array, sets the matching entry to `null`, and writes the entire re-encrypted array back with `prisma.user.update`. Because the read and write are not atomic (no transaction, no conditional update), two concurrent authorize() calls that both present the *same* code will both find it at a non-(-1) index and both succeed, defeating the single-use guarantee of a backup code. Two concurrent logins with *different* codes will also clobber each other, re-validating an already consumed code. Consider consuming the code inside a transaction or with an update guarded on the previous `backupCodes` value.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
resetState leaves stale form/backup-code state and leaks the blob URL

`resetState()` clears only `password`, `errorMessage` and `step`. The component is not unmounted when the dialog closes (state lives above the Radix `Dialog`), so `form`'s `totpCode`, `backupCodes`, `secret`, `dataUri` and `backupCodesUrl` persist. Consequences: (1) the previously entered 6-digit `totpCode` is still in the form on a subsequent setup, so pressing "Enable" immediately submits the stale code; (2) the object URL created with `URL.createObjectURL` is only revoked on the next successful setup, so it (and the plaintext backup codes it contains) is retained for the lifetime of the document. Reset the form (`form.reset()`) and clear/revoke the backup-code state too.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

false_positives.candidate:
"missing_backup_codes" tells users to generate codes in settings, but no such feature exists

`"missing_backup_codes": "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings."` is shown when `user.backupCodes` is null — which is the case for every account that enabled 2FA before this change, and for anyone who already spent all ten codes. There is no regenerate/backup-codes screen in settings: codes are only created by `/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup`, which rejects accounts that already have 2FA enabled (`TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled`). The only actual remedy is to disable and re-enable 2FA, so the message sends users on an impossible errand. Either add a regeneration path or change the text to describe the real recovery procedure.

Assertion on the 2FA switch is a no-op and was documented rather than fixed

`expect(page.locator(`[data-testid=two-factor-switch]`).isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` asserts on the Promise returned by `isChecked()`, which is always truthy, so this step can never fail — as the newly added FIXME admits. Since the enable flow now ends on the backup-codes dialog (the switch is not updated until `onEnable` runs), this test would not catch a regression where 2FA is never actually enabled. Replace it with `await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=two-factor-switch][data-state="checked"]')).toBeVisible()` as the second test already does.

Backup codes cannot be used by Google/SAML users with 2FA

`if (user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode) throw new Error(ErrorCode.ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled)` (and the analogous check on the next line) only allows the second-factor flow to proceed when a TOTP code is present. Users who authenticate via Google/SAML and have 2FA enabled are redirected to `/auth/login?totp=<jwt>` with no password; if they submit a backup code (totpCode empty) they get `ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled` / `IncorrectEmailPassword` instead of being logged in. The login page also hides the "Lost access" button in that flow (`ExternalTotpFooter`), so for these accounts backup codes are generated and stored but can never be redeemed — exactly the lock-out case the feature is meant to solve. The condition should also accept `credentials.backupCode`.

Backup codes stored with reversible encryption instead of hashed

`backupCodes: symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)` persists the plaintext codes under a single application-wide key, and both the login and disable paths decrypt them to compare. Unlike `twoFactorSecret`, backup codes never need to be recovered in cleartext — verification only requires an equality check — so they should be stored as hashes (e.g. bcrypt/sha-256 per code). As written, anyone who obtains the database plus `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (one secret shared by every other encrypted field) gets a usable 2FA bypass for every user.

No test covers the core new behaviour: authenticating with a backup code

The added test steps only exercise the download/copy/close buttons on the new backup-codes screen; the primary feature paths — logging in through "Lost access" with a backup code (including that a code is consumed and cannot be reused) and disabling 2FA with a backup code — are left as a TODO comment. Given the security sensitivity (single-use enforcement, re-encryption of the remaining codes, dash stripping), at least one end-to-end or unit test for a successful and a repeated backup-code redemption should be part of this PR.

Passing type="password" to PasswordField disables the show/hide toggle

`PasswordField` computes `type={isPasswordVisible ? "text" : "password"}` and then spreads `{...props}` *after* it (packages/ui/components/form/inputs/Input.tsx), so the explicit `type="password"` kept from the old `TextField` usage overrides the computed value. Clicking the eye icon toggles `isPasswordVisible` but the input stays `type="password"`, i.e. the reveal button does nothing. Drop the `type` prop here.

Submitting an empty/short backup code silently does nothing

The login form is rendered with `noValidate`, so the `required`/`minLength` attributes on the backup-code input (apps/web/components/auth/BackupCode.tsx) are never enforced, and the zod schema `passthrough()`es `backupCode` without validation. Submitting the backup-code step with an empty field sends `backupCode: ""`, the server falls through to the TOTP branch and throws `SecondFactorRequired`, which this handler maps to `setTwoFactorRequired(true)` — a no-op since it is already true — leaving no error message and no visible feedback. Add client-side validation for `backupCode` (or surface `SecondFactorRequired` as an error while in the lost-access state).

Unvalidated request body can crash the disable endpoint with a 500

`req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` assumes the field is a string. A client that posts `{"backupCode": 123}` or `{"backupCode": {}}` passes the truthiness check and then throws `TypeError: replaceAll is not a function`, producing an unhandled 500 instead of a 400. Likewise `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` on line 58 throws if the stored value cannot be decrypted/parsed (e.g. after an encryption-key rotation). Validate/coerce the body (zod or `typeof === "string"`) and wrap the decrypt/parse in a try/catch returning a defined ErrorCode.

onEnable() is only called from the Close button, so dismissing the dialog leaves stale UI and loses codes

Previously `onEnable()` fired as soon as the enable API returned 200. Now the success path only calls `setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes)` and `onEnable()` is invoked exclusively by the "Close" button handler. If the user dismisses the dialog with ESC, the X, or an overlay click (which triggers `onOpenChange`), 2FA is already enabled server-side but the parent settings view is never notified, so the two-factor switch stays in the "off" state until a manual reload. The user also loses the only display of their backup codes, with no way to regenerate them. `onEnable()` should be called when the code is accepted (or on `onOpenChange` while on the backup-codes step).

tabIndex={-1} makes the password reveal button keyboard-inaccessible

Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide-password button removes it from the tab order for all `PasswordField` consumers across the app (login, signup, 2FA modals). Keyboard-only and screen-reader users can no longer reach this control even though it has an `sr-only` label, which is an accessibility regression affecting every password input, not just the 2FA dialogs. If the goal was to stop the button from stealing focus during the 2FA flow, make it opt-in via a prop instead of changing global behaviour.

true_positives.golden_comment: A null reference occurs in GoogleCalendarService.createEvent() and updateEvent() when mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar but evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, causing mainHostDestinationCalendar to be undefined.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Google Meet fallback dereferences undefined destination calendar

`const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` yields `undefined` whenever the event has no destination calendar (empty array or null), and the next line reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Placeholder string overwrites a valid refresh token

`if (!refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token) refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token";` injects the literal string `"refresh_token"` whenever the provider response omits a refresh token — and it does this unconditionally, even when credential sharing is disabled. In `office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` the result is merged into the stored key (`{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`) and `refresh_token` is optional in `refreshTokenResponseSchema`, so a refresh response without a new refresh token will replace the user's real Microsoft refresh token with the garbage value, permanently breaking that credential. Only fill in a placeholder when the credential-sync path is active, and never let it clobber an existing refresh token.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
minimumTokenResponseSchema is not a valid schema and silently strips all token fields

The computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both stringify a ZodType object to the same literal key (`"[object Object]"`), so the schema is effectively `{ access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown }`. It therefore (a) never validates that an expiry field exists, despite the comment, and (b) because Zod objects strip unknown keys by default, the returned `data` contains only `access_token` — `refresh_token`, `expires_in`/`expiry_date`, `scope`, `instance_url`, `api_domain`, etc. are discarded. Any caller that persists this data (Google, Office365, Zoom) loses the fields it needs: e.g. Zoom computes `expiry_date = Date.now() + undefined * 1000` → `NaN`, after which `isTokenValid` never triggers a refresh again. Use an explicit schema such as `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), expires_in: z.number().optional(), expiry_date: z.number().optional() }).passthrough()`.

true_positives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Google credential key is overwritten with a Zod safeParse result wrapper

`parseRefreshTokenResponse()` returns the raw `safeParse` result (`{ success: true, data: {...} }`), not the parsed object, yet the return value is written straight into the DB: `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema); await prisma.credential.update({ ..., data: { key } })`. Previously the code stored `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)`. After this change the stored credential key becomes `{"success":true,"data":{...}}`, so the next `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` fails and the user's Google Calendar credential is permanently broken. The value should be `...data` (and the helper should return the parsed data, not the wrapper).

true_positives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

Token refresh success detected via `statusText === "OK"`

`if (response.statusText !== "OK") throw new HttpError(...)` is unreliable: `statusText` is an empty string for HTTP/2 responses (undici) and may carry other reason phrases for 2xx responses, so a successful refresh can be rejected with an empty error message while a non-2xx body could slip through. Check `response.ok` / `response.status` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Salesforce token is refreshed on every instantiation and the stale token is still used

`getClient()` is called from the constructor and now unconditionally POSTs to `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` with `grant_type=refresh_token`, regardless of whether the stored access token is still valid — an extra Salesforce round trip (and API-limit consumption) for every service construction, e.g. on each availability/booking path. Worse, after refreshing and persisting the new token the returned `jsforce.Connection` is still built with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` and `instanceUrl: credentialKey.instance_url` from the old key, so the freshly obtained token is discarded and requests may run with an expired token. Gate the refresh on expiry and build the connection from the refreshed values. (Note the `if (!accessTokenParsed.success)` branch below is dead code, since `parseRefreshTokenResponse` already throws on failure.)

true_positives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unvalidated input and decryption errors surface as unhandled 500s

`appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a `ZodError` for a malformed payload, and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, ...))` throws when the key is wrong or the ciphertext/JSON is invalid. Neither is caught, so callers get an opaque 500 (with a stack trace in the server logs and, in dev, the response) instead of a 400 with an actionable message, making integration debugging hard for self-hosters. Use `safeParse` plus a try/catch around decryption and return 400.

false_positives.candidate:
APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED evaluates to the encryption key, not a boolean

`process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` returns the value of `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` when both are set, so this exported "flag" is actually the secret string. `packages/lib/constants.ts` is imported broadly (including from client-reachable modules), so any place that logs or serialises this constant leaks the AES key. Wrap it in `!!(...)` so only a boolean is exported.

Apps wired to refreshOAuthTokens still validate with provider-specific strict schemas

Webex (and likewise `larkcalendar` via `handleLarkError`, `office365video`, `hubspot`, `zohocrm`, `zoho-bigin`) now call `refreshOAuthTokens`, but still parse the result with the provider's own strict contract — here `webexRefreshedTokenSchema` requires `refresh_token`, a literal `scope` of `"spark:kms meeting:schedules_read meeting:schedules_write"` and `token_type: "Bearer"`. The documented sync-endpoint contract ("The response should only contain the access token and expiry date") cannot satisfy these schemas, so with credential sharing enabled refresh fails ("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned") or yields `NaN` expiry dates. These call sites need to go through `parseRefreshTokenResponse` (once it is fixed) or the feature should be documented as unsupported for them.

Credential sync request carries no authentication and its status is never checked

The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` with no shared secret, signature, or auth header, so the self-hoster's endpoint has no way to verify the caller; anyone who learns the URL can request access tokens for arbitrary Cal.com user ids. The inbound direction (`/api/webhook/app-credential`) does use `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, so the asymmetry is clearly unintended. Additionally, `response.ok` is never checked, so a 4xx/5xx HTML error body is passed on to the per-app parsing code, producing confusing downstream failures instead of a clear error.

Custom webhook header name is case-sensitive

`req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"]` relies on the operator configuring the name in lowercase, because Node lowercases incoming header names. If a self-hoster sets `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME="Calcom-Webhook-Secret"` the lookup yields `undefined` and every request is rejected with "Invalid webhook secret" with no hint why. Apply `.toLowerCase()` to the configured name instead of relying on the .env comment.

No HTTP method restriction and non-constant-time secret comparison

The handler accepts any HTTP method (GET, DELETE, …) and compares the webhook secret with `!==` on the raw header value. A method guard (`POST` only) prevents accidental credential writes from GET/prefetch traffic, and `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers avoids leaking the secret through response-time differences on a write-capable, unauthenticated-by-default endpoint.

The PR adds an unauthenticated-by-default write endpoint that creates/updates OAuth credentials plus a shared `parseRefreshTokenResponse`/`refreshOAuthTokens` layer used by ~10 apps, with no unit or integration tests. Given that the helpers currently mis-handle schemas and return types (see other findings), at minimum there should be tests covering: rejected requests when sharing is disabled / secret mismatch, slug→metadata resolution for apps whose dirName differs from the slug, credential create vs update, and that `parseRefreshTokenResponse` preserves `refresh_token`/expiry in both sharing modes.

Webhook silently overwrites one of several credentials for the same user and app

The upsert uses `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })`. Users can legitimately have more than one credential for the same app (e.g. two Google Calendar accounts); the webhook will overwrite whichever row is returned first and leave the others stale, with no indication to the caller. The payload has no way to target a specific credential, so consider including an external identifier/account email in the schema or documenting the single-credential-per-app assumption.

Wrong app slug ("zoomvideo") sent to the credential sync endpoint

`refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoomvideo", credential.userId)` uses the app's directory name, not its slug. The Zoom app's slug is `zoom` (see `zoomvideo/api/callback.ts`, which creates the credential with `appId: "zoom"`, and the `App.slug` row used by the new `/api/webhook/app-credential` endpoint). A self-hoster's endpoint keyed on the Cal.com app slug will not recognise `zoomvideo`, so Zoom token sync silently fails.

`prisma` is used but never imported in Salesforce CalendarService

`getClient()` now calls `prisma.credential.update({...})`, but the file imports no Prisma client (only `getLocation`, `WEBAPP_URL`, `HttpError`, `logger`, types, `getAppKeysFromSlug`, `parseRefreshTokenResponse`). `prisma` is therefore an undefined identifier: TypeScript type-check/build will fail, and at runtime every instantiation of `SalesforceCalendarService` throws a `ReferenceError`, breaking all Salesforce bookings. Add `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma";`.

appStoreMetadata is indexed by slug, but it is keyed by app dirName

`appStoreMetadata[app.slug as keyof typeof appStoreMetadata]` casts the slug to a key of the generated metadata map, which is keyed by app directory name. For every app whose dirName differs from its slug — `googlecalendar`/`google-calendar`, `office365calendar`/`office365-calendar`, `zoomvideo`/`zoom`, `office365video`/`msteams` — the lookup returns `undefined` and the handler responds 404 "App not found. Ensure that you have the correct app slug". Those are precisely the apps this feature targets, so the webhook is unusable for them. Resolve the metadata via a slug lookup (e.g. `getAppFromSlug`) or by the app's `dirName`.

`getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials })` use the *caller's* credentials/destination calendar, but the handler explicitly allows team admins/owners and plain attendees to add guests. In those cases the calendar/video integration update (`eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)`) runs with credentials that have no access to the organizer's calendar event, so the external calendar invite is silently not updated (or errors out) and the new guests never appear on the real event. The query at line 35-40 already fetches `booking.user.credentials` but never uses them; the organizer's credentials should be used instead.

No guard for cancelled/past bookings or seated event types

The handler accepts any `bookingId` regardless of `booking.status` or start time, so a direct call can append attendees to a CANCELLED/REJECTED booking and send them a CONFIRMED ICS REQUEST for an event that no longer exists. It also ignores `eventType.seatsPerTimeSlot`: attendees are inserted with `createMany` without any corresponding `BookingSeat` record, which bypasses seat accounting for seated event types. Reject non-accepted/past bookings and either reject or correctly handle seated events.

No tests for the new addGuests handler

The PR adds a mutation that writes attendees to a booking, performs permission checks (organizer / team admin-owner / attendee), filters blacklisted and duplicate emails, updates external calendars and sends emails — with no unit or integration test. The permission expression bug (`&&` instead of `||`) and the raw-vs-filtered guest list bug would both have been caught by a basic handler test. Add tests covering: unauthorized caller rejected, team admin allowed, duplicate/blacklisted emails filtered, and the email payload containing only newly added guests.

Subject line dereferences attendees[0] and can render an empty name

`name: this.calEvent.attendees[0].name` throws a TypeError if the attendee list is empty, and newly added guests are created with `name: ""` in the handler, so if the ordering ever puts a new guest first the subject becomes `Guests Added: <eventType> with  at <date>`. Guard the access and fall back to the attendee email or organizer name.

Validation error state is never reset, leaving a stale error on reopen

`isInvalidEmail` is only cleared by the Cancel button. It is not reset in `onSuccess`, nor when the dialog is dismissed via Escape/overlay click (`onOpenChange={setIsOpenDialog}`), nor when the user edits the emails. As a result the red 'Emails must be unique and valid' message stays visible after a successful submit and reappears the next time the dialog is opened. Reset it when the dialog opens/closes and when `multiEmailValue` changes.

findFirstOrThrow on `booking.userId || 0` yields an unhandled 500 for bookings without a user

If `booking.userId` is null (possible for dynamic/managed or orphaned bookings), the lookup becomes `where: { id: 0 }` and `findFirstOrThrow` raises a Prisma `NotFoundError`, surfacing as an opaque INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR to the client instead of a meaningful tRPC error. Handle the null case explicitly (e.g. NOT_FOUND / BAD_REQUEST) rather than coercing to id 0.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Read-modify-write on retryCount instead of atomic increment

`retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` uses the value read at the start of the handler. If two cron invocations overlap (cron overlap, manual POST, retried request), both read the same value and one increment is lost, so a reminder can keep retrying beyond the intended limit. Use Prisma's atomic `{ increment: 1 }` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteMany OR branch has no method filter and deletes non-SMS reminders

The new `OR` branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` in `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany` is not scoped to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`. The SMS cron therefore deletes *any* WorkflowReminder row (EMAIL, WHATSAPP, mandatory reminders, etc.) whose retryCount exceeded 1, including rows with future scheduledDate. Today only this handler increments retryCount, but as soon as the email/WhatsApp schedulers (or any other code) reuse the same column, this cron will silently destroy their pending reminders. Add the method filter inside the OR branch (or combine it as `AND` with method/scheduled conditions).

false_positives.candidate:
No test covering the new retry/delete behaviour

The PR introduces a retry-and-delete policy (increment on failure, delete when retryCount > 1) with no accompanying test. A regression here either leaks reminders forever or deletes reminders that should still be sent, both of which are silent in production. A unit/integration test asserting (a) retryCount increments when scheduleSMS fails or returns falsy, (b) rows with retryCount > 1 are deleted, and (c) non-SMS reminders are untouched, would lock the behaviour in.

Reminders skipped for non-transient reasons (e.g. SMS sending locked) are permanently deleted

`twilio.scheduleSMS` returns a falsy value not only on send failures but also when sending is suppressed for the user/team (SMS lock state checks inside the provider). With this change such a skip increments `retryCount`, and after two cron runs the reminder row is deleted by the new `deleteMany` branch. Consequence: once a lock/review is lifted the reminder no longer exists and the customer never gets the SMS. Distinguish genuine scheduling errors from intentional skips before counting a retry.

prisma.update inside catch block can throw and abort the whole cron run

The `prisma.workflowReminder.update` added at the top of the `catch` block is itself unprotected. If this update fails (record removed concurrently, connection error, etc.) the exception propagates out of the `for` loop, so every remaining unscheduled reminder in the batch is skipped and the endpoint returns a 500 instead of the previous behaviour where a single failing reminder was only logged. Wrap the retry-count update in its own try/catch (or move it after logging and guard it).

retryCount is not incremented when sendTo or message is missing, so those reminders still loop forever

The retry increment only happens inside `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)` (else-branch) or in the catch. When `sendTo` is null (e.g. no smsReminderNumber on the booking / no sendTo on the step) or the template produced an empty message, the loop body does nothing: the reminder stays `scheduled: false`, keeps being picked up by the 7-day query on every cron run and is never cleaned up until scheduledDate passes. This is exactly the "keep scheduling it in our cron job until the date is reached" problem the PR claims to fix, so the fix is incomplete for that class of rows.

retryCount predicate is unindexed, forcing a full scan of WorkflowReminder on every cron tick

`retryCount` has no index (see `WorkflowReminder` indexes in schema.prisma), and because it is an `OR` branch Postgres can no longer satisfy the whole delete from the existing `[method, scheduled, scheduledDate]` index — it must sequentially scan WorkflowReminder. WorkflowReminder is one of the largest tables in this schema and this cron runs frequently, so this adds a repeated full-table scan plus row locks. Either add an index covering retryCount (e.g. `@@index([method, retryCount])`) or fold the retry condition into the existing method/scheduledDate-filtered predicate.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
Caching tests for auth/filter conditions were deleted with no replacement

The `describe("Caching")` block covering `getAuthorizationConditions()`/`getFilterConditions()` memoization was removed. That behaviour still exists in the service (`cachedAuthConditions`/`cachedFilterConditions` with the `=== undefined` sentinel check, which is specifically needed because `getFilterConditions()` legitimately caches `null`). With the tests gone, a regression such as switching the check to `if (!this.cachedFilterConditions)` — which would recompute and re-query on every call — would go unnoticed. Port the caching assertions to the new SQL expectations instead of dropping them.

Constructor option type widened so `scope: "team"` without `teamId` type-checks and silently returns no rows

The constructor now accepts `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` (`scope: "user" | "org" | "team"`, `teamId?: number`) instead of the zod-inferred discriminated union. A caller passing `{ scope: "team", userId, orgId }` with `teamId` undefined (a very likely shape when `teamId` comes from an optional request field) now compiles, but `insightsBookingServiceOptionsSchema.safeParse` fails, `this.options` becomes `null`, and `buildAuthorizationConditions` returns `1=0`. The user sees an empty insights result with no error and no log, instead of a compile-time error as before. Keep the exact union type for the public options, or surface the validation failure (throw / log) rather than degrading to an empty result set.

Only the user-scope SQL is ever executed; team/org `= ANY(...)` fragments are never run against Postgres

After this conversion the correctness of the generated SQL (column quoting, `= ANY($n)` parameter binding for integer arrays, `1=0`) can only be verified by executing it. The single `$queryRaw` test at line 481 exercises the user-scope condition plus an `eventTypeId` filter; the team-scope, org-scope and NOTHING conditions are asserted only by comparing `Prisma.sql` template objects, which would pass even if the SQL is syntactically invalid or the driver cannot infer the array parameter type for `= ANY($1)`. Add `$queryRaw` assertions for at least the org and team scopes (and the NOTHING condition) so a broken raw query is caught by CI rather than in production.

Public `findMany` removed and replaced by `getBaseConditions` without updating consumers

The only query-executing method on `InsightsBookingService` (`findMany(findManyArgs)`) is deleted and replaced with `getBaseConditions(): Promise<Prisma.Sql>`. Nothing else in the repository is updated in this PR, so any existing caller of `service.findMany(...)` will fail to compile (or, if typed loosely, fail at runtime). It also pushes raw-SQL assembly onto every consumer, which is where the parenthesization hazard above becomes dangerous. Either keep an execution helper on the service (e.g. a `findMany`/`query` that wraps `$queryRaw` with the base conditions correctly parenthesized) or update all call sites in the same change.

Returned SQL fragments contain un-parenthesized top-level OR, enabling authorization bypass when callers append conditions

`getBaseConditions()` returns `authConditions` verbatim when there are no filters (line 75), and `getAuthorizationConditions()`/`getFilterConditions()` are public. For org and team scope, `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition`/`buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` produce a fragment whose top-level operator is `OR` (e.g. `("teamId" = ANY($1)) AND ("isTeamBooking" = true) OR (("userId" = ANY($2)) AND ("isTeamBooking" = false))` after the reduce), and `buildFilterConditions` likewise returns a bare `OR` fragment when only `eventTypeId` is set. Since the service no longer executes any query, every consumer must interpolate these fragments into their own raw SQL, and the natural `WHERE ${baseConditions} AND "startTime" > ${x}` becomes `A OR (B AND x)` because SQL `AND` binds tighter than `OR`. That silently widens the authorized row set (bookings of users/teams the caller is not entitled to see). The service should wrap its final result in parentheses (e.g. `Prisma.sql`(${combined})`) before returning it from `getBaseConditions`/`getFilterConditions`/`getAuthorizationConditions`.

`sed -i '' -E "s|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|...|" "$ENV_FILE"` uses the BSD form where `-i` takes a separate (empty) backup suffix. With GNU sed (Linux, CI containers) `-i` does not consume the next argument, so `''` is parsed as the sed script and the substitution expression is treated as a filename, causing the command to fail and the env file to be left unmodified. true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteCache handler throws a plain Error and only authorizes user-owned credentials

The handler throws `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")` instead of a `TRPCError`. tRPC maps unknown errors to `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR`, so an authorization failure is reported to the client as a 500 and logged/alerted as a server bug rather than a 403/404. Additionally, the authorization check is `where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id }`, so credentials owned by a team (`userId` is null, `teamId` set) can never be matched; the UI will still render the "Delete cached data" action for such a credential and the user gets an opaque server error. true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache timestamp is hard-coded to the en-US locale and ignores the user's time format

`new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" })` formats the cache timestamp with a fixed US locale, so non-US users see MM/DD/YY and a 12-hour clock regardless of their configured locale/`timeFormat` (24h) preference. false_positives.candidate:
Cache deletion never invalidates the connectedCalendars query, leaving stale cache status in the UI

`deleteCacheMutation`'s `onSuccess` only shows a toast and calls the optional `onSuccess` prop. Confirm buttons are not disabled while mutations are in flight and errors lose server detail

`onConfirm` fires `deleteCacheMutation.mutate` / `disconnectMutation.mutate` and immediately closes the dialog without any pending/disabled state, so a user can re-open and re-trigger the mutation while the first request is still running. Also both `onError` handlers discard `error.message` and show a generic toast, so real failures (e.g. the "Credential not found or access denied" case from `deleteCache.handler.ts`) are indistinguishable from transient errors, making support/debugging harder. Wire `isPending` to the dialog's confirm button and surface the server message in the error toast.

ENV_FILE is resolved relative to the caller's CWD and can write a .env outside the repo

`ENV_FILE="../.env"` is relative to the current working directory, not to the script location. Running the script the obvious way from the repository root (`./scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh`) resolves to `<parent-of-checkout>/.env`: the script happily creates that file (`touch "$ENV_FILE"`) and writes `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` into it, polluting a directory outside the repo while the developer's real `.env` is never updated — so the webhook test silently does not work. Resolve the path from the script directory (e.g. `ENV_FILE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)/.env"`).

Migration header warning contradicts the SQL it documents

The generated warning block states "Added the required column `updatedAt` to the `CalendarCache` table without a default value. This is not possible if the table is not empty.", but the statement below adds the column `NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()`, which is safe for a non-empty table. Leaving the stale warning in place makes reviewers/operators believe this migration will fail or needs a manual backfill. Remove or correct the comment block.

No tests for the new deleteCache authorization or cache-status aggregation

This PR adds a destructive mutation (`viewer.calendars.deleteCache`) whose only protection is an ownership lookup, plus a new `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` aggregation and the credential→cache mapping in `connectedCalendars.handler.ts`, and none of them have unit tests. At minimum there should be tests asserting that (a) deleting cache for a credential belonging to another user is rejected, (b) a successful call removes only the rows for that credentialId, and (c) `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` returns the latest `updatedAt` per credential and maps correctly to `cacheUpdatedAt` (including the no-cache case).

UserWithCalendars now requires updatedAt and googleChannelId that nothing in this PR consumes

`UserWithCalendars.allSelectedCalendars` / `userLevelSelectedCalendars` were widened from `Pick<SelectedCalendar, "externalId" | "integration" | "eventTypeId">` to also require `updatedAt` and `googleChannelId`. This is a breaking contract change for every caller that builds this object from a narrower Prisma `select` (platform API v2 / `@calcom/platform-libraries` consumers of `getConnectedDestinationCalendars`), which will now fail type-check and need matching select changes. Neither field is used by the cache-status feature added here (the handler reads `cacheUpdatedAt` from `CalendarCache`), and adding them to `findUnlockedUserForSession`'s select also enlarges the session payload for no benefit. Revert the type widening unless there is a consumer.

cleanup() always exits 0, so failures report success

`cleanup()` ends with `exit 0` and is used both as the SIGINT/SIGTERM trap and as the failure path for "Rate limit hit" (line 49) and "Failed to extract Tunnelmole URL" (line 58). The script therefore terminates with status 0 even when it never obtained a tunnel URL and never configured `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL`, so any wrapper script or CI step cannot detect the failure. connectedCalendars always runs an extra cache groupBy and bypasses the CalendarCache feature-flag factory

The handler instantiates `new CalendarCacheRepository()` directly instead of going through `CalendarCache.init`, so the `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` (used when calendar-cache is disabled) is bypassed and an additional `calendarCache.groupBy` query is executed on every call to this frequently-used endpoint, even for users/teams that have the calendar-cache feature off. Either skip the query when the feature is disabled or short-circuit when `credentialIds` is empty, and go through the existing factory so the enabled/disabled behaviour is consistent with the rest of the calendar-cache code.

`"dev:cron": "npx tsx cron-tester.ts"` relies on `npx` fetching `tsx` from the network at run time; the package is not in `dependencies`/`devDependencies`, so the version is unpinned and unaffected by the lockfile, and the command fails in offline/sandboxed environments. Either add `tsx` as a devDependency and call it directly, or revert to `ts-node`.

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds ignores expiresAt and reports expired cache as present

The `groupBy` only filters on `credentialId`, so rows whose `expiresAt` is already in the past are included in the max-`updatedAt` result. `getCachedAvailability` refuses to serve those rows (`expiresAt: { gte: now }`), so the UI will show a "Cache Status / Last updated …" entry and offer "Delete cached data" for a credential whose cache can no longer be used — a misleading status for a diagnostics feature. The new method accepts `Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput` but forwards it to `prisma.selectedCalendar.updateMany`, which requires `Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateManyMutationInput`. `UpdateInput` permits nested relation operations (e.g. `user: { connect: { id } }`, `credential: { disconnect: true }`) that `updateMany` cannot execute, so such a call type-checks but fails at runtime with a Prisma validation error. true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.

Reminder cancellation promises are no longer awaited

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are async and are invoked inside `forEach` without `await` (the previous code collected the Prisma promises and awaited them in `Promise.all`). Nothing in the handler guarantees these DB writes (setting `cancelled: true`, deleting SMS reminder rows, Twilio cancellations) complete before the request returns. In a serverless deployment the execution context can be frozen as soon as the handler resolves, so the reminder may never be flagged as cancelled and the workflow email will still be sent — the exact bug being fixed. The same pattern was introduced in `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` (requestReschedule) and `packages/features/bookings/lib/handleNewBooking.ts`; in the latter the surrounding `try/catch` cannot catch anything either because the promise is not awaited.

This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.

immediateDelete branch cancels at SendGrid but never deletes the reminder row

In the `immediateDelete` branch the function returns right after the SendGrid cancel request, without deleting the `WorkflowReminder` row and without setting `cancelled`. The function name (`delete...`) and the other two branches (delete row / flag row) make this inconsistency a correctness problem, not just cosmetics.

true_positives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

The migration adds `cancelled BOOLEAN` with no default and no index, while the cron now runs `findMany({ where: { cancelled: true, scheduledDate: { lte: ... } } })` every 15 minutes against `WorkflowReminder`, a table that grows with every booking. Making the column `BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false` (and the Prisma field `Boolean @default(false)`) would also avoid the three-state null/false/true semantics that every future query has to account for.

The fix introduces a new state machine (flag `cancelled` on cancel/reschedule → cron cancels at SendGrid within one hour → delete row) spread across the cancel handler, the reschedule handler, the workflow router and this cron endpoint, but no test is added. Given that the previous attempt at this fix (#6991) shipped broken and silently stopped cancelling emails, at least a unit test for `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` (each of the three branches) and for the cron's cancellation loop (including a failing SendGrid request not blocking the remaining reminders) would prevent another silent regression.

The whole cancellation loop is wrapped in a single try/catch and the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` calls are collected as lazy Prisma promises that are only executed by `await Promise.all(...)` after the loop finishes. If any `client.request` call throws (SendGrid rejects a cancellation that is less than ~10 minutes before `sendAt`, or returns 400 because the batch already has a `cancel` status), the loop aborts and *none* of the already-cancelled reminders are deleted from the DB. On the next cron run the same rows are re-processed; the previously-cancelled batches now return an error themselves, so the run aborts again. The result is a poisoned queue in which no reminder is ever cancelled or removed — exactly the failure mode this PR is meant to fix. The failure is also only `console.log`ged and the endpoint still returns HTTP 200, so it is invisible to monitoring. The entry also lacks the trailing comma (`TimeUnit,\n  Prisma\n}`), which prettier will flag. Both will fail the lint/format check.

When a workflow is deleted (line 214) or a step is removed (line 521), reminders are cancelled with `immediateDelete = true` and immediately afterwards the workflow/step is deleted, which cascade-deletes the `WorkflowReminder` rows. If the direct `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` call fails — the failure mode this PR addresses, and failures are only `console.log`ged — the scheduled emails are still delivered and the DB record needed to retry the cancellation is gone. Deleting a workflow with many upcoming reminders can also exceed SendGrid's pending-cancellation limit in one burst, reintroducing the original bug for this path.

remindersToCancel query is not restricted to EMAIL reminders with a referenceId

The query selects every `WorkflowReminder` with `cancelled: true`, without filtering on `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` or on a non-null `referenceId`, and then posts `reminder.referenceId` as a SendGrid `batch_id`. Today only email reminders ever get the flag, but any row that is flagged with a Twilio SID or a null reference (now or after a future change) will produce a SendGrid 400 which, given the shared try/catch, aborts the whole cancellation batch (see the loop issue). Add the method/referenceId filters to make the query match the intent stated in the comment.

Rejected app-module imports become unhandled rejections at module load
