Recurring-booking calendar deletions are fire-and-forget and never awaited

In the recurring/`allRemainingBookings` branch the credentials are iterated with `.forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); … apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent) })`. The callback's promise is discarded, so the `await getCalendar(...)` and the subsequent `calendar.deleteEvent(...)` calls run after `forEach` returns. By the time `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` (line 652) copies `apiDeletes`, the array is still empty, so the handler returns "Booking successfully cancelled" without waiting for any external calendar event to be removed — in a serverless runtime the function can be frozen/torn down first, leaving cancelled recurring bookings still present on users' calendars. Errors from these calls also escape as unhandled rejections. The sibling non-recurring branch in this same diff was correctly converted to `for (const credential of …)`; this branch needs the same treatment (and should push the promise, not the awaited result).

false_positives.candidate:
Commented template entry points at a non-existent path

The commented-out example was changed from `./_example` to `// example: import("./example")`. The app template directory is `_example`, so a developer copying this line as a guide for registering a new app will reference a path that does not exist. Keep the directory name accurate (`import("./_example")`).

Dynamic imports are evaluated eagerly, so nothing is actually loaded lazily

The object literal calls `import("./applecalendar")`, `import("./caldavcalendar")`, … directly as property values. `import()` is invoked at module-evaluation time, so the moment anything imports `@calcom/app-store` all 28 app modules are requested and evaluated — exactly as before, only now asynchronously. The server/serverless bundle still contains every app and cold start still pays for loading all of them, so the PR's stated goal (async/lazy import of app packages) is not achieved while every call site has been forced to become `async`. To get real laziness the values need to be thunks (e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) resolved on demand, ideally with memoization.

getCalendarCredentials creates floating promises and changes the type of `calendar`

`getCalendar(credential)` is now async, but it is still invoked unconditionally inside the `flatMap` before the `app.variant === "calendar"` check. For every non-`calendar` variant credential the returned promise is created and immediately discarded; if it rejects (e.g. the app module fails to load) it becomes an unhandled rejection, which can crash the Node process. In addition, the `calendar` property of the returned items is now `Promise<Calendar | null>` instead of `Calendar | null`; this is a silent contract change for any consumer of `getCalendarCredentials()` other than `getConnectedCalendars` (which was updated), and such a consumer would call methods on a Promise at runtime. Move the `getCalendar` call behind the variant check and audit/convert all consumers.

requestReschedule: calendar/video cancellation is now an un-awaited async forEach

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) … })` discards every callback promise. The mutation continues to send the reschedule-request email and webhooks and returns while the `getCalendar` import and the `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` calls are still pending, so in a serverless environment the previous calendar entries and video meetings may never be deleted. Any error thrown inside the callback is now an unhandled rejection (it can terminate the process) rather than something the caller can observe. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (ref) => …))` instead.

try/catch around the cancellation loop is dead code after converting the callback to async

Same defect as in `vital/lib/reschedule.ts`: `forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); … })` discards the callback promises, so the surrounding `try/catch` that logs errors can never fire, failures from `getCalendar`/`deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` become unhandled rejections, and the function proceeds to send the reschedule email and return `true` before the external calendar/video entries have actually been deleted. Await the work explicitly (e.g. `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (ref) => …))`) inside the try block.

try/catch around the cancellation loop is dead code after converting the callback to async

The callback passed to `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach` was made `async` so it can `await getCalendar(...)`, but the callback's promise is thrown away. The enclosing `try { … } catch (error) { logger.error(...) }` can therefore never observe a failure from `getCalendar`, `calendar.deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting`: those rejections surface as unhandled promise rejections (process-level crash risk in modern Node) and are silently lost from the logs. The function also returns `true` and sends the reschedule email before the deletions have completed, so the stale calendar/video entries may never be removed. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (ref) => …))` inside the try block.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`end` is computed from the slot start, so the working-hours end boundary is never enforced

`const start = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute(); const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` — both variables are identical; `end` was clearly meant to be the slot end (`start + eventLength`, or derived from `slotEndTime`). As written, the `end > workingHour.endTime` test only ever compares the slot *start* against the end boundary, so a slot that starts inside working hours but ends after them (e.g. a 60-minute slot starting 30 minutes before the day's end time) is accepted, allowing bookings that run past the host's availability.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs objects compared with `===`, so the zero-length (whole-day unavailable) override branch is dead code

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two freshly created Dayjs objects by reference, which is always false. The intent (treat an override whose start equals its end as "unavailable all day") is never executed, so the handling of whole-day "mark unavailable" overrides depends on the later, unrelated comparisons. Use `.isSame(...)` (or compare `valueOf()`).

false_positives.candidate:
Date override on a day makes every slot available, skipping busy-time checks

In `checkIfIsAvailable`, the new block sets `dateOverrideExist = true` for any date override whose date matches the slot's date, and then `if (dateOverrideExist) return true;` returns early. This return happens *before* the `busy.every(...)` loop, so on any day that has a date override the function reports every slot as available and completely ignores existing bookings, external calendar busy times, event buffers and reserved (`selectedSlots`) entries. Any host with a date override can therefore be double-booked. The override check should only narrow availability, not short-circuit the busy evaluation.

Date-override check rejects slots when a date has multiple override ranges

`dateOverrides.find((date) => ...)` returns truthy for the first override that does *not* contain the slot, and that result is treated as "slot is not within the date override" -> unavailable. Cal.com allows several time ranges for the same override date (and several hosts' overrides are flattened into the same array when a team event is evaluated per host). With two ranges on one date (e.g. 09:00-11:00 and 14:00-16:00), a slot inside the first range is outside the second, so the slot is rejected and every slot on that date disappears. The condition should be "none of the overrides for this date contain the slot".

Missing `override.timeZone` silently falls back to the process/default timezone

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` is called with `timeZone` typed as optional (`timeZone?: string` in packages/types/schedule.d.ts). When a caller of `getSlots` passes date overrides without a `timeZone` (the type permits it, and only the slots tRPC router was updated to populate it), the dayjs timezone plugin falls back to the default/local timezone, so `organizerUtcOffset` is computed for the wrong zone and the override is shifted by an arbitrary amount instead of being treated as organizer-local. Either make `timeZone` required for date overrides or explicitly fall back to `organizerTimeZone` which is already passed into `getSlots`.

No test for the PR's main fix: date overrides of fixed hosts in round-robin events

The PR's primary claim is that date overrides of fixed hosts are now honoured for ROUND_ROBIN events (so slots where the fixed host is unavailable are no longer offered). The only new test added covers a single-user event with a different invitee timezone. There is no scenario with a ROUND_ROBIN event type, a fixed host carrying a date override and a non-fixed host available all day, which is exactly the behaviour added in `checkIfIsAvailable` and the riskiest part of the change (it currently also bypasses busy-time checks). Without such a test the regression this PR fixes can silently come back.

Override date comparison mixes server-local and UTC dates

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD")` formats in the *server's* local timezone (plain `dayjs(...)`, no `.utc()`), while it is compared against `slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")`, which is in UTC (`slotStartTime = time.utc()`). On any deployment whose process timezone is not UTC the two dates can differ by a day, so date overrides are matched to the wrong day: overrides are either ignored (making unavailable time bookable) or applied to the neighbouring day. Use `dayjs.utc(date.start)` for the comparison. Tests run with TZ=UTC will not catch this.

Override timezone shift loses the day when it crosses midnight

The new override conversion reduces the shifted instant to minutes-since-midnight via `hour() * 60 + minute()`. When `offset` (invitee offset minus organizer offset) pushes the override across a day boundary — e.g. an override 22:00-23:00 in the organizer's timezone viewed by an invitee 5 hours ahead — the computed `startTime`/`endTime` wrap around to small values and are applied to the invitee's *same* day, so the override's slots are generated on the wrong day. If only one of the two endpoints wraps, `endTime < startTime` and `buildSlots` silently discards the range (`if (start >= end) continue`), so the override yields no slots at all. The day offset produced by the shift has to be carried, not discarded.

Slots that only partially overlap a date override are treated as inside it

The override containment test marks a slot as outside the override only when `slotEndTime <= override.start` or `slotStartTime > override.end`. A slot that starts before the override start but ends inside it (slot 13:30-14:30 vs override 14:00-18:00) or starts inside but ends after the end (slot 17:30-18:30 vs 14:00-18:00) satisfies neither condition, so it is considered available. Combined with the early `return true` for `dateOverrideExist`, such partially overlapping slots are offered for booking outside the host's overridden availability. The correct test is `slotStartTime < override.start || slotEndTime > override.end`.

toHaveTimeSlots matcher does not compare lengths, so the new assertion can pass with missing slots

The matcher iterates `schedule.slots[dateString].map(...).every((actualSlotTime, index) => ...)` over the *actual* slots only and never checks that the number of returned slots equals `expectedSlots.length`. The new assertion for the Asia/Dhaka invitee would therefore still pass if the implementation returned only `08:30:00.000Z` (or any prefix of the expected list), which is precisely the kind of over-filtering the new date-override/working-hours code can cause. Add a length check to the matcher so the new timezone test actually guards against dropped slots.

working-hours check rejects slots when a user has more than one availability block per day

`workingHours.find((workingHour) => ...)` returns truthy as soon as *one* working-hours entry does not contain the slot, and the result is interpreted as "slot is outside of working hours" -> unavailable. A user whose schedule has several blocks on the same weekday (e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 14:00-18:00) produces two `WorkingHours` entries with the same `days`, so a 10:00 slot is inside the first and outside the second and gets dropped — all slots vanish for split schedules. The same happens for schedules that cross UTC midnight, where `getWorkingHours` emits two normalized entries covering the same days. The predicate must be "no entry contains the slot" (`!workingHours.some(contains)`), not "some entry does not contain it". Note this path applies to personal events too, because single-user events are treated as fixed hosts.

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth `state` uses `pipeline.signature`, which is not a per-session nonce

`OAuthLoginView.dispatch` sends `state = pipeline.signature` to GitHub and then validates the callback with `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature` (line 412). `Pipeline.signature` is derived from the pipeline view definitions, not from the user's session, so it is the same constant for every user and every installation attempt of the provider — the new tests hardcode `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` and reuse it across different users and organizations, which demonstrates this. As a result the `state` check provides no CSRF/replay protection (any party can supply the correct value), contrary to what the PR description claims. The established pattern in `sentry/identity/oauth2.py` (`OAuth2LoginView`) is to generate `secrets.token_hex()`, `pipeline.bind_state("state", ...)` it, and compare the callback value against the bound state; this view should do the same.

true_positives.matched_candidate:

false_positives.candidate:
GitHub user validation is skipped when no local Integration row exists

In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, if `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist` the pipeline continues immediately (`return pipeline.next_step()`) without comparing the OAuth-authenticated GitHub user to the owner/sender of the installation. `installation_id` is attacker-controllable (it is read straight from the query string at line 448, or from state bound from the query string in `OAuthLoginView`) and GitHub installation ids are small sequential integers. The ownership check should be made against the installation data fetched from GitHub (e.g. `installation["account"]`), not only in the branch where a local Integration happens to exist.

`assert_setup_flow` asserts the exact redirect query string including `state=9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`, and five other tests hardcode the same md5 value as the `state` parameter. This value is an implementation detail of `Pipeline.signature` (a hash over the pipeline views): adding, removing or renaming a pipeline view will silently change it and break all of these tests with an opaque "Invalid installation request." failure rather than a clear assertion error. Reading the `state` out of the redirect `Location` (or binding a real nonce, as suggested elsewhere) would make the tests robust and self-explanatory.

The PR description lists three new failure modes (GitHub user mismatch, `state` mismatch, and GitHub not returning an `access_token`), but only the user mismatch is covered by `test_github_user_mismatch`. There is no test asserting that a tampered/missing `state` or an access-token response without `access_token` (e.g. `error=bad_verification_code`, which GitHub returns with HTTP 200) renders the failure page, so regressions in those branches would go unnoticed. There is also no test for an existing `Integration` whose metadata lacks a `sender` key, which currently crashes (see the `metadata["sender"]` finding).

`safe_urlopen(...)` on line 423 is outside the try/except, and `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` on line 434 is not wrapped at all. `sentry.identity.github.get_user_info` performs an HTTP request and calls `raise_for_status()`, so a revoked/invalid token, a GitHub outage, or any network error raises out of the pipeline view and yields a 500 error page rather than the user-facing `github-integration-failed.html` page this PR is designed to show. The assertion was changed from `b"The GitHub installation could not be found."` to the generic `b"Invalid installation request."`, which is the default `error_short` emitted by nearly every failure path in the new code (state mismatch, failed token exchange, missing `login`, user mismatch). Public helpers removed from mark_failed without re-export; external importers will break

`mark_failed.py` no longer defines `mark_failed_threshold`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, `get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context` or `SimpleCheckIn`, and they are not re-exported from the module. Any other module, task, or test that does `from sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed import <one of these>` (or patches e.g. `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed.create_issue_platform_occurrence` in a test) will now fail with ImportError/AttributeError. The PR touches only these four files, so no callers/tests were updated — the whole tree should be grepped for the old names (including mock patch targets, which are string-based and won't be caught by static checks) before merging.

get_failure_reason docstring shows an output string the function can never produce

The docstring lists `"A failed check-in was detected"` as example output, but `SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP` only contains "An error check-in was detected", "A missed check-in was detected" and "A timeout check-in was detected"; there is no generic "failed" variant. The second example ("... were detected") also doesn't match the template `"%(problem_checkins)s check-ins detected"`. Also note the typos "humam readible". Misleading docs here make it harder to reason about the user-visible failure reason text.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent metric tag key: "shards" vs "shard"

`spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged with `{"shards": shard_tag}` while `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use `{"shard": shard_tag}` for the same value. Dashboards/alerts grouping by `shard` will silently miss the `wait_produce` timer. Pick one key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

Line 15 does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, so the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` on line 62 ("Give flusher threads time to process after drift change") does nothing at all. The comment is misleading and the test still relies entirely on `step.join()` busy-looping for the flusher thread to produce the message, so it remains timing-dependent. Either drop the sleep/comment or use an unpatched sleep (e.g. capture the original `time.sleep` before monkeypatching) / poll until `messages` is non-empty.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unhealthy flusher process is never killed before being restarted

`_ensure_processes_alive` now guards the kill with `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. The processes are created via `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, i.e. `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`, which derives from `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` and is *not* a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process` (`multiprocessing.context.Process`). The isinstance check is therefore always False, so `process.kill()` is never executed — the previous code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. Consequence: when a flusher is detected as hung (`cause == "hang"`, process still alive but `healthy_since` stale), the old process keeps running while `_create_process_for_shards` spawns a second process for the same shards. Two processes then flush the same Redis shards concurrently, which can produce duplicate/partial segments to the buffered-segments topic, and up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS+1 processes can accumulate per shard group. Use `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` (or check for `threading.Thread` instead) in the guard.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

Line 15 does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, so the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` on line 62 ("Give flusher threads time to process after drift change") does nothing at all. The comment is misleading and the test still relies entirely on `step.join()` busy-looping for the flusher thread to produce the message, so it remains timing-dependent. Either drop the sleep/comment or use an unpatched sleep (e.g. capture the original `time.sleep` before monkeypatching) / poll until `messages` is non-empty.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() skips termination of remaining processes once the deadline expires

In `join`, the loop over `self.processes.items()` does `if remaining_time <= 0: break` before waiting on each process. If the first process consumes the whole timeout budget, every remaining process is skipped entirely — it is neither waited for nor terminated. Combined with the `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` check at the end of the loop (always False for spawn-context `SpawnProcess`, see the kill() issue), `terminate()` is effectively never called on any flusher process, so hung flusher processes can outlive the shutdown/rebalance path. `remaining_time` is also computed and then unused except for the comparison. Consider terminating all processes after the wait loop regardless of which ones timed out, and fixing the isinstance check.

false_positives.candidate:
--flusher-processes 0 silently means "one process per shard"

`self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats 0 as falsy, so passing `--flusher-processes 0` (or any code path passing 0) results in one process per assigned shard rather than an error or a single process. The click option has no range validation. Use an explicit `if max_processes is None` and/or validate `>= 1` in the click option.

Class docstring claims one process per shard, which is not what the code does

The docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing." In practice the number of processes is `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` and shards are round-robined onto processes, and the CLI default for `--flusher-processes` is 1, so the default behaviour is a single process handling all shards. The new `max_processes` parameter is also undocumented while the docstring still documents a non-existent `topic` parameter. This misleads operators about the default behaviour.

Dead method _create_process_for_shard

`_create_process_for_shard(shard)` is not called anywhere after the refactor (`_ensure_processes_alive` calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly). It duplicates restart logic and will silently drift out of sync; remove it or wire it up.

New multiprocess flusher test only asserts bookkeeping, not behaviour

`test_flusher_processes_limit` submits no messages and only asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `max_processes`, `num_processes` and that the shard map totals 4. It does not assert that shards are partitioned without overlap (e.g. `{0,1,2,3}` exactly once across `process_to_shards_map`), nor that segments from all 4 shards are actually flushed/produced when more than one process is used. The core risk of this PR — multiple flushers each owning a disjoint shard subset and producing all segments exactly once — is untested. There is also no test for the unhealthy-process restart path that this PR rewrote.

Per-segment metric now tagged with a high-cardinality shard-list tag

`spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` is emitted for every flushed segment and is now tagged with `shard=shard_tag`, where `shard_tag` is the comma-joined list of all shards handled by that process (e.g. `"0,3,6,9"` or, with the default `--flusher-processes 1`, the full assigned-partition list). That tag value changes on every Kafka rebalance and differs per consumer instance, so this high-volume metric gains an effectively unbounded set of tag values. The same tag is added to the `spans.buffer.flusher.produce`/`wait_produce` timers and to `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy`. This risks cardinality blowup/cost in the metrics backend; consider emitting a per-shard tag only where the value is a single bounded shard id, or dropping the tag from the per-segment metric.

Redis memory info is now queried once per flusher buffer on every submit

`submit` previously called `self.buffer.get_memory_info()` once; it now iterates `self.buffers.values()` and calls `get_memory_info()` on each of the N per-process buffers (plus `record_stored_segments()` on each). Since each `SpansBuffer` holds its own client, these calls duplicate the Redis INFO round trips N times per submitted message batch when `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage < 1.0`, scaling with `--flusher-processes`. If a given Redis node is reported by more than one buffer, both `used` and `available` are also counted multiple times. Consider keeping a single buffer in the parent for memory/stat reporting.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
A gauge is emitted for every processed item on the hot path

`OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `metrics.gauge("remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth", ...)` in the `finally` block of every single work item, with only an `identifier` tag so all 20 workers overwrite the same series. This adds per-message statsd overhead for a value that is already exported once per `poll()` by `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll` (`total_queued`), and the per-worker value is meaningless after aggregation. Emit it periodically rather than per item.

Commit assertions race with the 1-second commit loop and will flake

`test_offset_committing` and `test_handles_invalid_messages` wait for the first `commit_event` and then assert an exact final offset (104, resp. 101). The commit thread runs independently every second and commits whatever contiguous prefix is complete at that moment, so a tick that happens after only some offsets have been processed sets `commit_event` with a lower offset (e.g. 100 or 102); the subsequent `commit_event.wait()` returns immediately because the event is never cleared again and the equality assertion fails. The tests should poll until the expected offset is observed (or clear/re-wait) instead of asserting on the first commit.

Failed work items have their offsets committed, contradicting the documented at-least-once guarantee

In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, any exception raised by `result_processor` is logged and the `finally` block still calls `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)`, so the offset becomes committable. The same happens in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` (lines 317-325) when `grouping_fn` or the queue put fails. This makes processing at-most-once: a transient failure (DB blip, timeout) permanently drops the message, while the class docstring claims "No item is lost" and "Only commits offsets after successful processing". Either failures must block the commit / be routed to a DLQ, or the documented guarantee must be corrected.

FilteredPayload messages are handled through the exception path, producing an error log per message

`decode_payload` in the result consumer starts with `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)`, which is outside its own try/except, so for every filtered message the `AssertionError` propagates into `submit()`'s broad `except Exception` and is reported via `logger.exception("Error submitting message to queue")`. Filtered payloads are a normal part of arroyo pipelines (e.g. when the stale-message DLQ wrapper is enabled), so this turns routine filtering into a flood of error-level exceptions with stack traces and relies on exceptions for ordinary control flow. `submit()` should check for `FilteredPayload` explicitly and complete the offset without logging.

OffsetTracker state is never reset between partition assignments

The `FixedQueuePool` (and therefore its single `OffsetTracker`) is created once per factory and shared across all `create_with_partitions()` calls. `OffsetTracker.last_committed` and `all_offsets` therefore survive partition revocation. If a partition is revoked and later reassigned at a lower offset (offset reset, another consumer having made less progress, topic re-creation), `get_committable_offsets()` computes `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` and only reports an offset when `highest_committable > last_committed`, so no offset for that partition will ever be committed again and the consumer group silently stops advancing. In-flight work items belonging to the previous assignment also remain tracked and can be committed by the new strategy for partitions the consumer no longer owns.

Offsets are committed from a background thread, outside arroyo's single-threaded strategy contract

`_commit_loop` runs in its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is arroyo's `commit` callable wired to `StreamProcessor`/`KafkaConsumer`. Arroyo strategies are only ever called from the main consumer thread, and `KafkaConsumer.stage_offsets`/`commit_offsets` mutate consumer state (staged offsets, assignment/state checks) without locking. Committing from this thread races with `poll()`/rebalance callbacks on the main thread and can stage offsets for partitions that were just revoked, which arroyo rejects with `ConsumerError`, or corrupt the staged-offset bookkeeping. The exception is merely logged by the loop's `except Exception`, so the failure is invisible while offsets stop advancing.

Queue pool is destroyed on strategy close, so the consumer silently drops every message after a rebalance

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` (and `terminate()`/`join()`) calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `worker.shutdown = True` and calls `queue.shutdown()` on every queue. The `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` (result_consumer.py:133) and reused for every `create_with_partitions()` call. Arroyo invokes `close()`/`join()` on the strategy whenever partitions are revoked and then builds a new strategy on the next assignment. After the first rebalance the factory hands the new strategy the already-shut-down pool: the worker threads are dead and `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`, which is swallowed by the broad `except Exception` in `submit()` (line 317) where the offset is then marked complete and committed. The result is that every subsequent message is committed without ever being processed – permanent, silent data loss after any rebalance or partition reassignment. The pool (and its workers) needs to be created per assignment, or `close()` must not destroy state owned by the factory.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and memory can grow without limit

`queue.Queue()` is created with the default `maxsize=0` (unbounded) and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`, so arroyo will keep feeding messages as fast as it can poll regardless of how far behind the workers are. The docstring of `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", which cannot happen. Each queued `WorkItem` additionally retains the full `Message[KafkaPayload]` (field `message`, never read anywhere), so a slow group pins both the decoded result and the raw Kafka payload in memory, and a backlogged consumer will OOM instead of applying backpressure.

Shutdown sets the worker stop flag before queue.shutdown(immediate=False), so queued items are discarded instead of drained

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` first sets `worker.shutdown = True` for every worker and only then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Because the worker loop is `while not self.shutdown:`, each worker exits right after finishing the item it currently holds, so the "non-immediate" shutdown that is supposed to let queued items drain has no effect and all pending items are dropped. Combined with `close()` joining the commit thread before the pool shuts down, the final set of completed offsets may also never be committed, so a normal restart re-reads and re-processes more messages than necessary.

Worker threads can block forever on queue.get(); shutdown failures are swallowed and leak threads

`OrderedQueueWorker.run` uses a blocking `self.work_queue.get()` with no timeout, so the `self.shutdown` flag is only observed after an item arrives. Termination relies entirely on `queue.Queue.shutdown()` succeeding, but `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` wraps that call in `except Exception: logger.exception(...)` (line 239). If it raises for any reason (e.g. the method is unavailable on the running Python version), every idle worker stays blocked in `get()`, `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` is executed sequentially for each worker, and shutdown stalls for 5s × num_queues (100s with the default of 20) before leaking the threads. Using `get(timeout=...)` would make the stop flag effective.

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts behaviour the implementation does not provide

The test makes the result processor raise and then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that a processing error prevents the offset from being committed. The implementation does the opposite: `OrderedQueueWorker.run` completes the offset in its `finally` block even when processing raises, so offsets 100 and 101 become committable. The assertion only holds because the polling loop breaks within ~0.3s while the commit thread ticks once per second; if the commit tick lands first the test fails. This test is both flaky and encodes a guarantee that does not exist – it should assert the real behaviour (or the behaviour should be fixed).

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every denied Check now performs a full permission re-query against the database

The permission-cache read was removed from `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions`, and `Check` now only short-circuits on a cached *allow*. Any cached-but-denied result falls through to `getIdentityPermissions`, which executes `GetUserPermissions` (plus basic-role/team lookups on their own cache misses) against the DB. The new denial cache only suppresses repeats of the exact same (user, action, name, folder) tuple, so a workload that checks many distinct resource names the subject cannot access (per-object checks from the resource server, UI pre-flight checks) issues one permission query per check. `singleflight` only dedupes concurrent calls, not sequential ones, so this is a significant increase in DB load compared with the previous behaviour where the 30s permission cache absorbed denies as well.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
"Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" test is vacuous and its comment is wrong

The comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but the permission cache is seeded with `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`. A `false` value means the scope lookup in `checkPermission` fails, so the request would be denied even if the denial cache were never consulted (the fallback DB query uses the default `fakeStore` with no permissions and also denies). The assertion therefore passes regardless of whether the new `permDenialCache` short-circuit works; the value must be `true` for the test to actually prove the denial cache takes precedence. There is also no test covering the write side of the new behaviour (that a DB-confirmed deny stores an entry under `userPermDenialCacheKey`), so the whole denial-cache feature is effectively untested.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache can persist a deny caused by a stale folder tree, doubling the staleness window

After a DB re-query the result is cached as a denial for `shortCacheTTL` (30s). The re-query only refreshes the *permission* map; `checkInheritedPermissions`/`buildFolderTree` still use `folderCache` (also 30s), which is not refreshed. Concrete failure: a user with a grant on folder A creates subfolder B and a dashboard D inside B. `Check(dashboards:read, name=D, folder=B)` fails the direct `folders:uid:B` lookup and then walks `tree.Ancestors("B")`, which is empty because B is not in the cached folder tree, so the request is denied — and that denial is now written to `permDenialCache` with its own independent 30s TTL. If the deny happens just before the folder tree entry expires, the user keeps being denied for up to ~60s even though the refreshed tree would allow it. This is exactly the "creator cannot access the resource they just created" case the PR intends to fix. Consider also invalidating/refetching the folder tree before caching a denial, or not caching denials that depend on folder inheritance.

Denial cache has unbounded key cardinality in a shared in-memory cache

Denial entries are keyed per (namespace, subject, action, resource name, parent folder), so their cardinality grows with the number of distinct resources any subject is denied on. They are stored in the same unbounded `cache.NewLocalCache` instance as the identity/permission/folder caches (configured in-proc with `CleanupInterval: 10 * time.Minute`), so although entries expire after 30s they are only reclaimed every 10 minutes. A burst of denied checks across many resource names can therefore retain a large amount of memory in the Grafana process; consider a bounded cache or a shorter cleanup interval for this cache.

Disabling the in-proc client cache moves per-request cost onto the server path

In-proc mode now passes `&NoopCache{}` to `authzlib.NewClient`, so no Check/List response is cached on the client side any more. Every authorization decision now goes through the in-proc channel into `Service.Check`, which reads the permission map out of the byte cache via `cacheWrap` and JSON-unmarshals it on every call. For users/service accounts with large permission sets (thousands of scopes) this adds a JSON decode of the whole scope map to every API request, where previously identical checks were served from the 30s client cache. Worth measuring before merge, or caching the decoded map in memory instead of re-decoding bytes per request.

Permission-denial cache key omits identity type (and group/resource) that the decision depends on

`userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent)` is built in `Check` from the raw `checkReq.UserUID` returned by `types.ParseTypeID`, without the identity type. Different identity types share the same identifier space: `anonymous:0` and `render:0` both yield userUID "0", so a denial cached for the render service is returned for the anonymous user (and vice versa) for the same namespace/action/name/folder. The key also omits group and resource, while the decision does depend on them (`checkPermission` uses `mapper.translation(req.Group, req.Resource)` to derive the scope prefix and the `folderSupport` flag); any two group/resource pairs that map to the same action string would therefore share denial entries and produce false denials. Finally, because the raw subject identifier is used (numeric user ID for `user:1`, UID for `user:abc`), the same user gets separate denial entries depending on how the caller addressed them. Include the identity type, group and resource (or the resolved internal UID) in the key.

permissionCacheUsage metric is misreported in Check

`s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", ...)` at line 137 is reached whenever the cached permissions did not yield an allow — including the case where the permission cache *did* hit but the decision was deny. Conversely, a hit in the new `permDenialCache` (line 118) is reported as a `permissionCacheUsage` hit even though it is a different cache. The resulting hit-rate metric no longer measures permission-cache effectiveness and will look much worse than it is, making it useless for tuning TTLs; use a distinct label/metric for the denial cache and only count a permission-cache miss when the cache actually missed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing `key` prop on GrafanaRuleListItem inside rules.map()

In `FilterViewResults`, the `grafana` branch of `rules.map(...)` now renders `<GrafanaRuleListItem ... />` without a `key`, while the `datasource` and `default` branches still pass `key={key}`. The pre-computed `key` (from `getRuleKey`) is destructured but unused for Grafana rules. This produces a React "Each child in a list should have a unique key" warning and makes reconciliation index-based; because this list grows by appending pages during infinite scroll, items can be re-created/re-ordered incorrectly and transient component state (e.g. an open action menu or drawer) can be attached to the wrong row.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
"Silence notifications" menu item is a no-op when only a Prometheus rule is available

The silence drawer is rendered only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true, where `rule` is the ruler rule. In the new list view only `promRule` is passed, so `rule` is undefined and `SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer` is never mounted. Meanwhile `AlertRuleMenu` now derives the Silence ability from the Prometheus rule (`useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`), so the "Silence notifications" item is shown (the new GrafanaGroupLoader test even asserts it exists). Clicking it sets `showSilenceDrawer` to true and nothing happens — a visible, clickable action with no effect and no feedback.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete and Pause menu items can never render in the ruler-less list view

`AlertRuleMenu` now computes Grafana abilities from `promRule` (so Pause/Delete can be "allowed" without a ruler rule), but the rendering conditions were not updated: the Delete item is gated on `canDelete && rulerRule` (line 165) and the Pause item on `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` (line 123). In the new rule list (`GrafanaRuleListItem` -> `RuleActionsButtons.V2` with only `promRule`), `rulerRule` is always undefined, so users can no longer pause or delete a rule from the list view even when they have permission. Note the delete handler itself only needs the identifier (`showDeleteModal(identifier, groupIdentifier)`), so the gate is unnecessary. The new assertion `expect(menuItems.length).toBe(4)` in GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx bakes this regression into the tests, and the `ui.menuItems.delete` selector added there is never used.

Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable in the existing rule views

`useAllAlertRuleAbilities` previously computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` from the `CombinedRule`, which disabled Update/Delete/Pause for Mimir federated rule groups. It now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, where `isFederated` is hardcoded to `false` (the `isFederatedRuleGroup` import was dropped). As a result, every consumer of `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` (RulesTable, rule details, etc.) will now offer Edit/Delete on federated rules, which the backend rejects. The group information is no longer plumbed into the hook, so this needs an explicit fix (or at least the group's `source_tenants` passed through) rather than a TODO.

Grafana-managed recording rules lose Pause/Export/Restore abilities in the Prometheus ability path

`useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` uses `isAlertingRule = prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` as the gate for `ModifyExport`, `Pause`, `Restore` and `DeletePermanently` (lines 324-330). The ruler-based equivalent used `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)`, which includes Grafana recording rules. Since Grafana-managed recording rules can be paused and exported, routing the list view through this hook silently removes the Pause, Export, Restore and Delete-permanently actions for every Grafana recording rule. Only `Silence` legitimately requires an alerting rule.

Provisioned-rule protection in the new list view is untested and depends on a newly declared optional field

`provenance?: string` is added to `GrafanaPromRuleDTOBase` and `isProvisionedPromRule` / `GrafanaRuleListItem` (`isProvisioned: Boolean(provenance)`) now rely exclusively on it to mark Grafana rules as provisioned in the ruler-less list view. No mock, fixture or test sets `provenance` on a Prometheus rule (e.g. `rulerRuleToPromRule` in GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx omits it), and no test asserts that a provisioned rule hides Edit/Delete through this path. If the Grafana Prometheus rules endpoint does not return `provenance`, provisioned rules will silently become editable/deletable in the list, so this behaviour needs a test that pins it down.

Rule view link lost the returnTo parameter

The deleted `GrafanaRuleLoader` built the rule href as `createRelativeUrl('/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view', { returnTo })` using `createReturnTo()`. The replacement omits `returnTo`, so navigating from the rule list into a rule detail page no longer provides the "return to previous" target and the user loses the back-navigation affordance to their filtered list.

Stale comment and variable name after removing ruler prefetching

The ruler prefetch (`alertRuleApi.util.prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup', ...)`) was removed, but the surrounding comment still says "This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules ... but doesn't need to wait for each group to be loaded" and the variable is still named `cacheAndRulerPreload`. Both now describe behaviour that no longer exists and will mislead future readers into thinking ruler data is still warmed up here.

logWarning is emitted during render for every affected row

`getEditableIdentifier` is called directly in the component body and calls `logWarning('Unable to construct an editable rule identifier')` whenever neither a ruler rule nor a Grafana Prometheus rule is supplied. Because this runs on every render — and the rule list polls Prometheus every 20s, re-rendering all rows — a single unsupported row will emit the same warning repeatedly, spamming the analytics backend. Move the reporting into an effect (or dedupe it) so it fires once per occurrence.

skipToken path grants Duplicate ability for non-Grafana rules

`useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(skipToken, ...)` calls `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined)`, which does not short-circuit: with `rule === undefined`, `loading` is false so `MaybeSupported = AlwaysSupported`, `isPluginProvided` is false so `duplicateSupported = true`, and `Duplicate` becomes `[true, ctx.hasPermission(AlertingRuleCreate)]`. `AlertRuleMenu` ORs this with the ruler ability (`canDuplicate = ruler || grafana`), so for data-source (Mimir/Loki/Prometheus) rules — which always pass `skipToken` — the "Duplicate" item is shown to any user holding the Grafana `alert.rules:create` permission, even when the data source has no ruler or the user lacks external-write permission. The hook should return an all-false ability map when no rule is supplied.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Assertion locks in redundant interpolation count

`expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` asserts that a single target is interpolated five times (once in `runShardSplitQuery` plus once per shard sub-request inside `runSplitQuery`). This encodes the redundant re-interpolation as expected behaviour, so a future fix that interpolates only once will fail this test, and the test is coupled to the number of shard groups rather than to the thing being verified (that queries are interpolated before being run). Prefer asserting that the targets reaching `runQuery` are interpolated, or `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)` once the duplicate interpolation is removed. Note also that the mock mutates `query.expr` in place and is only correct because the substitution happens to be idempotent.

New test does not cover the actual regression (step used for partitioning)

The bug being fixed is that an un-interpolated `step` (e.g. `step: '$step'`) does not match the interval regex in `calculateStep`, so the metric time-range partitioning falls back to `intervalMs` and produces wrong split boundaries. The new test only asserts that `targets[0].expr`/`targets[0].step` on the first `runQuery` call are interpolated; it never asserts that the partitions/ranges (or the number of sub-requests) now reflect the interpolated step. The existing 'Correctly splits queries with step' test shows how range boundaries differ by step, so the fix could regress (e.g. interpolation moved back after partitioning) while this test still passes.

Queries are now interpolated twice (ad hoc filters applied twice)

`runSplitQuery` now calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)` on every target, but the sub-requests it builds (`{ ...request, targets }`) still carry the original `scopedVars`/`filters` and are executed through `datasource.runQuery()` -> `DataSourceWithBackend.query()`, which calls `applyTemplateVariables(q, request.scopedVars, request.filters)` again for each target. The result is that interpolation runs twice on the same query: (a) `addAdHocFilters` is applied a second time to an expression that already contains those matchers, so ad hoc/adhoc-variable label matchers end up duplicated in the LogQL sent to Loki (e.g. `{app="x", env="prod", env="prod"}`), and (b) `templateSrv.replace` is re-run over a string that already contains substituted variable values, so any value that itself contains `$name`/`${name}` is expanded a second time, silently changing the query. Either strip `scopedVars`/`filters` from the sub-request, or flag the request as already interpolated so the downstream call is skipped.

Shard splitting path interpolates each query three times

`runShardSplitQuery` interpolates the targets with `applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)`, then hands the resulting sub-request (which still contains `scopedVars` and `filters`) to `runSplitQuery`, which interpolates again (querySplitting.ts:299), and finally `datasource.runQuery` -> `DataSourceWithBackend.query` interpolates a third time. The new assertion `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` in shardQuerySplitting.test.ts confirms the repeated calls (1 up-front + 1 per sub-request). Beyond wasted work (each call re-parses the LogQL expression in `addAdHocFilters`), repeated application of ad hoc filters duplicates label matchers and repeated `templateSrv.replace` can re-expand `$`-containing variable values in the already-interpolated expression, including the injected `__stream_shard__` selector context. Interpolation should happen exactly once per query.

Test's replace mock ignores scopedVars, so `$__auto` substitution is unrealistic

The test's `replace: (input = '') => input.replace('$__auto', '5m')...` ignores the `scopedVars` argument. The real Loki `applyTemplateVariables` deliberately passes macros such as `$__auto`, `$__interval` and `$__range` through by overriding them in the scopedVars it hands to `templateSrv.replace`, so in production `count_over_time({a="b"}[$__auto])` is left untouched on the frontend and interpolated on the backend. The test therefore asserts a substitution that cannot happen in the real data source and gives false confidence about macro handling. Using a user-defined variable (e.g. `$range`/`$step`) would exercise the same code path realistically.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, discarding recorded logs

`TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()` instead of the receiver, so the returned logger writes its `InfoLogs`/`DebugLogs`/... counters into a throwaway instance. Since `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` now always goes through `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info("Plugin Request Completed", ...)`, any test that injects `plog.NewTestLogger()` into the middleware and then asserts on `logger.InfoLogs.Calls`/`Message`/`Ctx` will observe zero calls — either failing outright or, worse, silently passing assertions that expect nothing to be logged. The fake should return `f` (optionally recording the ctx) so logging through the contextual path remains observable.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

false_positives.candidate:
Adding FromContext to the exported plugins/log.Logger interface is a breaking change

`plugins/log.Logger` is an exported interface consumed across the plugin packages and by out-of-tree code (e.g. grafana-enterprise). Adding the `FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger` method breaks every existing implementation that is not updated in this PR; only the two in-tree implementations (`grafanaInfraLogWrapper` and `TestLogger`) were adjusted, and the `var _ Logger = ...` compile checks only cover those. Any external or generated implementation will fail to compile after this change, so it needs to be coordinated/announced or the method should be introduced via an optional extension interface.

FromContext silently drops contextual fields if the concrete type assertion fails

`grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext` asserts the result of `d.l.FromContext(ctx)` to `*log.ConcreteLogger` and, on failure, falls back to `d.New()` — a logger with no context attributes at all. The failure path is silent: if `infra/log` ever returns a different `Logger` implementation from `FromContext`, every plugin request log line would silently lose `pluginId`, `endpoint`, `dsName`, `dsUID`, `uname` and `traceID`, with no error or warning to indicate why. Consider storing the `log.Logger` interface in the wrapper instead of the concrete `*ConcreteLogger`, so no assertion is needed.

Logger name still "plugin.instrumentation" after the rename

`NewLoggerMiddleware` is still constructed with `log.New("plugin.instrumentation")`, so the emitted log lines carry `logger=plugin.instrumentation` even though the instrumentation middleware has been renamed to the metrics middleware and the contextual logging has been split out. Since the goal of this change is naming consistency, and this name is user-visible in logs (and used for per-logger level configuration), it should be updated to something that matches the new structure (e.g. `plugin.logger`/`plugin.request`), keeping in mind that changing it affects existing log filters.

New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no tests and the moved log fields are unverified

This PR moves the `pluginId`, `endpoint`, `dsName`, `dsUID` and `uname` fields out of the explicit log params in `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` and into context attributes set by the brand-new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware`, but no test is added for the new middleware and no test asserts that the "Plugin Request Completed" log line still carries those fields. The correctness now depends on (a) the middleware being registered ahead of `LoggerMiddleware` in the chain and (b) `log.WithContextualAttributes` attributes being picked up by `Logger.FromContext`. A silent regression here would drop fields that log-based dashboards/alerts rely on, with nothing in CI to catch it.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Count-then-insert is not atomic, so the device limit can be exceeded

`CreateOrUpdateDevice` first runs `CountDevices` and then, if under the limit, performs the upsert in a separate session. Concurrent requests from different new devices (very likely for anonymous traffic across multiple Grafana instances or goroutines) can all read a count below the limit and all insert, pushing the stored device count above `AnonymousDeviceLimit`. Enforcement needs to be atomic (e.g. insert guarded by a conditional statement/transaction with appropriate locking) if the limit is meant to be a hard cap.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Any zero-row UPDATE is reported as "device limit reached"

`updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever `RowsAffected() == 0`. That is true not only for unknown devices but also for a device row that exists yet whose `updated_at` falls outside the `[now-30d, now+1m]` window (rows are only purged after 61 days), and on MySQL for an update that changes no column values. The caller turns this into an authentication failure, so legitimate but stale devices are denied with a misleading error that makes the real cause impossible to diagnose from logs. Distinguish "row not matched" from "limit reached", or at minimum log the device id/reason.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit is bypassed after the first rejection because the cache is populated before the DB write

`tagDeviceUI` writes the device key into `localCache` (`a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})`) *before* calling `anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice`. With the new limit enforcement, the first request from a device that exceeds the limit returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` (and `Anonymous.Authenticate` rejects it), but the key is already cached. Every subsequent request from the same `X-Grafana-Device-Id` within the cache TTL (29 min) short-circuits at the cache check, returns nil, and the anonymous user is authenticated without ever being recorded. So the limit only blocks a single request per device per ~29 minutes and is trivially bypassed by a page reload. The cache entry should only be set after a successful store write (or removed on error).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Backend sends 0 for "no limit" while the frontend type declares `number | undefined`

`AnonymousDeviceLimit int64` has no `omitempty`/pointer, so when no limit is configured the payload contains `anonymousDeviceLimit: 0`, yet `GrafanaConfig.anonymousDeviceLimit` is typed `number | undefined` and `GrafanaBootConfig` initialises it to `undefined`. Frontend code that distinguishes "unset" via `=== undefined` will treat an unlimited instance as having a limit of 0. Use `*int64` with `omitempty` (or document that 0 means unlimited) so the two sides agree.

Device tagging moved into the synchronous auth path, adding a COUNT query per cache miss

The previous implementation tagged devices in a background goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout and panic recovery; tagging is now done inline on the request's context during `Authenticate`. For every cache miss (once per device per 29 min) an anonymous request now blocks on `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device WHERE updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ?` plus the upsert. `anon_device` has no index supporting a range scan on `updated_at`, so on instances with many anonymous devices this is a table scan in the request path, and any DB slowness/latency is now visible to the user instead of being absorbed asynchronously. Consider caching the count or indexing `updated_at`, and only performing the count when the limit is configured.

Exported provider signatures changed without updating DI wiring / generated code

`ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` no longer takes `anonstore.AnonStore` but a `db.DB`, and `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` gained a second `deviceLimit int64` parameter. These are the providers referenced by the checked-in wire graph (`pkg/server/wire.go` and the generated `wire_gen.go`), plus enterprise wiring. Neither file is part of this PR, so the generated code still calls the old signatures and the build will fail (and/or wire now has a stale `ProvideAnonDBStore` provider with no `int64` binding). Regenerate wire and update all callers. Note this also removes the ability to inject a fake `AnonStore` into the service, which reduces testability of `AnonDeviceService`.

Limit-enforcement tests do not cover the update path or the client behaviour

`TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only asserts that a *new* device is rejected when the limit is reached. The core new logic — that an *existing* device is still updated successfully (and therefore still authenticates) once the limit is hit, including the `updated_at BETWEEN` window boundaries — is untested, as is the new synchronous `Anonymous.Authenticate` behaviour (returns error for `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, logs and continues for other errors) and the interaction with the local cache. Without those tests the limit-bypass via the local cache and the stale-row rejection path go unnoticed.

New `[auth.anonymous] device_limit` option is undocumented

`cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit` is read from `auth.anonymous.device_limit`, but the PR does not add the key to `conf/defaults.ini` / `conf/sample.ini` nor to docs/sources/setup-grafana/configure-grafana. Operators have no way to discover the option, its default (0 = unlimited), or the fact that exceeding it blocks anonymous authentication. Grafana convention requires every new ini setting to appear in defaults.ini and the configuration docs. Also consider rejecting/normalizing negative values, which are currently silently treated as "unlimited" by the `s.deviceLimit > 0` check.

Raw `ErrDeviceLimitReached` returned from Authenticate yields an opaque 500 to the user

`ErrDeviceLimitReached` is created with `fmt.Errorf("device limit reached")` in anonstore/database.go and is returned verbatim from `Anonymous.Authenticate`. The authn stack maps non-`errutil` client errors to a generic internal server error, so a user hitting the configured anonymous device limit gets a 500 with no actionable message instead of a well-defined 4xx/403 with a user-facing reason. Define the error with `errutil` (public message, proper status) so the rejection is reported correctly to the browser and logs.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Debug logging left in at Error level, dumping entire ID batches

Six new log calls use `r.log.Error(...)` for purely informational progress messages (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579), e.g. `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, ...)`. Consequences: (1) every cleanup cycle emits error-level log lines on a healthy system, which pollutes logs and will trigger error-rate alerting/monitoring; (2) the full `ids` slice is logged, so with a configured `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` (the test in this PR uses 32767) each iteration writes tens of thousands of IDs per log line, which can be megabytes of logs per cleanup run; (3) the `"err", err` field in the "to clean" messages is always nil at that point because the error path returned earlier, so it is misleading. These should be `Debug` level without the raw ID list (or removed).

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup job interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute (looks like leftover debug change)

The background cleanup ticker was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (splitting the annotation cleanup query) and has broad consequences: every cleanup job (temp files, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history) now runs 10x more often, increasing database and I/O load on every Grafana instance. It also interacts badly with the 9-minute timeout in `clean()`: a cleanup pass that takes longer than one minute will be immediately followed by another pass, effectively making cleanup run continuously. Unless this is intentional and documented, it should be reverted to 10 minutes.

false_positives.candidate:
Bind-parameter path can exceed Postgres/MySQL parameter limits for large configured batch sizes

For non-SQLite databases `deleteByIDs` always builds `DELETE ... WHERE id IN (?,?,...)` with one placeholder per ID. Postgres and MySQL cap the number of bind parameters in a statement at 65535, so an operator who sets `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` above that will make annotation cleanup fail permanently with a driver error ("extended protocol limited to 65535 parameters" / "Prepared statement contains too many placeholders"). The previous implementation used a single parameterless DELETE with a subquery, so any batch size worked; this is therefore a regression. Also note the branch condition tests `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` instead of `len(ids)`, which couples the delete path to an assumption about how many IDs the caller fetched; checking `len(ids)` (and applying an inline/chunked strategy for all dialects above the limit) would be safer.

Quadratic string concatenation when inlining IDs for SQLite

In `deleteByIDs`, the SQLite inline-values path builds the ID list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside the loop. Each iteration reallocates and copies the whole accumulated string, giving O(n^2) copying. With the batch sizes this code path is specifically designed for (>999, and the new test uses 32767 IDs), this copies on the order of gigabytes per batch and allocates one string per ID, for every cleanup iteration. Use a `strings.Builder` (or `strconv.AppendInt` into a byte slice, as done in `getAccessControlFilter`) instead.

Test cleanup registered after data creation and assertions, leaking rows across subtests on failure

`createTestAnnotations` and the two `assertAnnotationCount`/`assertAnnotationTagCount` calls run before `t.Cleanup` is registered, and all subtests share the single `fakeSQL` database. If insertion or either initial assertion fails (they use `require`, so the subtest aborts immediately), the `DELETE FROM annotation` / `DELETE FROM annotation_tag` cleanup is never registered, leaving rows behind and causing every subsequent subtest to fail with confusing count mismatches instead of a single clear failure. Register the `t.Cleanup` before creating the test data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete puts the bare logger in the context instead of the enriched one

`ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` uses `d.Log` rather than the `log` built one line earlier with `name`, `kind` and `method` values. Downstream code that retrieves the logger via `klog.FromContext(ctx)` loses all of the request-specific context, unlike every other method in this file which stores `log`. Should be `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
DeleteCollection records the legacy call duration into the storage metric

Inside the async goroutine of `DeleteCollection` the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration`. The legacy delete-collection latency/error rate is therefore never visible in the legacy metric and instead corrupts the storage metric (which was already recorded a few lines above for the same request), double-counting storage observations.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records the object name in the metric's `kind` label, causing unbounded cardinality

`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. Each distinct resource name becomes a new Prometheus label value on the storage duration histogram, so the series count grows with the number of objects ever deleted. This is a metrics cardinality explosion that can blow up the registry and the scraping backend. It should be `options.Kind`.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will be canceled when the request finishes

All four async legacy writes (`Create` line 51, `Delete` line 110, `Update` line 135, `DeleteCollection` line 163) build their context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming request context. In net/http (and therefore in the apiserver), the request context is canceled as soon as the handler returns, which happens immediately after the dual writer returns the unified-storage result. The spawned goroutine therefore usually starts or continues with an already-canceled context, so the legacy write is aborted (and silently only shows up as an error in the duration metric). Since the whole point of mode 3 is to keep legacy in sync as a safety net, legacy would systematically fail to be written. Use a detached context (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` as the parent, preserving the auth/user values) before applying the timeout.

Destroy can tear down the stores while async legacy writes are still in flight

`Destroy()` immediately calls `d.Storage.Destroy()` and `d.Legacy.Destroy()`, but nothing tracks the goroutines spawned by Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection. On shutdown an in-flight legacy write can run against an already-destroyed store (closed DB handles/connection pools), producing errors or panics. A WaitGroup (or a shared lifecycle context) that Destroy waits on would make shutdown deterministic.

Legacy update now re-runs the caller's objInfo instead of applying the object already written to storage

The previous implementation fetched the current object, computed `updated`, and passed `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}` to the legacy store so that legacy received exactly the object persisted in unified storage. The new code hands the raw `objInfo` to `d.Legacy.Update`, so the legacy store re-evaluates the update/patch against *its own* copy of the object, including resource-version precondition checks. For PUT requests the resourceVersion in the request body comes from unified storage and will generally not match the legacy row, so the legacy update can fail with a conflict, and for PATCH/Apply the transformation is applied to a possibly divergent legacy object. Either way legacy silently drifts from unified storage, defeating the purpose of the mode-3 safety write. The failure is only visible as a metric label, since the error is not even logged.

New mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy write

All of the new tests share a single `mock.Mock` between `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock`, so an expectation registered by `setupLegacyFn` is indistinguishable from the one registered by `setupStorageFn` (e.g. in `TestMode3_Update` both register `"Update"` with identical argument matchers). Combined with the fact that no test waits for (or asserts on) the goroutine that performs the legacy write, and no `AssertExpectations`/`AssertCalled` is used, the tests cannot show that the legacy store is written at all — which is the core behaviour this PR adds. They also cannot show that a legacy failure does not affect the response. Separate mocks per store (or distinct expectations) plus a synchronization point (channel/WaitGroup signalled from the legacy mock) are needed.

Storage failures in Create/Update are recorded as legacy-storage durations

In `Create` (line 45) and `Update` (line 129) the error path calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` even though the failure came from `d.Storage`. The success paths correctly call `recordStorageDuration`. As a result the legacy histogram is polluted with unified-storage failures and the storage error rate is under-reported, which makes the mode-3 dashboards/alerts misleading. Both should call `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

The input object is shared with the async legacy write without a deep copy

`d.Legacy.Create(ctx, obj, ...)` is called from the goroutine with the same `obj` pointer that was just passed to `d.Storage.Create` and that the request handler still owns (admission/audit layers may read it, and generic registry code mutates object metadata in place such as resourceVersion/UID/name on name generation). Writing to that object from the legacy store concurrently with the handler's continued use is a data race that can also mean the legacy store persists metadata mutated by the unified store. Pass `obj.DeepCopyObject()` to the goroutine.

Unrecovered panic in async legacy write will crash the whole process

The legacy writes are now executed in bare `go func()` goroutines (lines 50, 108, 134, 161) with no `defer recover()`. Previously these calls were synchronous and any panic inside the legacy store was caught by the apiserver's panic-recovery filter for that request. Now a panic in `d.Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection` (or in the validation callbacks it invokes) happens on a goroutine with no recovery and takes down the entire Grafana process. Wrap the goroutine body with a recover (e.g. `runtime.HandleCrash` semantics) or a helper that logs and swallows panics.

Unrelated, duplicated and unsorted go.work.sum entries
