The added block contains `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` which is already present a few lines above, and inserts `github.com/grafana/grafana-azure-sdk-go/v2` out of sort order. These entries are unrelated to the dual-writer change and look like a hand-edited/stale generated file; they should be regenerated (`go work sync`) or dropped from this PR to avoid confusing future dependency updates.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write lock acquired without re-checking the cache (no double-checked locking)

After the fast path under `RLock` sees a nil cache, every goroutine falls through, takes the exclusive `Lock`, and unconditionally re-reads `assets-manifest.json` (or performs the CDN HTTP request) before setting the cache. There is no second check of `entryPointAssetsCache` after the write lock is acquired, so on a cold start with N concurrent requests the manifest is parsed N times, serialized one after another while holding the exclusive lock. Re-checking `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after `Lock()` makes the load happen exactly once and avoids the serialized duplicate I/O.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is overwritten with nil when loading the manifest fails

`entryPointAssetsCache = result` runs unconditionally, including when `readWebAssetsFromFile`/`readWebAssetsFromCDN` returned `nil, err`. A transient failure therefore stores nil in the shared cache and the function returns a nil `*dtos.EntryPointAssets` together with the error; any caller that logs the error but still dereferences the returned pointer will panic. Guard the assignment with `if err == nil && result != nil` (and return the previous cached value on error) so a failed reload cannot poison the cache.

false_positives.candidate:
No test exercising concurrent GetWebAssets calls

The PR fixes a data race but adds no test that calls `GetWebAssets` from multiple goroutines, so the race fix is not covered and a future refactor (for example removing the lock or mutating the cached struct) could reintroduce the race without any CI signal. A small `t.Parallel`/`sync.WaitGroup` test run under `-race` would pin the behaviour.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions has unreachable logic and silently neutralises the feature toggle

`enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` from both the `if enabled` branch and the fall-through, so the function is a constant `false` and the feature-flag lookup is completely dead. The negation is also inverted relative to the variable name (`enabled` is true when the flag is *off*), which makes the code read as a logic error rather than an intentional kill switch. Consequences: (a) the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle no longer has any effect on this code path, which is surprising for anyone later trying to re-enable the feature by flipping the flag; (b) static analysis/lint (ineffectual assignment, identical branch returns) is likely to flag it. If the intent is a hard disable, the function should simply `return false` with a comment explaining why, or the type case should return the error directly.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

false_positives.candidate:
Feature gate only added to the new reader path; legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path relies solely on the stubbed DB

The explicit disable check was added only in `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` (pkg/expr/reader.go). The other entry point, `UnmarshalSQLCommand` -> `NewSQLCommand` (used by the classic/non-apiserver expression pipeline), has no toggle or disable check at all; it is only prevented from working because `sql.DB.RunCommands`/`QueryFramesInto` in the new `pkg/expr/sql/db.go` stub return `errors.New("not implemented")`. If `sql.DB` is ever re-implemented (which is the obvious next step for this package), that path silently becomes reachable again with no gate, re-opening the vulnerable surface. The gate should be applied at command construction/execution as well, not just in the query reader. Additionally, every such request now takes the `logger.Warn("invalid sql query", "sql", rawSQL, ...)` branch and surfaces an opaque `error reading SQL command` BadRequest, which both logs user-supplied query text on every attempt and gives no indication the feature is disabled.

No test asserts that SQL expressions are rejected

This change is a security fix that disables a code path, but no test is added or updated. There is nothing verifying that `ReadQuery` returns an error for `QueryTypeSQL` (with the toggle both on and off), nor that `NewSQLCommand`/`SQLCommand.Execute` fail safely against the new stub `sql.DB`. Without such a test, a future refactor (e.g. "fixing" the obviously odd `enableSqlExpressions` helper, or implementing `sql.DB`) can silently re-enable the vulnerable path with a green CI.

User-facing error says "not implemented" while the sqlExpressions toggle is still registered and documented

Requests of `QueryTypeSQL` are now rejected with `sqlExpressions is not implemented`. The `sqlExpressions` feature toggle remains registered in featuremgmt and documented as an available (experimental) flag, so an operator who enables it, and users who already have saved SQL expression queries, will get an error that contradicts the documentation and gives no hint that the feature was deliberately removed/disabled for security reasons. Either the toggle/docs should be marked as unavailable, or the message should state that SQL expressions are currently disabled.

tablesFromAST indexes ast[0] without a length check

`tablesFromAST` does `flatten.Flatten(ast[0], ...)` immediately, so an empty JSON array (`[]`) returned from the serialization step causes an index-out-of-range panic. Today this is unreachable because `DB.RunCommands` is a stub that always errors, but the DuckDB-specific code in `TablesList` (the `SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')` command, the single-quote escaping) is left in place and will be the starting point if/when a real backend is wired up again. Either add a length guard, or remove this now-dead DuckDB-specific parser along with the dependency it was built for so it cannot be reactivated by accident.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dropping the BuildIndex-wide lock allows concurrent duplicate builds of the same key

The write lock that previously covered the whole of `BuildIndex` is now only taken around the cache assignment. `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` does a lock-free `GetIndex` followed by `build`, so two concurrent requests (or a watch event plus a search) for the same NamespacedResource can now execute `BuildIndex` for the same key at the same time. Consequences: (a) for file-backed indexes both goroutines call `bleve.New` on the identical directory `Root/namespace/resource.group`, which at best fails with ErrorIndexPathExists and at worst leaves two writers on the same on-disk index; (b) both perform a full re-list/re-index of the resource (wasted DB and CPU work); (c) the loser's index object silently overwritten in the cache is never closed, leaking its file handles/memory, while callers that already got the old handle keep searching a discarded index. Finer-grained locking is fine, but it needs to be per-key (e.g. a per-key build mutex or singleflight) rather than removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs reads b.cache without holding cacheMu — concurrent map read/write panic

`TotalDocs()` iterates `b.cache` with no lock, while `BuildIndex` now writes the map (line 138) outside any long-held lock, from the N concurrent index-build workers and from lazy builds triggered by search/watch events. A concurrent map read and map write is a fatal runtime panic in Go (not just a benign race), taking down the process. This path is newly exercised by the `s.search.TotalDocs()` call added in search.go:216 and by any metric/diagnostic caller. Take `cacheMu.RLock()` in `TotalDocs` (and avoid holding it while calling `index.DocCount()` if that is expensive, e.g. snapshot the slice of indexes first).

false_positives.candidate:
BuildIndex still discards the span context, so the indexing work is not under its span

This PR's stated goal includes fixing trace propagation (`ctx, span := ...` in search.go and sql/backend.go), but `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` still uses `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` and never passes the derived context anywhere. The `builder(idx)` callback executed at line 126 captures the caller's context instead, so all the list/iterate/document-build spans produced during the actual indexing attach to the parent `unified_search.Build` span rather than to `unified_search.bleve.BuildIndex`, leaving BuildIndex as an empty leaf span and making it impossible to attribute index build time in traces.

Data race on shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` in searchSupport.init

Inside `group.Go(...)` the closure writes the function-scoped `err` variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increments `totalBatchesIndexed++`. With `group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers)` these closures run concurrently, so both are unsynchronized writes from multiple goroutines: a genuine data race (the race detector will flag it), an undercounted `namespaced_indexed` span attribute, and — worse — error misattribution: one goroutine can overwrite `err` with `nil` before another returns it (swallowing a build failure) or a goroutine can return an error produced by a different build. Since init failure now aborts server startup (server.go:258), a spuriously propagated error can block the whole process. Use a local `err :=` inside the closure and an atomic/counter for the batch count.

Index/lifecycle init failure now aborts server construction (and therefore process startup)

`NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` and returns the error. Previously initialization was lazy, so a failure only broke the individual gRPC call that triggered it. Now any failure in `lifecycle.Init`, `search.init` (which lists all resource stats and builds every index), or `initWatcher` makes the constructor fail, which propagates up through DI and prevents the storage server / Grafana from starting at all. This is a real, reachable scenario: for file-backed bleve indexes `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` (pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:98) returns `ErrorIndexPathExists` when the directory from a previous run is still on disk (the code itself has a TODO about not yet checking the persisted RV), and transient DB errors during `GetResourceStats` have the same effect. Startup also now blocks for the full duration of indexing all namespaces. Consider keeping init asynchronous/retryable, or at least making index build failures non-fatal.

Removing per-request Init() checks makes the shutdown guard dead code

`Stop` sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping" / "service is stopped", which used to be surfaced to clients because every handler started with `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil { return nil, err }`. All of those checks were removed in this diff, so no handler ever reads `initErr` again. After `Stop()` has cancelled the background context and the backend lifecycle has shut down, Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search now proceed into a stopped backend instead of returning a clear "service is stopping" error, producing confusing driver-level errors (or worse, work against a closed DB). Either keep a lightweight state check in the handlers or remove the now-misleading `initErr` assignments in `Stop`.

Storage-server integration test silently disabled for postgres in CI

The only integration test that boots the `StorageServer` module target is now skipped for postgres with the comment "test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally." This PR moves unified storage initialization (index build, watcher start) into `NewResourceServer`, i.e. into module startup — exactly the code path this test exercises — so disabling it removes CI coverage of the change for one of the supported databases and hides whatever failure prompted the skip (it may well be caused by this PR's startup-blocking init rather than by Drone). The root cause should be identified before the skip is merged, or the skip should link to a tracking issue with the observed failure.

cancel() is not called when Init fails in NewResourceServer, leaking goroutines

The cancelable context created at line 229 is only cancelled via `server.Stop`. On the new error path (`err := s.Init(ctx); if err != nil { return nil, err }`), the constructor returns without calling `cancel()`, so the context (and anything already started under it) is leaked. This matters because `search.init` may already have called `storage.WatchWriteEvents` and started the SQL poller/event-handling goroutines before the error occurred; nothing will ever stop them, and the caller has no handle to the server to call `Stop`. Call `cancel()` (and ideally `lifecycle.Stop`) before returning the error.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup registers a non-existent alias, leaking 21 identity providers into the shared test realm

`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` (lines 381 and 425) uses the literal string "alias" instead of the alias of the provider just created (`idpRep.getAlias()`). Consequently the 20 providers `idp-alias-0..19` plus `idp-alias-20` are never deleted after the test, and the cleanup action itself targets a provider that does not exist (404 at teardown). Because `OrganizationCacheTest` uses the shared test realm across test methods, these leftover providers change the IDP counts other tests in this class rely on (e.g. `testCacheIDPForLogin` asserts exactly 5/5/10 login providers and `testCacheIDPByOrg` asserts 6/2/4), making results order-dependent and flaky. Note that the same mistake already exists at line 303 and is being copied here.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Cached getForLogin returns providers in non-deterministic order, unlike the delegate path

On a cache hit, `getForLogin()` returns `identityProviders.stream()` built from a `HashSet`, so the iteration order is arbitrary, whereas the fallback paths (lines 218 and 249) return the delegate's stream, which for `FetchMode.ALL` is realm-level providers followed by organization providers in query order. The order of providers returned by the same call therefore differs depending on whether the cache is warm or cold. Current login beans sort the result, but any consumer that relies on the stream order (or picks the first element) will behave non-deterministically; this should at least be documented in `IdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin`, which says nothing about ordering.

Login-cache invalidation decision uses the org-aware wrapped model, so required invalidations can be skipped

In `update()` the "original" model passed to `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate()` comes from `getById(model.getInternalId())`, which returns the model wrapped by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel()`. That wrapper's `isEnabled()` returns `false` whenever the linked organization (or the realm's organization support) is disabled, even though the underlying IDP row is enabled. The login cache, however, is populated from the JPA query, which only filters on the IDP's own `enabled` flag and therefore *does* contain such IDPs. The result is an asymmetry: for an org-linked IDP whose organization is currently disabled, `getLoginPredicate().test(original)` is `false`, so an update that also makes the raw model non-eligible (e.g. setting `hideOnLogin=true`, `enabled=false`, or `broker_public=false`) takes the first early-return branch and no login cache is invalidated, while the cached id list still contains the provider. After the organization is re-enabled (organization updates do not invalidate the login keys), `getForLogin()` keeps returning that id from the cache, so a hidden or non-public (private) organization broker is still offered on the login page. Note that `create()` and `remove()` evaluate the predicate on raw models (`model`, `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)`), so only `update()` is inconsistent; the fix is to evaluate the predicate on the unwrapped model (e.g. `idpDelegate.getById(...)`).

No coverage for the new create/remove login-cache invalidation

The new test only exercises the negative cases for the invalidation hooks added to `create()` and `remove()`: it creates an IDP with `hideOnLogin=true` and removes a disabled IDP, then asserts the login caches are still present. There is no case that creates a login-eligible IDP (enabled, not link-only, not hidden) or removes one and asserts that all three `cacheKeyForLogin(realm, mode)` entries are invalidated. Those are exactly the paths added by `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(model)` in `create()` and `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp)` in `remove()`, so a regression that drops either call (leaving stale login lists that hide a new broker or still advertise a deleted one) would not be caught.

One login cache entry per realm+fetch mode aggregates all organizations, causing cluster-wide invalidation churn

`getForLogin()` stores all results for a given realm and `FetchMode` in a single cache object keyed by `cacheKeyForLogin(realm, mode)`, using the organization id as the inner search key. Whenever a request asks for an organization that is not yet present in that object, line 236 calls `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)`, which drops the entry locally and broadcasts an invalidation to the whole cluster, then re-adds a merged copy. `OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean` calls `getForLogin(ALL, organization.getId())` on the login path, so in a realm with many organizations the first login for each new organization on each node wipes every other node's cached login IDP lists for that fetch mode, which must then be rebuilt from the database; the merged entry itself also grows with one id set per organization without any bound. Keying the cache per `(mode, organizationId)` (as `getByOrganization` does per organization) would avoid the shared-entry contention. Additionally, for `FetchMode.REALM_ONLY` the `organizationId` argument is documented as ignored, yet it is still used as the search key, so passing different organization ids creates redundant duplicate entries with identical content.

Test asserts only on cache internals, never on what getForLogin returns

`testCacheIDPForLogin` discards the stream returned by `session.identityProviders().getForLogin(...)` and only inspects the sizes of the internal `IdentityProviderListQuery` entries. Nothing verifies that the cached code path returns the same providers as the uncached delegate path (for example that the aliases match, that disabled/hidden/non-public providers are excluded, or that the second, cache-hit call returns the same result as the first). A bug in the cache-hit branch (e.g. the `getById` loop returning wrapped models whose `isEnabled()` is false, or the fallback on a missing id) would pass this test unnoticed.

getLoginPredicate() silently gains an organization/BROKER_PUBLIC criterion that getLoginSearchOptions() does not have

`LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate()` now additionally rejects any IDP that is linked to an organization and does not have `BROKER_PUBLIC=true`. This criterion is not represented by any `LoginFilter` constant and is therefore absent from `getLoginSearchOptions()`, so the query-based and predicate-based helpers of the same enum no longer agree on what "available for login" means; the enum's javadoc ("contains all fields that are considered when deciding if a provider should be available for login") is now inaccurate. The change also affects every existing caller of `getLoginPredicate()` (e.g. `IdentityProviderBean.federatedProviderPredicate()`, which `OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean` builds on): non-public organization brokers that previously passed the predicate are now filtered out. If that behavior change is intended it should be documented; otherwise the extra condition belongs in the Infinispan invalidation logic rather than in the shared SPI predicate.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code: two ASN1Encoder instances created and discarded in concatenatedRSToASN1DER

Lines 114-115 (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);`) build encoders whose results are thrown away; the actual DER sequence is produced from freshly created encoders on lines 117-121. These two statements have no effect and only confuse readers (they look like they are part of the encoding). They should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Indefinite-length encoding (-1 from readLength) is not handled by readInteger/readSequence

readLength() returns -1 for the indefinite-length form (0x80). readInteger() passes that value straight to read(length), which executes `new byte[-1]` and throws NegativeArraySizeException - an unchecked exception escaping a method that declares IOException, so callers that catch IOException will not handle it. readSequence() with a -1 length simply skips the while loop and returns an empty list, hiding the malformed input. Malformed or BER-encoded input (asn1derToConcatenatedRS is called with externally supplied bytes) should be rejected with a clear IOException instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() added as a non-default interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is a public SPI in keycloak-common. Adding the abstract method `int order();` is a source- and binary-incompatible change: any out-of-tree implementation (and, per the PR description, the authz-client copy maintained in the keycloak-client repository which compiles against a released keycloak-common) will no longer compile, and pre-compiled implementations will fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration sorts the providers. Declaring it as `default int order() { return 0; }` (or some neutral baseline) keeps compatibility while still allowing the new provider to lower/raise its precedence.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)

false_positives.candidate:
Multiple crypto providers are now silently tolerated, with non-deterministic tie-breaking

detectProvider() no longer throws when more than one CryptoProvider is found on the classpath; it just sorts by order() and picks the first. All three in-tree providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider) return order() == 200, and Stream.sorted() is stable, so when two of them are on the classpath the selected provider is decided purely by ServiceLoader/classpath discovery order. The removed IllegalStateException was the guard that caught exactly this misconfiguration; now a deployment that accidentally has both the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider and the FIPS provider on the classpath can silently run non-FIPS crypto (or vice versa) with no error, and the behaviour can change between environments or build layouts. Either keep failing when two providers share the same order, or give the real providers distinct orders and log at WARN/ERROR when more than one is present.

Test uses the default EC curve for ES384/ES512 and never validates the produced DER with a verifier

The key pair is generated once with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` using the JDK default curve (P-256 on current JDKs), so testES384/testES512 sign with a P-256 key while asserting against signature lengths 96/132. The round-trip assertion still passes because r/s are simply zero-padded, so the real P-384/P-521 r/s widths produced by concatenatedRSToASN1DER are never exercised. Additionally the test only asserts rsConcat == rsConcat2; it never feeds the DER output of concatenatedRSToASN1DER into Signature.verify(), which is the actual production use of that method (JWS signature verification), so an encoder that produces structurally parseable but non-DER output would not be caught. Generate keys with the curve matching each algorithm (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) and verify the re-encoded DER with a JCA Signature.

integerToBytes silently truncates integers larger than the expected signature half-length

When `qLength < bytes.length` the method keeps only the low-order qLength bytes of the BigInteger, silently discarding high-order bytes. The BouncyCastle-based implementation this replaces uses BigIntegers.asUnsignedByteArray(len, value), which raises an error when the value does not fit. With this implementation a DER signature containing an r/s value wider than the algorithm's half-length (corrupt input, or a mismatch between the key curve and the declared ES* algorithm) is converted to a wrong concatenated R||S value instead of failing, which turns a detectable error into a silently invalid signature. It should throw IOException when the value does not fit in qLength bytes.

logger.debugf() called with a dynamically built string as the format

`logger.debugf(builder.toString())` passes runtime-constructed text as the format string. If any ignored provider class name ever contains a '%' the formatter will throw or produce garbage, and static analysis/IDE format checks cannot validate it. Use `logger.debugf("%s", builder)` (or logger.debug(Object)). The message should also be built lazily (guarded by isDebugEnabled) and, given that silently ignoring a crypto provider used to be a fatal error, logged at WARN rather than DEBUG so misconfigured classpaths are visible. The message also ends with a dangling ", ".

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feature guard stops cleanup of legacy fine-grained permission policies

Previously the role/client/group removal listener ran unconditionally and invoked `setPermissionsEnabled(..., false)`, which deletes the V1 fine-grained permission policies/resources associated with the removed object. With the new `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)` guard, deployments that created V1 FGAP data and later disabled the preview feature will leak orphan policies and resources into the authorization store when the corresponding roles/clients/groups are deleted, leaving the data inconsistent if the feature is re-enabled. If the intent was only to avoid the V2 `UnsupportedOperationException`, the guard should select the V1 management implementation rather than skipping cleanup entirely.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission returns the literal "Clients" and never a real client id

`getClientsWithPermission()` iterates `resourceStore.findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)` and adds `resource.getName()` to the result. Only the aggregate resource created in `AdminPermissionsSchema.init()` has its type set to `Clients` (`resource.setType(type)`); per-client resources created by `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource()` are created with `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, owner)` and never get a type. Consequently this method (1) can only ever return the string `"Clients"`, which is not a client id, and (2) never returns the ids of clients that actually have a permission granted. Any caller using this set to decide which clients an admin may act on will both miss all legitimately permitted clients and receive a bogus entry. Either set the resource type when creating per-client resources, or resolve the granted clients differently (and exclude the aggregate resource name).

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NPE when the aggregate "Clients" resource does not exist

In `hasPermission(ClientModel, String)`, when no per-client resource exists the code falls back to `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` and immediately passes the result to `authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource)` without a null check. `getResourceTypeResource()` returns `null` in two reachable situations: (a) `supportsAuthorizationSchema()` is false, i.e. the realm still has an admin-permissions client (so `root.realmResourceServer()` is non-null) but `realm.isAdminPermissionsEnabled()` was turned off, and (b) the realm's resource server has no resource named `Clients` (e.g. a realm whose FGAP client was created before this PR, see the missing migration). The policy store dereferences `resource.getId()`, so this throws a NullPointerException, and because `canManage/canConfigure/canView/canMapRoles` all go through this method, every admin REST call touching a client would fail with HTTP 500. Add a null check and return `false`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code and unused imports copied from the V1 implementation

`getEvaluationContext(ClientModel, AccessToken)` (line 262) is private and never called, the `logger` field (line 51) is unused, and the imports `org.keycloak.authorization.model.Scope`, `ClientModelIdentity`, `DefaultEvaluationContext`, `EvaluationContext` and the static import of `AdminPermissionManagement.TOKEN_EXCHANGE` are unused. This dead code (apparently copied from `ClientPermissions`) suggests token-exchange support was intended but is not implemented, and it will mislead future readers. Remove it (or implement the missing behaviour).

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Javadoc for void require* methods says they return true

`requireView()` (line 98) and `requireViewClientScopes()` (line 103) are `void`, but the new Javadoc states "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}" / "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canViewClientScopes()} returns {@code true}". These should follow the convention used for the other require* methods in this file: "Throws ForbiddenException if ... returns {@code false}". As written the contract documented for implementors/callers is wrong.

Listener guard does not protect against V1+V2 both enabled; client removal will fail with 500

The removal listener is now only executed when `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` (V1) is enabled, presumably because `ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled()` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. But `management()` (line 67) prefers `MgmtPermissionsV2` whenever `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` is enabled, and the two preview features are not mutually exclusive. When both are enabled, a `ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent` reaches `management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(cast.getClient(), false)`, which now throws `UnsupportedOperationException` and aborts the client deletion transaction (HTTP 500). The same applies to the `/clients/{id}/management/permissions` admin endpoints, which call `clients().isPermissionsEnabled()`/`getPermissions()` after the V1 feature check passes. The guard should select the V1 implementation explicitly (or V2 should no-op instead of throwing) for these legacy operations.

New Clients scopes and all-clients fallback combinations are untested

The added tests cover `manage`, `configure`, `view`, `map-roles` and `map-roles-composite`, but there is no test for the newly introduced `map-roles-client-scope` scope (`canMapClientScopeRoles`), none for `getClientsWithPermission()` (which, as implemented, cannot return any client id), and none for the combination of an all-clients permission with an unrelated per-client permission — a case where `hasPermission(ClientModel, scope)` stops consulting the aggregate `Clients` resource as soon as a per-client resource exists, so a previously granted all-clients permission silently stops applying to that client. These are exactly the paths most likely to regress.

No migration for realms whose admin-permissions client already exists

`init()` returns early when `realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() != null`, so realms where FGAP v2 was already enabled before this change never receive the newly added `Clients` resource nor the new scopes (`configure`, `map-roles-client-scope`, `map-roles-composite`). In such realms: creating a Clients permission reaches `getOrCreateResource()` and hits `throw new ModelException("No scopes found.")` (line 108) for the missing scopes, all-clients evaluation silently returns `false` because `resourceStore.findByName(server, "Clients", ...)` is null, and per-client evaluation NPEs on the null aggregate resource (ClientPermissionsV2 line 219). The PR adds no upgrade/migration step to create the missing scopes and resource for existing admin-permissions clients.

canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException on a runtime (non-admin) code path

`canExchangeTo(...)` now throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. This method is not only an admin-console concern: the legacy token-exchange flow calls `AdminPermissions.management(session, realm).clients().canExchangeTo(...)` to authorize exchanging to a target client, and `AdminPermissions.management()` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2` whenever the `admin-fine-grained-authz:v2` feature is enabled — independently of whether the legacy FGAP feature is enabled. With both the (legacy) token-exchange feature and FGAP v2 enabled, token-exchange requests will produce an HTTP 500 from the unchecked exception instead of a clean 403 denial. The V1 implementation returned `false` when no resource server/permission existed; this override should do the same (or the caller must be made V2-aware).

canView() ignores the manage scope, breaking "manage implies view" for client scopes/listing

`canView()` is implemented as `canViewClientDefault() || hasPermission(VIEW)`. Unlike every other place in this class (`canView(ClientModel)` falls back to `canManage(client)`, `canView(ClientScopeModel)` checks VIEW *or* MANAGE) and unlike V1 where the `manage-clients` role implies view, the global `manage` permission does not imply `canView()`. Since `canList()`, `canListClientScopes()`, `canViewClientScopes()` and `requireView()` (not overridden) are all derived from `canView()`, an admin granted only the all-clients `manage` permission is denied listing/viewing realm client scopes (`requireListClientScopes()` → 403) while `canManageClientScopes()` returns true, so the same admin may create and modify client scopes but cannot list them. `canView()` should also consider the `manage` scope.

getResourceName has no handling for the Clients resource type

`getResourceName()` translates resource names to human-readable values only for the `Users` resource type ("All users" for the aggregate resource, the username for per-user resources) and otherwise returns `resource.getDisplayName()`. Per-client resources are created in `getOrCreateResource()` without a display name, and the aggregate `Clients` resource has none either, so every Clients permission exposed through the admin REST API/console will report a `null` resource name instead of the client id/clientId or an "All clients" label. The new resource type needs a branch here (resolving the client via `session.clients().getClientById()`), consistent with the Users handling.

resolveClient allows permissions to target the admin-permissions client itself

`resolveClient()` resolves any client in the realm, including the realm's own admin-permissions (FGAP policy) client and `realm-management`, even though the class already provides `throwExceptionIfAdminPermissionClient()` for exactly this kind of guard and it is not used here. As a result an administrator can create a Clients permission whose resource is the admin-permissions client and grant `manage`/`configure` on it; since the client authorization admin endpoints are gated on being able to manage the owning client, the grantee can then modify or delete all fine-grained admin permission policies — a privilege escalation out of the restricted scope they were given. Target clients that back the FGAP/admin infrastructure should be rejected when resolving the resource.

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Exit-code contract changed: 4 now means "feature disabled" instead of "recreate required"

`RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE` was changed from 4 to 3 and 4 is reused for the new `FEATURE_DISABLED` result. Any consumer written against the previously released behaviour of the `update-compatibility check` command (automation/DevOps pipelines, as explicitly encouraged by the guide, and the Operator's auto-update logic that inspects the Job's exit code) will now mis-interpret results: a check that tested `exit == 4` for "recreate needed" will now trigger a downtime upgrade when the only problem is that the preview feature is not enabled, and will not recognise exit code 3 at all. The reverse mapping is just as harmful: code expecting 3 to be unused will now receive it for the common recreate case. Since both codes are swapped in the same release, consumers must be updated in lockstep (operator source is not touched in this PR) and the change should be called out in release notes / upgrade notes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

false_positives.candidate:
CR-only instructions for enabling rolling-updates are incomplete for custom/optimized images

The new CAUTION and the example tell users to enable the preview feature only via `spec.features.enabled: [rolling-updates]`. For deployments using a custom image (`spec.image`), the Operator starts the server with `--optimized`, so build-time options such as `features` must already be baked into the image - exactly what this PR does for the test image in `operator/scripts/Dockerfile-custom-image` (`kc.sh build ... --features=rolling-updates`). Without mentioning this, users of custom images will either see the server reject the build-time option or run without the feature while believing it is enabled. The CAUTION also does not say how the Operator "will fail", which makes it hard to diagnose.

Documented command appends --features=rolling-updates, silently replacing the user's feature set

The `updatecompatibility` macro now renders `bin/kc.[sh|bat] update-compatibility <params> --features=rolling-updates`. `--features` is a list option that replaces, not extends, the configured feature set, so a deployment that runs with e.g. `--features=admin-fine-grained-authz` will be analysed with a different feature configuration than the running server. This directly contradicts the warning in update-compatibility.adoc ("Ensure that all configuration options ... are included ... Omitting any configuration options will result in incomplete metadata") and can yield a wrong rolling/recreate verdict. The docs should instead instruct the user to add `rolling-updates` to their existing `--features` value. The same rendered command also breaks for pre-built/optimized distributions, where passing the build-time `--features` option together with `--optimized` is rejected.

New feature enum requires regenerating CLI help/doc snapshots

`ROLLING_UPDATES` is added to `Profile.Feature`, which feeds the `--features` option's enumerated "Possible values" text in the CLI help and the generated configuration documentation. The approved help output files under `quarkus/tests/integration/src/test/resources/help/` (compared verbatim by the help dist tests) are not updated in this PR, so those tests will fail or the documented feature list will be stale. Regenerate the approved help output after adding the feature.

New/changed exit codes are not asserted by any test

`testFeatureNotEnabled` only asserts the stderr message and only for the `metadata` sub-command; it never asserts that the process exits with `CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED` (4), and the `check` sub-command is not covered at all. Likewise `testWrongVersions` asserts only the error text, not the new `RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE` (3). Because the exit codes are the documented, scriptable contract of this command (and were just renumbered from 4 to 3), a regression in either value would pass CI unnoticed. Add assertions on `result.exitCode()` for the feature-disabled case (both sub-commands) and for the incompatible-version case.

setEnabledFeatures overwrites any features already configured in the test deployment

`kc.getSpec().getFeatureSpec().setEnabledFeatures(List.of(Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES.getKey()))` replaces the whole list. The preceding null check on `getFeatureSpec()` implies the base deployment produced by `getTestKeycloakDeployment(true)` may already carry a FeatureSpec with enabled features; those would be silently dropped, changing what the test actually exercises (and potentially breaking the test if a required feature is removed). Append to the existing list instead of overwriting it.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() grants manage when only the VIEW scope is permitted

`canManage()` evaluates `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)` - i.e. it returns `true` when the caller only has the `view` scope on the "all groups" resource (looks like a copy/paste from `canView()` two methods above). `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup` calls `auth.groups().requireManage()`, so an administrator who was granted only a read-only all-groups permission can create top-level groups. This is a privilege escalation; the check must only accept `MANAGE`. The new Javadoc added to `GroupPermissionEvaluator#canManage()` documents the same wrong semantics and should be fixed as well.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authorization resource IDs, not group IDs

In the V2 implementation the authorization `Resource` created for a group uses the *group id as the resource name* (see `AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup`/`getOrCreateResource`), while `Resource#getId()` is the unrelated internal UUID of the authz resource. This method adds `groupResource.getId()` to the returned set and also passes `groupResource.getId()` into `hasPermission(String groupId, ...)`, which resolves the group via `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`.

Consequences:
1. `hasPermission` never finds the per-group resource for the id it is given, so it always falls through to the "all groups" resource-type resource - the per-group evaluation intended here does not happen.
2. The returned set is consumed as a set of *group ids*: `UsersResource.searchForUser` puts it in `session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, groupIds)` (restricting the user query to members of those groups) and `UsersResource.getUsersCount` passes it to `session.users().getUsersCount(realm, ..., groupIds)`. Because the ids are authz resource ids, they match no group, so an admin holding an all-groups `view-members`/`manage-members` permission gets zero users and a count of 0 from `/users` and `/users/count`.

The V1 implementation deliberately strips the resource-name prefix (`resource.getName().substring(RESOURCE_NAME_PREFIX.length())`) to produce group ids; V2 should use `groupResource.getName()`. Note also that resources created by `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` never get `setType(...)`, so `findByType(server, "Groups", ...)` only returns the single "Groups" resource-type resource, never the per-group resources - the loop can therefore never enumerate individual groups. No test covers this code path (the existing tests pass via the per-user `canView(user)` filter).

false_positives.candidate:
All-groups permissions are silently ignored for any group that has its own permission

`hasPermission` only falls back to the "all groups" resource when no resource exists for the specific group. A per-group resource is created as soon as *any* group-scoped permission references that group (`AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource`). Because per-group resources are created without a resource type, type-based policy evaluation does not apply either. Result: once an admin creates, say, a `manage-membership` permission for group G, all broader all-groups permissions (e.g. `view`, `view-members`) stop applying to G, so an administrator who could previously view G loses that access as a side effect of an unrelated permission being created for G. The scopes granted at the resource-type level should be evaluated in addition to, not instead of, the group-specific resource.

Group deletion breaks when both FGAP v1 and v2 features are enabled

`MgmtPermissionsV2` now overrides `groups()` to return `GroupPermissionsV2`, whose `setPermissionsEnabled(...)`/`isPermissionsEnabled(...)` throw `UnsupportedOperationException`. `AdminPermissions.registerListener` (registered whenever `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` is enabled) handles `GroupModel.GroupRemovedEvent` by calling `management(session, realm).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false)`, and `management(...)` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2` as soon as `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` is enabled. With both features enabled, deleting any group in any realm therefore throws `UnsupportedOperationException`, failing the delete request (500) and aborting the transaction. The same override also makes `GET/PUT /groups/{id}/management/permissions` fail with 500 instead of operating on the v1 permission model. Either the listener/endpoints must be gated to the v1 implementation, or these methods must degrade gracefully (no-op/false) in v2.

Incorrect Javadoc on new GroupPermissionEvaluator methods

Two of the newly added Javadoc blocks are wrong: `requireManageMembers(GroupModel)` is documented as "Throws ForbiddenException if {@link #canManageMembership(GroupModel)} returns false" (it actually checks `canManageMembers`), and `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` documents "@return Stream of IDs of groups with view permission" although the method returns a `Set<String>`. Since these interfaces are the contract used by other modules (admin-ui-ext, services), the wrong text is likely to be copied into new implementations.

NPE when the "Groups" resource-type resource does not exist

When no per-group resource is found, the code falls back to `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` and immediately dereferences the result via `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` and later `resource.getScopes()`, without a null check. `getResourceTypeResource` returns `null` whenever the resource named "Groups" is absent for the admin-permissions client. This is reachable for any realm where admin permissions were enabled before this change: `AdminPermissionsSchema.init()` returns early when the admin permissions client already exists, and there is no migration that adds the newly introduced "Groups" resource/scopes to existing resource servers. Any group-related permission check in such a realm will then fail with a NullPointerException (HTTP 500) instead of simply denying access.

No negative test that a view-only group permission does not grant manage

`testViewGroups` creates an all-groups `VIEW` permission and only asserts that groups become visible. There is no assertion that this read-only permission does not allow write operations (creating a top-level group, updating a group, adding a child). Such an assertion would have caught that `GroupPermissionsV2.canManage()` returns `true` for the `view` scope, which currently lets a view-only admin create top-level groups. Similarly, no test exercises `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` (all-groups `view-members` permission combined with `GET /users` and `GET /users/count`), which is why the id/name mix-up in that method goes unnoticed.

getResourceName does not handle the new Groups resource type

`getResourceName` only special-cases `USERS` (returning "All users" or the username). For the newly added `Groups` resource type it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`, which is `null` for resources created by `getOrCreateResource` (they are created with name = group id and no display name). Admin API/console responses that list the resources of a group scope permission will therefore show `null`/empty instead of the group name or "All groups", unlike the Users resource type. The method needs a `GROUPS` branch resolving the group by id (and a name for the all-groups resource).

switch over resourceType throws NPE for a null resource type

The previous implementation used `USERS.getType().equals(resourceType)` chains, which tolerated a `null` `resourceType` and ended up throwing the descriptive `IllegalStateException("Could not map resource object ...")`. `switch (resourceType)` on a `String` throws `NullPointerException` when the argument is null, which surfaces as an opaque HTTP 500 for any caller that reaches `getOrCreateResource` without a resource type. Add an explicit null check that raises `ModelValidationException` (consistent with `throwExceptionIfResourceTypeOrScopesNotProvided`).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').
Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants

false_positives.candidate:
Anchor-mismatch message omits file and key, and the `key` parameter is unused

`messages.add("Didn't find anchor tag " + matcher.group() + " in original string")` gives no indication of which properties file or which message key failed, unlike the HTML message a few lines above which includes both. Since the plugin is run over hundreds of bundles, a failure produces an unactionable message. The method already receives `key` but never uses it; include `key` and `file` in the text (and reword "original string" to something like "in the English source value").

Byte-exact comparison against the sanitizer output rejects semantically identical HTML The check is `!Objects.equals(sanitized, value)`, i.e. the translation must match the sanitizer's *serialization* exactly, not just be free of disallowed markup. The OWASP sanitizer always emits void elements as `
`, so a perfectly safe `
` is flagged as "Illegal HTML" – which is why this PR has to rewrite `
` to `
` in ~20 translation files. Every future translation contribution (including machine/Weblate imports) that writes `
`, `
`, extra whitespace inside a tag, etc. will fail the build with a confusing "Illegal HTML" diff even though nothing unsafe is present. Consider comparing a canonicalized form of both sides (e.g. sanitize the value twice and compare the two sanitizer outputs) so only real policy violations are reported.

Diff trimming can throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException while building the error message

The two while-loops compute a common prefix length (`start`) and a common suffix length (`end`) independently, so `start + end` can exceed the length of the shorter string. Example: value `abb`, sanitized `ab` gives start=2 and end=2, and `value.substring(2, 3 - 2)` → `substring(2, 1)` throws `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` (the same happens on the `sanitized.substring(...)` call for value `aa`/sanitized `a`). This happens exactly when a violation has been detected, so instead of reporting the offending key the plugin aborts the build with an unrelated exception and the real problem is hidden. Clamp with e.g. `end = Math.min(end, Math.min(value.length(), sanitized.length()) - start)`.

Missing English counterpart aborts the build with a bare RuntimeException

The English reference bundle is derived purely by string surgery on the absolute path (`replaceAll("resources-community", "resources")` plus `replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")`). If the derived file does not exist – e.g. a community-only theme/message directory that has no counterpart under `resources`, a bundle whose file name does not follow the `_<locale>.properties` convention, or a future directory rename – the code throws an unchecked `RuntimeException("unable to read file ...")` from inside the `forEach`/verify path. That bypasses the `MojoExecutionException` contract of `verify()` and fails the whole build with a raw stack trace instead of a readable validation message. The missing-English case should either be skipped (treat as "no HTML allowed", as `getEnglishValue` already does for missing keys) or reported via `MojoExecutionException` with guidance.

No negative test and weakened assertions hide false positives The assertions were relaxed from `Matchers.contains` to `Matchers.hasItem`, so a test now passes even if the verifier emits additional, unexpected messages. Combined with the fact that there is no test asserting an *empty* result for a legitimate file (e.g. a `_de` bundle whose English source contains ``/`

`/`
` and whose translation uses the same allowed tags, or a bundle containing `{{0}}` placeholders and `{N,choice,...}` constructs), the suite cannot detect the false positives this checker is most likely to produce – which is exactly the risk that forced the large number of cosmetic edits in this PR. Add a test asserting `verify()` returns an empty list for a valid translation.

Property bundles are read as ISO-8859-1 while the files are UTF-8

`new PropertyResourceBundle(FileInputStream)` loads the file with `Properties.load(InputStream)`, which decodes ISO-8859-1, whereas `verifyNoDuplicateKeys` reads the same file with `Files.readString` (UTF-8). Keycloak theme message bundles are UTF-8, so every non-ASCII value is mojibake inside the sanitizer check and, more importantly, in the reported "Illegal HTML in key ..." messages, which makes failures for Arabic/Chinese/Cyrillic bundles very hard to read. Use `new PropertyResourceBundle(new InputStreamReader(fis, StandardCharsets.UTF_8))`.

i18next placeholders replaced with Java MessageFormat syntax breaks the account console message

`error-invalid-multivalued-size` was changed from `Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).` to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`. This bundle is consumed by the React account console through i18next, whose interpolation syntax is double braces (see every other entry in this file, e.g. `error-invalid-length-too-short='{{0}}' must have minimal length of {{1}}.`). With single braces none of the arguments are substituted and the ICU/MessageFormat choice construct is not supported by i18next either, so the user will literally see `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.` instead of the attribute name and the allowed bounds. If pluralization is desired here it has to be done with i18next plural keys (`_one`/`_other`), as already done for `resourceSharedWith_one`/`_other`.

i18next placeholders replaced with Java MessageFormat syntax breaks the admin console message

`error-invalid-multivalued-size` was changed to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`. The `maven-resources` admin bundle is loaded by the admin console via i18next, which only interpolates `{{...}}` placeholders and does not understand MessageFormat `choice` constructs. The rendered error will therefore show the raw format string instead of the attribute name and the min/max limits, making the validation error useless for the administrator. Only the server-side bundles (`themes/.../theme/base/*/messages/*`) are formatted with `java.text.MessageFormat` and may use single braces/choice.

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Null check for rawTokenId actually re-checks grantType

`Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");` validates `grantType` a second time instead of `rawTokenId`. As a result a `null` rawTokenId is accepted, and the failure only surfaces later as a token id literally ending in `":null"` produced by `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId()` (string concatenation of null), i.e. a corrupt `jti`, instead of failing fast at construction time with a clear message.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId() grant-shortcut check is inverted and reads the wrong characters

The new matcher is supposed to assert that the `jti` of an access token encodes the expected grant shortcut. Two defects make it a no-op:

1. The condition is inverted: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` fails the match when the shortcut *matches* instead of when it differs.
2. The offsets are wrong. The encoded prefix is `<sessionType:2><tokenType:2><grantType:2>`, so the grant shortcut is `substring(4, 6)`, not `substring(3, 5)`. `substring(3,5)` returns the second char of the token type plus the first char of the grant type (e.g. for `onrtac` it returns `"ta"`).

Because of (2) the comparison can never be true for any currently defined shortcut, so with (1) the method always falls through to the UUID check and never verifies the grant type at all. Every call site (`expectCodeToToken`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectAuthReqIdToToken`) therefore silently passes, leaving the main new behaviour of this PR untested. Fixing only the offsets without fixing the inversion would invert all those assertions and break the suite.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getShortcut() javadoc says 3 letters, but the decoder requires exactly 2

The javadoc states the shortcut is "usually like 3-letters shortcut of specific grants", while `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider` encodes/decodes a fixed 6-character prefix (2 chars session type + 2 chars token type + 2 chars grant type) and rejects anything else with `IllegalArgumentException("...Expected length of 6")`. A custom grant factory that follows the javadoc and returns a 3-character shortcut will produce token ids that this very provider cannot decode (and a 1-character shortcut would silently shift the grant type characters). Fix the javadoc to require exactly 2 characters and validate the length (and the absence of the `:` delimiter) in `postInit()` so misbehaving providers fail at boot rather than producing undecodable token ids.

true_positives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
testIncorrectGrantType passes on a NullPointerException, not on the intended validation error

The test sets up the factory by calling only `init(null)` and populating the maps directly; `postInit()` is never called, so `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.sessionFactory` stays `null`. Decoding `"ofrtac:5678"` misses the cache and `getGrantTypeByShortcut()` dereferences `sessionFactory`, throwing a `NullPointerException`. Since the test catches the broad `RuntimeException`, it passes for the wrong reason and never exercises the intended `IllegalArgumentException("...Unknown value 'ac' for grant type")` path. Assert on the concrete exception type and make the factory usable (or inject a session factory) so the real validation path is covered.

false_positives.candidate:
Format change of the access token `jti` is not documented / no upgrade note

Every access token's `id` (`jti` claim, and the `token_id` event detail) changes from a plain UUID to `<6-char-context>:<uuid>`. This is a client-visible contract change: integrations that store `jti` in a UUID column, parse it with `UUID.fromString()`, or assume a 36-char value will break after upgrade. The PR contains no documentation or upgrading/release-note entry describing the new format, its stability guarantees, or the fact that old (pre-upgrade) tokens still carry a bare UUID that decodes to `UNKNOWN`. Add the corresponding documentation/upgrade note before merging.

Lazy shortcut-map refresh bypasses duplicate-shortcut validation and can map a shortcut to the wrong grant

`postInit()` validates that no two grants share a shortcut (by comparing map sizes), but `getShortcutByGrantType()` and `getGrantTypeByShortcut()` later mutate the same maps at runtime for "newly deployed" grant types without re-running that validation. `getGrantTypeByShortcut()` simply takes `findFirst()` of all factories whose shortcut matches, and `getShortcutByGrantType()` unconditionally overwrites the `grantsByShortcuts` entry for that shortcut. If a newly registered grant collides with an existing shortcut, decoding a token id will silently resolve to the wrong grant type (and the reverse mapping becomes inconsistent) instead of being rejected.

New abstract SPI method breaks existing grant-type factories and can fail server startup

`getShortcut()` is added as a non-default abstract method to the `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` SPI interface. Existing third-party grant type factories no longer compile and, if deployed as an already-compiled jar, will fail with `AbstractMethodError` when `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit()` iterates all grant factories. The backing map lives only in the factory's memory, so after a server restart (or if the federated link survives removal from the map) `getMyUser()` returns null and any call going through `SubjectCredentialManager.getFederatedCredentialsStream()` – which is now on the login path via `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()` – fails with a NullPointerException instead of returning an empty stream.

`testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only sets the codes up and logs in once with code #0 (`enterRecoveryCodes(..., 0, recoveryKeys)`). Beyond the recovery codes needed for this PR, `getCredentials()` now also returns the stored OTP credential (and `updateCredential` assigns it a generated id). `configureBrowserFlowWithRecoveryAuthnCodes` adds a REQUIRED `delayed-authenticator` execution (with the config alias typo "delayed-suthenticator-config") to the copied browser flow, and the only call site passes `delay = 0`. The delay serves no purpose for this test while adding a hard dependency on an unrelated test-only authenticator provider: if `delayed-authenticator` is not deployed, flow creation/login in this test fails for reasons unrelated to recovery codes. Either drop the extra execution or explain/exercise the delay.

`RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE` was changed from 4 to 3 and 4 is reused for the new `FEATURE_DISABLED` result. Any consumer written against the previously released behaviour of the `update-compatibility check` command (automation/DevOps pipelines, as explicitly encouraged by the guide, and the Operator's auto-update logic that inspects the Job's exit code) will now mis-interpret results: a check that tested `exit == 4` for "recreate needed" will now trigger a downtime upgrade when the only problem is that the preview feature is not enabled, and will not recognise exit code 3 at all. The reverse mapping is just as harmful: code expecting 3 to be unused will now receive it for the common recreate case. Since both codes are swapped in the same release, consumers must be updated in lockstep (operator source is not touched in this PR) and the change should be called out in release notes / upgrade notes.

Omitting any configuration options will result in incomplete metadata") and can yield a wrong rolling/recreate verdict. Unlike every other place in this class (`canView(ClientModel)` falls back to `canManage(client)`, `canView(ClientScopeModel)` checks VIEW *or* MANAGE) and unlike V1 where the `manage-clients` role implies view, the global `manage` permission does not imply `canView()`. canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException on a runtime (non-admin) code path

The V1 implementation returned `false` when no resource server/permission existed; this override should do the same (or the caller must be made V2-aware).

The removal listener is now only executed when `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` (V1) is enabled, presumably because `ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled()` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. But `management()` (line 67) prefers `MgmtPermissionsV2` whenever `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` is enabled, and the two preview features are not mutually exclusive. When both are enabled, a `ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent` reaches `management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(cast.getClient(), false)`, which now throws `UnsupportedOperationException` and aborts the client deletion transaction (HTTP 500). The same applies to the `/clients/{id}/management/permissions` admin endpoints, which call `clients().isPermissionsEnabled()`/`getPermissions()` after the V1 feature check passes. The guard should select the V1 implementation explicitly (or V2 should no-op instead of throwing) for these legacy operations.

`init()` returns early when `realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() != null`, so realms where FGAP v2 was already enabled before this change never receive the newly added `Clients` resource nor the new scopes (`configure`, `map-roles-client-scope`, `map-roles-composite`). In such realms: creating a Clients permission reaches `getOrCreateResource()` and hits `throw new ModelException("No scopes found.")` (line 108) for the missing scopes, all-clients evaluation silently returns `false` because `resourceStore.findByName(server, "Clients", ...)` is null, and per-client evaluation NPEs on the null aggregate resource (ClientPermissionsV2 line 219). The PR adds no upgrade/migration step to create the missing scopes and resource for existing admin-permissions clients.

getResourceName has no handling for the Clients resource type

`getResourceName()` translates resource names to human-readable values only for the `Users` resource type ("All users" for the aggregate resource, the username for per-user resources) and otherwise returns `resource.getDisplayName()`. Per-client resources are created in `getOrCreateResource()` without a display name, and the aggregate `Clients` resource has none either, so every Clients permission exposed through the admin REST API/console will report a `null` resource name instead of the client id/clientId or an "All clients" label. The new resource type needs a branch here (resolving the client via `session.clients().getClientById()`), consistent with the Users handling.

resolveClient allows permissions to target the admin-permissions client itself

`resolveClient()` resolves any client in the realm, including the realm's own admin-permissions (FGAP policy) client and `realm-management`, even though the class already provides `throwExceptionIfAdminPermissionClient()` for exactly this kind of guard and it is not used here. As a result an administrator can create a Clients permission whose resource is the admin-permissions client and grant `manage`/`configure` on it; since the client authorization admin endpoints are gated on being able to manage the owning client, the grantee can then modify or delete all fine-grained admin permission policies — a privilege escalation out of the restricted scope they were given. Target clients that back the FGAP/admin infrastructure should be rejected when resolving the resource.

Javadoc for void require* methods says they return true

`requireView()` (line 98) and `requireViewClientScopes()` (line 103) are `void`, but the new Javadoc states "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}" / "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canViewClientScopes()} returns {@code true}". These should follow the convention used for the other require* methods in this file: "Throws ForbiddenException if ... returns {@code false}". As written the contract documented for implementors/callers is wrong.

New Clients scopes and all-clients fallback combinations are untested

The added tests cover `manage`, `configure`, `view`, `map-roles` and `map-roles-composite`, but there is no test for the newly introduced `map-roles-client-scope` scope (`canMapClientScopeRoles`), none for `getClientsWithPermission()` (which, as implemented, cannot return any client id), and none for the combination of an all-clients permission with an unrelated per-client permission — a case where `hasPermission(ClientModel, scope)` stops consulting the aggregate `Clients` resource as soon as a per-client resource exists, so a previously granted all-clients permission silently stops applying to that client. These are exactly the paths most likely to regress.

The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

`canManage()` evaluates `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)` - i.e. it returns `true` when the caller only has the `view` scope on the "all groups" resource (looks like a copy/paste from `canView()` two methods above). `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup` calls `auth.groups().requireManage()`, so an administrator who was granted only a read-only all-groups permission can create top-level groups. In the V2 implementation the authorization `Resource` created for a group uses the *group id as the resource name* (see `AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup`/`getOrCreateResource`), while `Resource#getId()` is the unrelated internal UUID of the authz resource. This method adds `groupResource.getId()` to the returned set and also passes `groupResource.getId()` into `hasPermission(String groupId, ...)`, which resolves the group via `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`.

1. `hasPermission` never finds the per-group resource for the id it is given, so it always falls through to the "all groups" resource-type resource - the per-group evaluation intended here does not happen.

The V1 implementation deliberately strips the resource-name prefix (`resource.getName().substring(RESOURCE_NAME_PREFIX.length())`) to produce group ids; V2 should use `groupResource.getName()`. `MgmtPermissionsV2` now overrides `groups()` to return `GroupPermissionsV2`, whose `setPermissionsEnabled(...)`/`isPermissionsEnabled(...)` throw `UnsupportedOperationException`. `AdminPermissions.registerListener` (registered whenever `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` is enabled) handles `GroupModel.GroupRemovedEvent` by calling `management(session, realm).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false)`, and `management(...)` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2` as soon as `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` is enabled. `hasPermission` only falls back to the "all groups" resource when no resource exists for the specific group. A per-group resource is created as soon as *any* group-scoped permission references that group (`AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource`). Because per-group resources are created without a resource type, type-based policy evaluation does not apply either. Result: once an admin creates, say, a `manage-membership` permission for group G, all broader all-groups permissions (e.g. `view`, `view-members`) stop applying to G, so an administrator who could previously view G loses that access as a side effect of an unrelated permission being created for G. The scopes granted at the resource-type level should be evaluated in addition to, not instead of, the group-specific resource.

`getResourceName` only special-cases `USERS` (returning "All users" or the username). For the newly added `Groups` resource type it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`, which is `null` for resources created by `getOrCreateResource` (they are created with name = group id and no display name). Admin API/console responses that list the resources of a group scope permission will therefore show `null`/empty instead of the group name or "All groups", unlike the Users resource type. The method needs a `GROUPS` branch resolving the group by id (and a name for the all-groups resource).

The previous implementation used `USERS.getType().equals(resourceType)` chains, which tolerated a `null` `resourceType` and ended up throwing the descriptive `IllegalStateException("Could not map resource object ...")`. `switch (resourceType)` on a `String` throws `NullPointerException` when the argument is null, which surfaces as an opaque HTTP 500 for any caller that reaches `getOrCreateResource` without a resource type. Add an explicit null check that raises `ModelValidationException` (consistent with `throwExceptionIfResourceTypeOrScopesNotProvided`).

Two of the newly added Javadoc blocks are wrong: `requireManageMembers(GroupModel)` is documented as "Throws ForbiddenException if {@link #canManageMembership(GroupModel)} returns false" (it actually checks `canManageMembers`), and `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` documents "@return Stream of IDs of groups with view permission" although the method returns a `Set<String>`. Since these interfaces are the contract used by other modules (admin-ui-ext, services), the wrong text is likely to be copied into new implementations.
