`testViewGroups` creates an all-groups `VIEW` permission and only asserts that groups become visible. There is no assertion that this read-only permission does not allow write operations (creating a top-level group, updating a group, adding a child). Such an assertion would have caught that `GroupPermissionsV2.canManage()` returns `true` for the `view` scope, which currently lets a view-only admin create top-level groups. Similarly, no test exercises `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` (all-groups `view-members` permission combined with `GET /users` and `GET /users/count`), which is why the id/name mix-up in that method goes unnoticed.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Indefinite-length encoding (-1 from readLength) is not handled by readInteger/readSequence

readLength() returns -1 for the indefinite-length form (0x80). readInteger() passes that value straight to read(length), which executes `new byte[-1]` and throws NegativeArraySizeException - an unchecked exception escaping a method that declares IOException, so callers that catch IOException will not handle it. readSequence() with a -1 length simply skips the while loop and returns an empty list, hiding the malformed input. Malformed or BER-encoded input (asn1derToConcatenatedRS is called with externally supplied bytes) should be rejected with a clear IOException instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() added as a non-default interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is a public SPI in keycloak-common. Adding the abstract method `int order();` is a source- and binary-incompatible change: any out-of-tree implementation (and, per the PR description, the authz-client copy maintained in the keycloak-client repository which compiles against a released keycloak-common) will no longer compile, and pre-compiled implementations will fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration sorts the providers. Declaring it as `default int order() { return 0; }` (or some neutral baseline) keeps compatibility while still allowing the new provider to lower/raise its precedence.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same problem: adding an abstract `order()` method to the `CryptoProvider` interface breaks backward compatibility for existing implementations.

false_positives.candidate:
Multiple crypto providers are now silently tolerated, with non-deterministic tie-breaking

detectProvider() no longer throws when more than one CryptoProvider is found on the classpath; it just sorts by order() and picks the first. All three in-tree providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider) return order() == 200, and Stream.sorted() is stable, so when two of them are on the classpath the selected provider is decided purely by ServiceLoader/classpath discovery order. The removed IllegalStateException was the guard that caught exactly this misconfiguration; now a deployment that accidentally has both the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider and the FIPS provider on the classpath can silently run non-FIPS crypto (or vice versa) with no error, and the behaviour can change between environments or build layouts. Either keep failing when two providers share the same order, or give the real providers distinct orders and log at WARN/ERROR when more than one is present.

logger.debugf() called with a dynamically built string as the format

`logger.debugf(builder.toString())` passes runtime-constructed text as the format string. If any ignored provider class name ever contains a '%' the formatter will throw or produce garbage, and static analysis/IDE format checks cannot validate it. Use `logger.debugf("%s", builder)` (or logger.debug(Object)). The message should also be built lazily (guarded by isDebugEnabled) and, given that silently ignoring a crypto provider used to be a fatal error, logged at WARN rather than DEBUG so misconfigured classpaths are visible. The message also ends with a dangling ", ".

integerToBytes silently truncates integers larger than the expected signature half-length

When `qLength < bytes.length` the method keeps only the low-order qLength bytes of the BigInteger, silently discarding high-order bytes. The BouncyCastle-based implementation this replaces uses BigIntegers.asUnsignedByteArray(len, value), which raises an error when the value does not fit. With this implementation a DER signature containing an r/s value wider than the algorithm's half-length (corrupt input, or a mismatch between the key curve and the declared ES* algorithm) is converted to a wrong concatenated R||S value instead of failing, which turns a detectable error into a silently invalid signature. It should throw IOException when the value does not fit in qLength bytes.

Test uses the default EC curve for ES384/ES512 and never validates the produced DER with a verifier

The key pair is generated once with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` using the JDK default curve (P-256 on current JDKs), so testES384/testES512 sign with a P-256 key while asserting against signature lengths 96/132. The round-trip assertion still passes because r/s are simply zero-padded, so the real P-384/P-521 r/s widths produced by concatenatedRSToASN1DER are never exercised. Additionally the test only asserts rsConcat == rsConcat2; it never feeds the DER output of concatenatedRSToASN1DER into Signature.verify(), which is the actual production use of that method (JWS signature verification), so an encoder that produces structurally parseable but non-DER output would not be caught. Generate keys with the curve matching each algorithm (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) and verify the re-encoded DER with a JCA Signature.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getSubGroupsCount() now returns null, which is not part of the GroupModel contract

`GroupAdapter.getSubGroupsCount()` returns `null` when the underlying group no longer exists. `GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount()` returns a boxed `Long` but no implementation (e.g. the JPA adapter) ever returns `null` and the interface documents no nullability, so callers are free to unbox or compare the result. Any such caller now gets a NullPointerException at the call site instead of here – i.e. the NPE is relocated rather than removed – and REST responses can silently carry `subGroupCount: null`. Prefer returning `0L` (or handling the removed-group case explicitly, e.g. by skipping the group) instead of leaking `null` through the model API.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same problem as the golden comment: `getSubGroupsCount()` returning `null` violates the `GroupModel` contract and will lead to NullPointerExceptions in callers expecting a non-null value.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined, so the regression test can pass while the NPE happens

`createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti` starts a background thread that repeatedly lists groups and records exceptions into `caughtExceptions`, but the main thread only sets `deletedAll = true` and immediately runs `assertThat(caughtExceptions, Matchers.empty())`. There is no `Thread.join()` (and no synchronization between setting the flag and the assertion), so an exception thrown by the very iteration that races with the last deletions – exactly the window this test is meant to cover – can be appended after the assertion has already run, making the test green even when the regression is present. In addition the thread is non-daemon and keeps issuing admin requests after the test method returns (until it observes the flag), which can produce errors/log noise or interfere with teardown of the managed realm and admin client. The thread reference should be kept and joined before asserting.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same concurrency problem: the background reader thread is not waited for (joined) after setting `deletedAll` to true and before asserting on `caughtExceptions`, causing a race condition where exceptions occurring near the end of the test can be missed.

false_positives.candidate:
Same concurrent-removal NPE still present in the getSubGroupsStream overloads

The fix only guards `getSubGroupsCount()` against `modelSupplier.get()` returning `null`. The three `getSubGroupsStream(...)` overloads (lines 256, 262 and 268) call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` with no null check, and `modelSupplier` resolves to `cacheSession.getGroupDelegate().getGroupById(realm, cached.getId())`, which returns `null` for a group removed by a concurrent transaction after the cache entry was obtained. Under the same race that motivated this PR (listing groups while groups are being deleted) those paths will still throw a NullPointerException, so the reported bug is only partially fixed for group tree/search endpoints.

populateGroupHierarchyFromSubGroups still dereferences a possibly-removed parent group

In `populateGroupHierarchyFromSubGroups`, `session.groups().getGroupById(realm, currGroup.getParentId())` can return `null` when the parent group is deleted concurrently with the listing request. `parentModel` is then passed to `groupEvaluator.canView(parentModel)` (line 51), to `toRepresentation(groupEvaluator, parentModel, full)` (line 57) and to `populateSubGroupCount(parentModel, parent)` (line 60) without any null check, producing a NullPointerException on exactly the concurrent read/delete path this PR aims to fix (and unconditionally when fine-grained admin permissions are enabled, since the `canView` block is skipped). A null `parentModel` should abort the walk for that branch (e.g. remove the current group from the map and break), analogous to the existing not-viewable handling.

Shared admin client used from two threads may yield spurious failures

The background reader calls `managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(...)` while the main thread performs deletes through the same injected `Keycloak` admin client. The admin client's token manager/JAX-RS proxy is not documented as thread-safe; concurrent token refresh from two threads can produce intermittent 401/`NotAuthorizedException`, which this test would record in `caughtExceptions` and report as a failure of the group-listing code. Using a separate admin client instance (or at least a dedicated token) for the reader thread would avoid attributing client-side races to the server fix being tested.

Tight busy loop issuing unbounded group queries

The reader thread loops with no pause, each iteration requesting `groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true)`. This saturates a CPU and floods the server with full-table group listings for the whole duration of the 100 deletions, slowing the test suite and making timing-sensitive neighbouring tests more flaky. A small sleep between iterations (and a bounded `maxResults`) would keep the race window without the load.

Created groups are not registered for cleanup

The 100 groups created in `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti` are only removed by the explicit delete loop; nothing is registered with `managedRealm.cleanup()`. If any `remove()` call or an earlier assertion fails, the remaining `Test Group N` entries stay in the realm, which is shared by all other test methods in this class, so a single failure here can cascade into unrelated failures in group-listing tests.

true_positives.matched_candidate:

true_positives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. true_positives.matched_candidate:
isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, disabling passkeys on the normal login page

`isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` returns true only when `user != null`. Both call sites use it to decide whether to call `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)`: `authenticate()` (line 115) and the error `challenge(context, error, field)` override (line 137). Before this change the condition was exactly the opposite (`context.getUser() == null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()`), i.e. the webauthn/conditional-UI data was filled when the user had not yet been identified. `fillContextForm` is what sets the challenge auth note and the `enableWebAuthnConditionalUI`/challenge/rpId form attributes that the login template needs to render the `webauth` form and start conditional mediation. With the new condition, a first-time visitor (user == null) no longer gets any of that, so the primary ID-less passkey login (auto-login with a discoverable key, 'Sign in with passkey' link, passkey autofill on the username/password page) is silently removed, and the same happens on the error re-render after a bad username/password. Existing tests in all three Passkeys* test classes assert the presence of `//form[@id='webauth']` on the initial login page and auto-login with a discoverable key, so they will fail. true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` requiring `user != null` prevents `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` from being called on the initial login page where the user is null, breaking ID-less / conditional passkey login for unidentified users.

false_positives.candidate:
Overriding shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators() to false removes the 'user has no passkey' guard during re-authentication

`WebAuthnAuthenticator.fillContextForm()` used the `user != null` branch not only to publish `ALLOWED_AUTHENTICATORS`, but also to bail out (`return null`) when the identified user has no credential of the relevant type. By overriding `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators()` to always return `false` in the conditional-UI authenticator, that branch is never taken, so during re-authentication (where the user is already known) the passkey/conditional-UI markup is now injected unconditionally for every user in a passkeys-enabled realm, including users that have no passwordless WebAuthn credential at all. Combined with the `UsernameForm` change (which no longer skips the username form during re-authentication when passkeys are enabled), such users get an extra, useless screen with a passkey prompt, and any passkey they pick from the platform list that belongs to another account ends in a WEBAUTHN_ERROR_DIFFERENT_USER error page. A check that the already-identified user actually has the passwordless credential configured is needed before enabling the conditional UI.

reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey does not test a user without a passkey

The test name and the inline comment at line 304 ('Passkeys login should not be available on the page as this user does not have passkey') claim it covers re-authentication of a user that has no passkey, but the test sets `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE)`, i.e. passkeys are disabled for the whole realm. The absence of the `webauth` form therefore proves nothing about per-user credentials. The actually interesting (and currently unverified) scenario introduced by this PR - passkeys enabled for the realm, user already identified for re-authentication but owning no passwordless WebAuthn credential - remains untested, which is exactly the path where the conditional UI is now shown unnecessarily. Either rename/retarget this test or add a second test with passkeys enabled and a user without a passkey credential.

Overly broad try/catch(Exception) used to assert element absence

The blocks at lines 291-296 and 312-317 call `driver.findElement(...)` inside `try { ...; fail(...); } catch (Exception nsee) { /* expected */ }`. Catching `Exception` swallows any WebDriver failure (e.g. TimeoutException, StaleElementReferenceException, WebDriverException from a broken page), so the assertion can pass for a completely unrelated reason and hide a real regression. The rest of the suite uses `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, () -> driver.findElement(...))`; use that here so only the expected exception type satisfies the assertion.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

Line 15 does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, so the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` on line 62 ("Give flusher threads time to process after drift change") does nothing at all. The comment is misleading and the test still relies entirely on `step.join()` busy-looping for the flusher thread to produce the message, so it remains timing-dependent. true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unhealthy flusher process is never killed before being restarted

`_ensure_processes_alive` now guards the kill with `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. The processes are created via `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, i.e. `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`, which derives from `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` and is *not* a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process` (`multiprocessing.context.Process`). The isinstance check is therefore always False, so `process.kill()` is never executed — the previous code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. Consequence: when a flusher is detected as hung (`cause == "hang"`, process still alive but `healthy_since` stale), the old process keeps running while `_create_process_for_shards` spawns a second process for the same shards. Two processes then flush the same Redis shards concurrently, which can produce duplicate/partial segments to the buffered-segments topic, and up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS+1 processes can accumulate per shard group. Use `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` (or check for `threading.Thread` instead) in the guard.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: processes created with `multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process` are instances of `SpawnProcess`, which is not a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process`, causing the `isinstance` check to always return False and preventing hung processes from being killed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() skips termination of remaining processes once the deadline expires

In `join`, the loop over `self.processes.items()` does `if remaining_time <= 0: break` before waiting on each process. If the first process consumes the whole timeout budget, every remaining process is skipped entirely — it is neither waited for nor terminated. Combined with the `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` check at the end of the loop (always False for spawn-context `SpawnProcess`, see the kill() issue), `terminate()` is effectively never called on any flusher process, so hung flusher processes can outlive the shutdown/rebalance path. `remaining_time` is also computed and then unused except for the comparison. Consider terminating all processes after the wait loop regardless of which ones timed out, and fixing the isinstance check.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue directly identifies the same problem as the golden comment: breaking out of the loop when the deadline expires (`remaining_time <= 0: break`) skips terminating the remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown.

false_positives.candidate:
Per-segment metric now tagged with a high-cardinality shard-list tag

`spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` is emitted for every flushed segment and is now tagged with `shard=shard_tag`, where `shard_tag` is the comma-joined list of all shards handled by that process (e.g. `"0,3,6,9"` or, with the default `--flusher-processes 1`, the full assigned-partition list). That tag value changes on every Kafka rebalance and differs per consumer instance, so this high-volume metric gains an effectively unbounded set of tag values. The same tag is added to the `spans.buffer.flusher.produce`/`wait_produce` timers and to `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy`. This risks cardinality blowup/cost in the metrics backend; consider emitting a per-shard tag only where the value is a single bounded shard id, or dropping the tag from the per-segment metric.

Class docstring claims one process per shard, which is not what the code does

The docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing." In practice the number of processes is `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` and shards are round-robined onto processes, and the CLI default for `--flusher-processes` is 1, so the default behaviour is a single process handling all shards. The new `max_processes` parameter is also undocumented while the docstring still documents a non-existent `topic` parameter. This misleads operators about the default behaviour.

Dead method _create_process_for_shard

`_create_process_for_shard(shard)` is not called anywhere after the refactor (`_ensure_processes_alive` calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly). It duplicates restart logic and will silently drift out of sync; remove it or wire it up.

--flusher-processes 0 silently means "one process per shard"

`self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats 0 as falsy, so passing `--flusher-processes 0` (or any code path passing 0) results in one process per assigned shard rather than an error or a single process. The click option has no range validation. Use an explicit `if max_processes is None` and/or validate `>= 1` in the click option.

Redis memory info is now queried once per flusher buffer on every submit

`submit` previously called `self.buffer.get_memory_info()` once; it now iterates `self.buffers.values()` and calls `get_memory_info()` on each of the N per-process buffers (plus `record_stored_segments()` on each). Since each `SpansBuffer` holds its own client, these calls duplicate the Redis INFO round trips N times per submitted message batch when `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage < 1.0`, scaling with `--flusher-processes`. If a given Redis node is reported by more than one buffer, both `used` and `available` are also counted multiple times. Consider keeping a single buffer in the parent for memory/stat reporting.

New multiprocess flusher test only asserts bookkeeping, not behaviour

`test_flusher_processes_limit` submits no messages and only asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `max_processes`, `num_processes` and that the shard map totals 4. It does not assert that shards are partitioned without overlap (e.g. `{0,1,2,3}` exactly once across `process_to_shards_map`), nor that segments from all 4 shards are actually flushed/produced when more than one process is used. The core risk of this PR — multiple flushers each owning a disjoint shard subset and producing all segments exactly once — is untested. There is also no test for the unhealthy-process restart path that this PR rewrote.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes nodestore preserves input ordering

`fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids`, calls `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` (which returns a dict keyed by node id), and then pairs them positionally with `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. The result is `ErrorEvent.id` being attached to the wrong error's title/message/timestamp, so the summary sent to Seer references incorrect event ids. Iterate `node_ids` and look up `events.get(node_id)` per id instead.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Analytics event recorded before the feature check and request validation

`analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` is the first statement in `post()`, so it fires even when the organization lacks `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` (404 response) or when the body fails schema validation (400 response). The resulting metric therefore counts rejected calls as assemble attempts. Move the `analytics.record` call after the feature/validation gates (or after the task is queued) so it reflects actual assembles.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify that the analytics event is recorded before the feature flag check, which causes analytics to be logged even when the feature is disabled and the request returns a 404, leading to inaccurate metrics.

false_positives.candidate:
Error/breadcrumb merge compares timestamps in different units

`gen_request_data` interleaves errors and replay events with `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)`. Error timestamps come from the nodestore event payload and are epoch *seconds* (e.g. 1718900000.0), while rrweb replay event `timestamp` values are epoch *milliseconds* (e.g. 1718900000000). With real data every error timestamp is ~1000x smaller than every breadcrumb timestamp, so all errors are emitted before all breadcrumbs regardless of when they actually occurred, defeating the purpose of the chronological merge (and the log text prints raw, mismatched numbers). Normalise both to the same unit before comparing. The new unit test passes only because it uses hand-written second-scale event timestamps.

React Query key no longer includes the organization

The hook was switched from `useApiQuery([path, options])` (where `path` contained `/organizations/${organization.slug}/...`) to `useQuery({queryKey: ['use-trace-item-attribute-keys', queryOptions]})`, and `makeTraceItemAttributeKeysQueryOptions` only contains itemType, attributeType, project ids and the datetime range. When the project selection is "all projects" (`projects: []`), two different organizations produce an identical cache key, so attribute keys fetched for one org can be served from cache to another org. Add the organization slug (and ideally the endpoint path) to the query key.

60s processing deadline is likely too short for a 100-identity chunk

`check_auth_identities` is scheduled by `check_auth` with `chunk_size=100` and sequentially calls `check_single_auth_identity` for each id; each call does a DB read, an RPC membership check and `provider.refresh_identity()`, which performs an external IdP request. A 60s `processing_deadline_duration` gives ~0.6s per identity. If the deadline is hit, the task is killed mid-chunk and (a) the remaining identities were already stamped with `last_synced=now` in `check_auth`, so they will not be re-selected for roughly another AUTH_CHECK_INTERVAL, and (b) the trailing `check_auth.apply_async(...)` that chains the next chunk never runs, stalling the whole sweep. Either raise the deadline substantially or reduce the chunk size.

Both saved-search conversion migrations turned into no-ops pointing at a migration not in this change

`0917_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views` and `0920_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_revised` both have their `RunPython` bodies replaced with `return` and a comment saying "See 0921_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_rerevised.py for the correct migration". No such migration is added in this PR, and the only test covering the conversion (`tests/sentry/migrations/test_0917_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views.py`) is deleted. If 0921 does not exist, organization-visibility `SavedSearch` rows are never converted into `GroupSearchView` rows anywhere, and the codebase is left with two dead migrations whose comments reference a nonexistent file plus zero test coverage for the conversion logic.

One invalid report rejects the entire browser report batch

The loop validates each report and returns `422` for the whole request as soon as any single report fails validation, so all other valid reports in the same batch are dropped. Browsers send Reporting API payloads as batches and will retry the whole batch, meaning a single persistently malformed/unsupported report (e.g. a `type` not in `BROWSER_REPORT_TYPES`, or a `url` the `URLField` regex rejects) permanently blocks metrics for every other report delivered with it. Prefer skipping/counting the invalid entries (with a metric or log) and returning 200 for the rest.

get_environment_info issues a per-issue recommended-event lookup while building PR comments

`get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` for every issue included in a merged-PR comment. That helper runs a search/Snuba query plus a nodestore fetch per group, so building one comment now performs up to 5 extra event lookups (per PR, for both GitHub and GitLab comment workflows) purely to render an environment name. Consider resolving environments with a single cheap query (e.g. GroupEnvironment) instead of fetching recommended events, and note that the broad `except Exception` silently degrades to no environment on any failure.

Issue titles are interpolated into a markdown link without escaping

`MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE = "* \u203c\ufe0f [**{title}**]({url}){environment}\n"` now puts the (truncated) issue title inside markdown link text, whereas the previous template only bolded it. Issue titles frequently contain `[` / `]` (e.g. `KeyError: 'items[0]'`), which terminates the link text early and renders a broken link/raw brackets in the PR comment. Escape `[`, `]` (and backslashes) in the title before formatting.

Custom cell renderers returning falsy React nodes are silently overridden

Both `renderDefaultHeadCell` and `renderDefaultBodyCell` do `const cell = render...(...); if (cell) return cell;`. The documented contract (see tableWidgetVisualization.stories.tsx and the prop JSDoc) is that only `undefined` falls through to the default renderer, but `null`, `''` and `0` are valid React nodes meaning "render this" and will instead be replaced by the default rendering. Check `cell !== undefined` so a custom renderer can intentionally render nothing.

Dead _handle_regex_match helper left in parametrize_w_experiments

After removing `ParameterizationRegexExperiment`, the experiment loop always calls `experiment.run(content, _incr_counter)`, but the inner `_handle_regex_match` closure (lines 335-343) is still defined and is now unreachable dead code duplicating the helper in `parametrize_w_regex`. Remove it to avoid confusion about which callback experiments use.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative queryset slicing raises ValueError; the "Django handles it" comment is wrong

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset` (and often a negative `stop`, since `stop = start_offset + limit + extra`). Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly rejects negative start/stop values with `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`; there is no SQL equivalent of a negative OFFSET. So the inline comment "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually false, and any request carrying a cursor with a negative offset on this path returns an unhandled 500. Since cursor strings are fully client-controlled (`Cursor.from_string` accepts negative offsets), this is a trivially reachable error/DoS vector. The whole negative-offset branch should be removed, or negative offsets rejected with `BadPaginationError`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator attempts to use negative slice offsets on a Django queryset, which Django does not support (resulting in an exception). The minor difference in the specific exception type (AssertionError vs ValueError, which changed across Django versions) does not detract from the exact match of the core issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`organization_context.member` can be None, causing AttributeError on every request

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated unconditionally for every GET, before the `use_optimized` check. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `None` whenever the caller is not an organization member — e.g. requests authenticated with an org-level/integration token (where `request.user` is an AnonymousUser and `is_superuser` is False), or a staff/superuser-less service account. In those cases the short-circuit does not fire and `None.has_global_access` raises `AttributeError`, turning a previously working audit-log listing into an unhandled 500. Guard with `organization_context.member and organization_context.member.has_global_access`, and only compute the flag when `use_optimized` is true.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: accessing `organization_context.member.has_global_access` without checking if `organization_context.member` is `None` (which happens when requests are authenticated with org-level/API tokens), leading to an AttributeError crash.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle datetime sort keys, which is what the audit-log endpoint uses

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(getattr(item, self.key)))` and `value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unchanged — i.e. it copies `Paginator`'s numeric-key semantics. The only caller, `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`, instantiates it with `order_by="-datetime"` on `AuditLogEntry`, whose `datetime` field is a `datetime` object: `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`. Even if the first page somehow succeeded, `value_from_cursor` would hand an integer to `build_queryset`, which injects it into `WHERE "datetime" <= %s` against a timestamp column, producing a database error. The optimized path therefore fails for every request that reaches it; it needs `DateTimePaginator`-style key/value conversion (or should subclass `DateTimePaginator`).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: `get_item_key` uses `math.floor` assuming a numeric key, while the audit logs endpoint uses it with `order_by='-datetime'`, causing a `TypeError` when called on a `datetime` object.

false_positives.candidate:
Authorization gate does not restrict the feature to administrators

The comment says the new pagination path is for "authorized administrators", but the check is `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. Two problems: (1) `request.user.is_superuser` is the raw DB flag; Sentry requires `is_active_superuser(request)` (or the staff equivalent) so that superuser powers only apply within an elevated/validated superuser session — using the raw flag bypasses that elevation requirement; (2) `member.has_global_access` is not an admin signal at all: it is true for ordinary members in organizations with open membership / global access, so essentially any regular org member can turn on the "admin-only" code path by appending `?optimized_pagination=true`. The gate should use an explicit permission/scope check.

Cursors are not interchangeable between the two paginators selected by a query param

The endpoint switches between `DateTimePaginator` (cursor value = epoch milliseconds) and `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (cursor value = floor/ceil of the raw sort value) based on the client-supplied `optimized_pagination` flag. A cursor minted by one paginator is meaningless to the other, so a client that follows a `Link` header while the flag changes (or that caches cursors) will get wrong pages, skipped/duplicated rows, or a query error. Pagination state must not depend on a mutable request flag; pick one cursor encoding or namespace the cursors.

BasePaginator silently clamps negative forward offsets, changing behavior for every paginated endpoint

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes the shared `BasePaginator.get_result` used by most paginated Sentry endpoints: a forward cursor with a negative offset, which previously surfaced as an error from Django slicing, now silently returns the first page's rows. That masks malformed/tampered cursors and can produce duplicated results across pages. Note also that the clamp is deliberately not applied when `cursor.is_prev`, so the previous-page path still crashes with `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` — the stated justification ("the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions") is incorrect. Invalid offsets should raise `BadPaginationError` consistently for both directions.

No tests for the new paginator or the new endpoint branch

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` (including its negative-offset branch) and the new `optimized_pagination` branch in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` ship with no tests, and the behavior change in `BasePaginator.get_result` (offset clamping) is likewise untested. Basic tests would have caught the `math.floor(datetime)` TypeError, the negative-slice `ValueError`, and the `organization_context.member is None` AttributeError. Add paginator unit tests for negative/zero/positive offsets plus endpoint tests covering member, non-member-token and superuser callers.

Comment documents a non-existent feature of Cursor

The added comment claims "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios", but no code changed here — `int(offset)` has always accepted any integer and nothing validates or makes use of negative offsets. The comment asserts that negative offsets are a supported, intentional capability, which is false: every consumer eventually feeds the offset into a Django queryset slice, which rejects negative values. This will mislead future readers into producing negative-offset cursors. Remove the comment or, better, add explicit validation that rejects negative offsets.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dropping the BuildIndex-wide lock allows concurrent duplicate builds of the same key

The write lock that previously covered the whole of `BuildIndex` is now only taken around the cache assignment. `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` does a lock-free `GetIndex` followed by `build`, so two concurrent requests (or a watch event plus a search) for the same NamespacedResource can now execute `BuildIndex` for the same key at the same time. Consequences: (a) for file-backed indexes both goroutines call `bleve.New` on the identical directory `Root/namespace/resource.group`, which at best fails with ErrorIndexPathExists and at worst leaves two writers on the same on-disk index; (b) both perform a full re-list/re-index of the resource (wasted DB and CPU work); (c) the loser's index object silently overwritten in the cache is never closed, leaking its file handles/memory, while callers that already got the old handle keep searching a discarded index. Finer-grained locking is fine, but it needs to be per-key (e.g. a per-key build mutex or singleflight) rather than removed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same race condition: narrowing the scope of the lock in `BuildIndex` to only cover the final cache assignment allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same index for the same key.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs reads b.cache without holding cacheMu — concurrent map read/write panic

`TotalDocs()` iterates `b.cache` with no lock, while `BuildIndex` now writes the map (line 138) outside any long-held lock, from the N concurrent index-build workers and from lazy builds triggered by search/watch events. A concurrent map read and map write is a fatal runtime panic in Go (not just a benign race), taking down the process. This path is newly exercised by the `s.search.TotalDocs()` call added in search.go:216 and by any metric/diagnostic caller. Take `cacheMu.RLock()` in `TotalDocs` (and avoid holding it while calling `index.DocCount()` if that is expensive, e.g. snapshot the slice of indexes first).
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same concurrency bug: `TotalDocs()` iterates over `b.cache` without synchronization/locks while `BuildIndex` (triggered by watch events or workers) writes to it concurrently, resulting in a concurrent map read/write panic when `s.search.TotalDocs()` is called.

false_positives.candidate:
Index/lifecycle init failure now aborts server construction (and therefore process startup)

`NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` and returns the error. Previously initialization was lazy, so a failure only broke the individual gRPC call that triggered it. Now any failure in `lifecycle.Init`, `search.init` (which lists all resource stats and builds every index), or `initWatcher` makes the constructor fail, which propagates up through DI and prevents the storage server / Grafana from starting at all. This is a real, reachable scenario: for file-backed bleve indexes `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` (pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:98) returns `ErrorIndexPathExists` when the directory from a previous run is still on disk (the code itself has a TODO about not yet checking the persisted RV), and transient DB errors during `GetResourceStats` have the same effect. Startup also now blocks for the full duration of indexing all namespaces. Consider keeping init asynchronous/retryable, or at least making index build failures non-fatal.

cancel() is not called when Init fails in NewResourceServer, leaking goroutines

The cancelable context created at line 229 is only cancelled via `server.Stop`. On the new error path (`err := s.Init(ctx); if err != nil { return nil, err }`), the constructor returns without calling `cancel()`, so the context (and anything already started under it) is leaked. This matters because `search.init` may already have called `storage.WatchWriteEvents` and started the SQL poller/event-handling goroutines before the error occurred; nothing will ever stop them, and the caller has no handle to the server to call `Stop`. Call `cancel()` (and ideally `lifecycle.Stop`) before returning the error.

Removing per-request Init() checks makes the shutdown guard dead code

`Stop` sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping" / "service is stopped", which used to be surfaced to clients because every handler started with `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil { return nil, err }`. All of those checks were removed in this diff, so no handler ever reads `initErr` again. After `Stop()` has cancelled the background context and the backend lifecycle has shut down, Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search now proceed into a stopped backend instead of returning a clear "service is stopping" error, producing confusing driver-level errors (or worse, work against a closed DB). Either keep a lightweight state check in the handlers or remove the now-misleading `initErr` assignments in `Stop`.

Data race on shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` in searchSupport.init

Inside `group.Go(...)` the closure writes the function-scoped `err` variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increments `totalBatchesIndexed++`. With `group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers)` these closures run concurrently, so both are unsynchronized writes from multiple goroutines: a genuine data race (the race detector will flag it), an undercounted `namespaced_indexed` span attribute, and — worse — error misattribution: one goroutine can overwrite `err` with `nil` before another returns it (swallowing a build failure) or a goroutine can return an error produced by a different build. Since init failure now aborts server startup (server.go:258), a spuriously propagated error can block the whole process. Use a local `err :=` inside the closure and an atomic/counter for the batch count.

BuildIndex still discards the span context, so the indexing work is not under its span

This PR's stated goal includes fixing trace propagation (`ctx, span := ...` in search.go and sql/backend.go), but `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` still uses `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` and never passes the derived context anywhere. The `builder(idx)` callback executed at line 126 captures the caller's context instead, so all the list/iterate/document-build spans produced during the actual indexing attach to the parent `unified_search.Build` span rather than to `unified_search.bleve.BuildIndex`, leaving BuildIndex as an empty leaf span and making it impossible to attribute index build time in traces.

Storage-server integration test silently disabled for postgres in CI

The only integration test that boots the `StorageServer` module target is now skipped for postgres with the comment "test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally." This PR moves unified storage initialization (index build, watcher start) into `NewResourceServer`, i.e. into module startup — exactly the code path this test exercises — so disabling it removes CI coverage of the change for one of the supported databases and hides whatever failure prompted the skip (it may well be caused by this PR's startup-blocking init rather than by Drone). The root cause should be identified before the skip is merged, or the skip should link to a tracking issue with the observed failure.

false_positives.candidate:
Stale TODO comment about stateful detectors

true_positives.matched_candidate:

`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a dataclass default, which Python evaluates a single time when the class body executes (i.e. at module import). Every `AssignmentSource` created for the lifetime of the process therefore carries the process-start timestamp rather than the time the assignment was queued, making the field useless for debugging/ordering and misleading to anyone who later relies on it (e.g. to expire stale sources). true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource round-trip through Celery kwargs corrupts the `queued` type and silently drops the source on any mismatch

`to_dict()` (via `asdict`) emits a raw `datetime` for `queued`, and that dict is passed as a Celery task kwarg in `sync_group_assignee_outbound`. With the JSON task serializer the datetime is encoded as an ISO string and is never decoded back, so `from_dict` reconstructs an instance whose `queued` field is a `str` even though it is annotated `datetime` (and with a stricter serializer the publish would fail outright, breaking assignee sync). `from_dict` performs no type validation and only catches `ValueError`/`TypeError`, returning `None` without logging, which means any future schema drift (renamed/extra key) silently yields no assignment source and re-enables the sync loop this PR is meant to fix. false_positives.candidate:
Abstract `sync_assignee_outbound` was not updated for the new `assignment_source` kwarg that the task now passes

`assignment_source` added to abstract `sync_status_outbound` but never passed or implemented

The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature gains `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None` before `**kwargs`, yet no call site (e.g. `sentry/integrations/tasks/sync_status_outbound.py`) passes it and no concrete integration implementation declares it. `assert result.get("queued") is not None` always passes because `queued` has a class-level default, so the test gives no coverage of the timestamp actually reflecting when the source was created, nor of the dict surviving a serialize/deserialize cycle (`to_dict()` -> Celery JSON -> `from_dict()`), which is the path that actually breaks the loop. false_positives.candidate:
Queue pool is destroyed on strategy close, so the consumer silently drops every message after a rebalance

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` (and `terminate()`/`join()`) calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `worker.shutdown = True` and calls `queue.shutdown()` on every queue. The `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` (result_consumer.py:133) and reused for every `create_with_partitions()` call. Arroyo invokes `close()`/`join()` on the strategy whenever partitions are revoked and then builds a new strategy on the next assignment. After the first rebalance the factory hands the new strategy the already-shut-down pool: the worker threads are dead and `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`, which is swallowed by the broad `except Exception` in `submit()` (line 317) where the offset is then marked complete and committed. The result is that every subsequent message is committed without ever being processed – permanent, silent data loss after any rebalance or partition reassignment. The pool (and its workers) needs to be created per assignment, or `close()` must not destroy state owned by the factory.

OffsetTracker state is never reset between partition assignments

The `FixedQueuePool` (and therefore its single `OffsetTracker`) is created once per factory and shared across all `create_with_partitions()` calls. `OffsetTracker.last_committed` and `all_offsets` therefore survive partition revocation. If a partition is revoked and later reassigned at a lower offset (offset reset, another consumer having made less progress, topic re-creation), `get_committable_offsets()` computes `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` and only reports an offset when `highest_committable > last_committed`, so no offset for that partition will ever be committed again and the consumer group silently stops advancing. In-flight work items belonging to the previous assignment also remain tracked and can be committed by the new strategy for partitions the consumer no longer owns.

Offsets are committed from a background thread, outside arroyo's single-threaded strategy contract

`_commit_loop` runs in its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is arroyo's `commit` callable wired to `StreamProcessor`/`KafkaConsumer`. Arroyo strategies are only ever called from the main consumer thread, and `KafkaConsumer.stage_offsets`/`commit_offsets` mutate consumer state (staged offsets, assignment/state checks) without locking. Committing from this thread races with `poll()`/rebalance callbacks on the main thread and can stage offsets for partitions that were just revoked, which arroyo rejects with `ConsumerError`, or corrupt the staged-offset bookkeeping. The exception is merely logged by the loop's `except Exception`, so the failure is invisible while offsets stop advancing.

Failed work items have their offsets committed, contradicting the documented at-least-once guarantee

In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, any exception raised by `result_processor` is logged and the `finally` block still calls `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)`, so the offset becomes committable. The same happens in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` (lines 317-325) when `grouping_fn` or the queue put fails. This makes processing at-most-once: a transient failure (DB blip, timeout) permanently drops the message, while the class docstring claims "No item is lost" and "Only commits offsets after successful processing". Either failures must block the commit / be routed to a DLQ, or the documented guarantee must be corrected.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and memory can grow without limit

`queue.Queue()` is created with the default `maxsize=0` (unbounded) and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`, so arroyo will keep feeding messages as fast as it can poll regardless of how far behind the workers are. The docstring of `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", which cannot happen. Each queued `WorkItem` additionally retains the full `Message[KafkaPayload]` (field `message`, never read anywhere), so a slow group pins both the decoded result and the raw Kafka payload in memory, and a backlogged consumer will OOM instead of applying backpressure.

Shutdown sets the worker stop flag before queue.shutdown(immediate=False), so queued items are discarded instead of drained

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` first sets `worker.shutdown = True` for every worker and only then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Because the worker loop is `while not self.shutdown:`, each worker exits right after finishing the item it currently holds, so the "non-immediate" shutdown that is supposed to let queued items drain has no effect and all pending items are dropped. Combined with `close()` joining the commit thread before the pool shuts down, the final set of completed offsets may also never be committed, so a normal restart re-reads and re-processes more messages than necessary.

Worker threads can block forever on queue.get(); shutdown failures are swallowed and leak threads

`OrderedQueueWorker.run` uses a blocking `self.work_queue.get()` with no timeout, so the `self.shutdown` flag is only observed after an item arrives. Termination relies entirely on `queue.Queue.shutdown()` succeeding, but `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` wraps that call in `except Exception: logger.exception(...)` (line 239). If it raises for any reason (e.g. the method is unavailable on the running Python version), every idle worker stays blocked in `get()`, `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` is executed sequentially for each worker, and shutdown stalls for 5s × num_queues (100s with the default of 20) before leaking the threads. Using `get(timeout=...)` would make the stop flag effective.

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts behaviour the implementation does not provide

The test makes the result processor raise and then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that a processing error prevents the offset from being committed. The implementation does the opposite: `OrderedQueueWorker.run` completes the offset in its `finally` block even when processing raises, so offsets 100 and 101 become committable. The assertion only holds because the polling loop breaks within ~0.3s while the commit thread ticks once per second; if the commit tick lands first the test fails. This test is both flaky and encodes a guarantee that does not exist – it should assert the real behaviour (or the behaviour should be fixed).

Commit assertions race with the 1-second commit loop and will flake

`test_offset_committing` and `test_handles_invalid_messages` wait for the first `commit_event` and then assert an exact final offset (104, resp. 101). The commit thread runs independently every second and commits whatever contiguous prefix is complete at that moment, so a tick that happens after only some offsets have been processed sets `commit_event` with a lower offset (e.g. 100 or 102); the subsequent `commit_event.wait()` returns immediately because the event is never cleared again and the equality assertion fails. The tests should poll until the expected offset is observed (or clear/re-wait) instead of asserting on the first commit.

FilteredPayload messages are handled through the exception path, producing an error log per message

`decode_payload` in the result consumer starts with `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)`, which is outside its own try/except, so for every filtered message the `AssertionError` propagates into `submit()`'s broad `except Exception` and is reported via `logger.exception("Error submitting message to queue")`. Filtered payloads are a normal part of arroyo pipelines (e.g. when the stale-message DLQ wrapper is enabled), so this turns routine filtering into a flood of error-level exceptions with stack traces and relies on exceptions for ordinary control flow. `submit()` should check for `FilteredPayload` explicitly and complete the offset without logging.

A gauge is emitted for every processed item on the hot path

`OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `metrics.gauge("remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth", ...)` in the `finally` block of every single work item, with only an `identifier` tag so all 20 workers overwrite the same series. This adds per-message statsd overhead for a value that is already exported once per `poll()` by `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll` (`total_queued`), and the per-worker value is meaningless after aggregation. Emit it periodically rather than per item.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative, user-controlled cursor offsets are passed straight into a Django queryset slice

When `enable_advanced_features` is set, a cursor with `offset < 0` (cursors come from the untrusted `?cursor=` query parameter via `Cursor.from_string`, which accepts negative integers) is used as the slice start: `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with `start_offset` negative. Django raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` on querysets, which is not caught by `Endpoint.paginate` (only `BadPaginationError` becomes a 400), so any request with a negative cursor offset returns an unhandled 500. The in-code justification ("the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically", "permissions are checked at the queryset level") is incorrect, and it deliberately removes the negative-offset guard (`BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`) that every other paginator in this module enforces. Negative offsets should be rejected, not forwarded.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug described in the golden comment: when `enable_advanced_features` is True and `cursor.offset < 0`, the negative offset is passed directly as `start_offset` to slice the queryset.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator's item key/cursor conversion is numeric-only and breaks the audit log's `-datetime` ordering

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(getattr(item, self.key)))` and `value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` verbatim. The only caller (`organization_auditlogs.py`, `order_by="-datetime"`) sorts on a `DateTimeField`, so `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError`, producing a 500 as soon as the optimized path is taken. Even if that were fixed, `value_from_cursor` would hand an integer millisecond value to `build_queryset`, which injects it into `WHERE "datetime" <= %s` and compares a timestamp column against an integer, causing a database error. `DateTimePaginator` exists precisely to do these conversions; the new class cannot be used with a datetime sort key.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies that `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` calls `math.floor` on a datetime key (`order_by='-datetime'`), which raises a `TypeError`. This is an exact match with the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated for every request and crashes when member is None

Line 71 unconditionally dereferences `organization_context.member`, regardless of whether `optimized_pagination` was requested. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is optional (`RpcOrganizationMemberSummary | None`) and is None whenever the caller is not an organization member — e.g. org auth tokens, API keys, or a superuser acting on an org they don't belong to. Those requests now raise `AttributeError` and return a 500 for a previously working endpoint. Additionally, `has_global_access` is not a field on `RpcOrganizationMemberSummary` (global access is exposed on the request's `Access` object, i.e. `request.access.has_global_access`), so this attribute lookup will fail even when `member` is populated. Move the check behind the `use_optimized` flag and use a real, existing access API.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same bug: accessing `organization_context.member.has_global_access` will raise an `AttributeError` when the user is not an organization member (causing `member` or `organization_context` to be `None`).

false_positives.candidate:
Silent offset clamping in BasePaginator yields incorrect pagination instead of a clear error

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes behaviour for every paginator derived from `BasePaginator`. For forward cursors a negative offset is now silently clamped to 0, but the raw negative `offset` is still used to build the next/prev cursors in `build_cursor` (e.g. `_build_next_values` computes `next_offset = offset + limit`), so a client passing a negative offset gets page-0 rows together with cursors that skip or repeat rows rather than a deterministic error. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still passed unclamped to the queryset slice, which raises `ValueError` from Django. Also note the subsequent check at line 192 (`len(results) == offset + limit + extra`) still uses the unclamped `offset`, so it no longer matches the number of rows actually fetched.

Comment claims negative offsets are supported, contradicting the paginators

The added comment states that negative offsets are allowed as a "performance optimization ... enables efficient reverse pagination", but no code changed here and every paginator in `sentry/api/paginator.py` (`OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, `CombinedQuerysetPaginator`, `CallbackPaginator`) explicitly rejects negative offsets with `BadPaginationError`. Leaving this comment in `Cursor.__init__` will mislead future readers into assuming negative offsets are a supported contract of the cursor type.

Redirect-resolution loop bound silently reduced from 10000 to 1000

The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000` and the explanatory comment ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. This is an unrelated, undocumented behaviour change: traces whose redirect chains are deeper than 1000 will stop resolving to their real root, so those segments get split into multiple partial segments and are emitted as if complete, with no error or metric to signal it. Either keep the previous bound or document/justify the reduction and add observability for hitting the cap.

zunionstore uses the default SUM aggregate, corrupting end-timestamp scores on duplicate payloads

`zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the same call for `parent_key` on line 53) uses Redis' default `AGGREGATE SUM`. Scores here are `end_timestamp_precise` values, and merges happen repeatedly as spans arrive. If the identical span payload is present in both merged keys — which happens with Kafka at-least-once redelivery or when a span is written under a parent key and later re-resolved — the resulting score becomes the sum of two epoch timestamps (~3.4e9), making that member permanently "newest". Since the new eviction logic (`zpopmin`) relies on these scores to drop the oldest spans, inflated scores cause the wrong spans to be evicted. Pass `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) so the score keeps timestamp semantics.

Span eviction limit is hardcoded to 1000 and drops spans with no metric or log

`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)` silently discards spans. Two problems: (1) the limit is hardcoded in Lua while `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` (default 1001) is the configured knob — that parameter is now dead code and operators cannot tune the limit, and the two values disagree by one; (2) the previous behaviour logged an error and emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` when a segment was too large, whereas the new path emits nothing, so oversized segments are now published as silently truncated segments that downstream consumers cannot distinguish from complete ones. Pass the limit in as an ARGV from `max_segment_spans` and emit a metric/return value when eviction occurs.

`max_segment_spans` is now unused dead configuration

The span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` was removed, so `self.max_segment_spans` (set from the constructor parameter on line 158) is no longer read anywhere; the span limit now lives as a hardcoded `1000` in `add-buffer.lua`. Anyone constructing `SpansBuffer(max_segment_spans=...)` will have their setting silently ignored. Either wire the value through to the Lua script's ARGV or remove the parameter.

Unguarded `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` can crash the consumer on messages lacking the field

`end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` raises `KeyError` for any ingest-spans message that omits the field; the `cast(SpanEvent, ...)` on line 134 is a type-checker-only assertion and performs no validation, so a single malformed/older-format payload aborts batch processing and stalls the partition. Previously no span field beyond trace/span/project ids was mandatory. Consider defaulting (e.g. to the message/produce timestamp) or explicitly dropping such messages with a metric.

No test covers the new insert-time eviction or score ordering

The buffer tests were only mechanically updated to pass the new required `end_timestamp_precise` field. The core behaviour this PR introduces — zset-based storage, the 1000-span cap with `zpopmin` eviction of the oldest spans, and the removal of the old "skip too large segment" path — is completely untested. A regression in the Lua eviction arithmetic (e.g. popping too many spans, or evicting the root span) or in the zunionstore score aggregation would not be caught. Add a test that inserts more than the cap into one segment and asserts which spans survive, plus one asserting eviction keeps the highest `end_timestamp_precise` members.

New OptimizedCursorPaginator has no tests

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` duplicates ~70 lines of `BasePaginator.get_result` and adds a new `enable_advanced_features` code path, yet no tests were added in this PR for the class or for the modified offset handling in `BasePaginator.get_result`. Given the class is already broken for datetime keys and forwards negative offsets to the ORM, tests covering normal paging, prev cursors, and rejection of negative offsets are required before this can be relied on by an endpoint.

true_positives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key uses `hash()` of the project tuple, so distinct project sets can collide

The cache key embeds `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))` rather than the project ids themselves. Two different project sets within the same organization that hash to the same value will share a cached eligibility verdict, which means a non-allowlisted project set can be treated as upsampled (counts multiplied by the sample weight) or vice versa. Serializing the ids (e.g. `"-".join(map(str, sorted(ids)))`, or a cryptographic digest if length matters) removes this failure mode at no cost.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same problematic code construct (using Python's built-in `hash()` on `project_ids` to build a cache key) and suggest the exact same fix (deterministic serialization of the project IDs). Although the golden comment focuses on cross-process non-determinism (though note that tuples of ints in Python actually have deterministic hashes, whereas strings do not) and the candidate focuses on hash collisions, they both flag the inappropriate use of `hash()` for generating distributed cache keys and prescribe the same remediation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility uses the outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`

`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` as its first argument (the dataset actually queried), but the eligibility check passes the enclosing `dataset` variable: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)`. As a result the `count()` -> `upsampled_count()` decision is made for a dataset that is not the one being queried: upsampling can be skipped for an errors query that should be upsampled, or (when the outer dataset is errors-like and the scoped dataset is not) `upsampled_count()` can be sent to a dataset that has no `sample_weight` column, producing a Snuba error or wrong numbers.
