true_positives.matched_candidate:
`organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated for every request and crashes when member is None

Line 71 unconditionally dereferences `organization_context.member`, regardless of whether `optimized_pagination` was requested. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is optional (`RpcOrganizationMemberSummary | None`) and is None whenever the caller is not an organization member — e.g. org auth tokens, API keys, or a superuser acting on an org they don't belong to. Those requests now raise `AttributeError` and return a 500 for a previously working endpoint. Additionally, `has_global_access` is not a field on `RpcOrganizationMemberSummary` (global access is exposed on the request's `Access` object, i.e. `request.access.has_global_access`), so this attribute lookup will fail even when `member` is populated. Move the check behind the `use_optimized` flag and use a real, existing access API.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify an unsafe organization_context.member.has_global_access dereference that can raise AttributeError for users without organization membership. The candidate emphasizes member being None rather than organization_context being None, but points to the same access-check failure.

false_positives.candidate:
Comment claims negative offsets are supported, contradicting the paginators

The added comment states that negative offsets are allowed as a "performance optimization ... enables efficient reverse pagination", but no code changed here and every paginator in `sentry/api/paginator.py` (`OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, `CombinedQuerysetPaginator`, `CallbackPaginator`) explicitly rejects negative offsets with `BadPaginationError`. Leaving this comment in `Cursor.__init__` will mislead future readers into assuming negative offsets are a supported contract of the cursor type.

Redirect-resolution loop bound silently reduced from 10000 to 1000

The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000` and the explanatory comment ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. This is an unrelated, undocumented behaviour change: traces whose redirect chains are deeper than 1000 will stop resolving to their real root, so those segments get split into multiple partial segments and are emitted as if complete, with no error or metric to signal it. Either keep the previous bound or document/justify the reduction and add observability for hitting the cap.

zunionstore uses the default SUM aggregate, corrupting end-timestamp scores on duplicate payloads

`zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the same call for `parent_key` on line 53) uses Redis' default `AGGREGATE SUM`. Scores here are `end_timestamp_precise` values, and merges happen repeatedly as spans arrive. If the identical span payload is present in both merged keys — which happens with Kafka at-least-once redelivery or when a span is written under a parent key and later re-resolved — the resulting score becomes the sum of two epoch timestamps (~3.4e9), making that member permanently "newest". Since the new eviction logic (`zpopmin`) relies on these scores to drop the oldest spans, inflated scores cause the wrong spans to be evicted. Pass `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) so the score keeps timestamp semantics.

Span eviction limit is hardcoded to 1000 and drops spans with no metric or log

`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)` silently discards spans. Two problems: (1) the limit is hardcoded in Lua while `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` (default 1001) is the configured knob — that parameter is now dead code and operators cannot tune the limit, and the two values disagree by one; (2) the previous behaviour logged an error and emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` when a segment was too large, whereas the new path emits nothing, so oversized segments are now published as silently truncated segments that downstream consumers cannot distinguish from complete ones. Pass the limit in as an ARGV from `max_segment_spans` and emit a metric/return value when eviction occurs.

`max_segment_spans` is now unused dead configuration

The span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` was removed, so `self.max_segment_spans` (set from the constructor parameter on line 158) is no longer read anywhere; the span limit now lives as a hardcoded `1000` in `add-buffer.lua`. Anyone constructing `SpansBuffer(max_segment_spans=...)` will have their setting silently ignored. Either wire the value through to the Lua script's ARGV or remove the parameter.

Unguarded `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` can crash the consumer on messages lacking the field

`end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` raises `KeyError` for any ingest-spans message that omits the field; the `cast(SpanEvent, ...)` on line 134 is a type-checker-only assertion and performs no validation, so a single malformed/older-format payload aborts batch processing and stalls the partition. Previously no span field beyond trace/span/project ids was mandatory. Consider defaulting (e.g. to the message/produce timestamp) or explicitly dropping such messages with a metric.

No test covers the new insert-time eviction or score ordering

The buffer tests were only mechanically updated to pass the new required `end_timestamp_precise` field. The core behaviour this PR introduces — zset-based storage, the 1000-span cap with `zpopmin` eviction of the oldest spans, and the removal of the old "skip too large segment" path — is completely untested. A regression in the Lua eviction arithmetic (e.g. popping too many spans, or evicting the root span) or in the zunionstore score aggregation would not be caught. Add a test that inserts more than the cap into one segment and asserts which spans survive, plus one asserting eviction keeps the highest `end_timestamp_precise` members.

New OptimizedCursorPaginator has no tests

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` duplicates ~70 lines of `BasePaginator.get_result` and adds a new `enable_advanced_features` code path, yet no tests were added in this PR for the class or for the modified offset handling in `BasePaginator.get_result`. Given the class is already broken for datetime keys and forwards negative offsets to the ORM, tests covering normal paging, prev cursors, and rejection of negative offsets are required before this can be relied on by an endpoint.

true_positives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sample-rate extraction silently swallows all errors and drops a 0 rate

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` wraps both the context lookup and the `float()` conversion in bare `except Exception: pass`, and gates on `if client_sample_rate:` (falsy), so a malformed or zero `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` results in no `sample_rate` on the event with no signal at all. A test that intends to store an upsampled event but passes a slightly wrong value will instead silently assert against raw counts, making failures hard to diagnose. Narrow the exception handling (e.g. `(TypeError, ValueError)`) and check `is not None` rather than truthiness.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same truthiness bug in _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling: a client_sample_rate of 0.0 is skipped by `if client_sample_rate:`, leaving sample_rate unset. Its additional exception-handling concerns do not negate the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility uses the outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`

`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` as its first argument (the dataset actually queried), but the eligibility check passes the enclosing `dataset` variable: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)`. In the dashboard-widget-split code path, `_get_event_stats` is intentionally invoked with a different dataset (`discover`, or the widget's split dataset) while the outer `dataset` is the metrics/discover dataset selected from the request. As a result the `count()` -> `upsampled_count()` decision is made for a dataset that is not the one being queried: upsampling can be skipped for an errors query that should be upsampled, or (when the outer dataset is errors-like and the scoped dataset is not) `upsampled_count()` can be sent to a dataset that has no `sample_weight` column, producing a Snuba error or wrong numbers. The check should use `scoped_dataset`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same incorrect dataset argument in the upsampling eligibility check: using the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset can skip upsampling when dashboard-split queries run against discover. The candidate's additional potential consequences do not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Caching allowlist eligibility for 60s can serve 10x-wrong counts and cannot be invalidated

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` stores the result of the allowlist check in the shared cache under `error_upsampling_eligible:{org}:{hash(project_ids)}` for 60 seconds. The underlying value comes from `options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist")`, which is already cached by the options store, so there is no meaningful performance gain; what it does add is up to a minute of stale behavior. After an operator removes a project from the allowlist (e.g. to stop bad data or roll back the feature), charts keep returning `sum(sample_weight)` values that are inflated by the inverse sample rate (10x in the tests here) — and conversely, newly allowlisted projects keep returning raw counts. Because the cache key is per (org, exact project-id set), there is no practical way to purge all affected entries. Additionally, if the cache backend (redis/memcached) outlives a database reset in CI or local dev, project ids can be reused and a stale `True`/`False` will be applied to an unrelated project set. Consider removing the cache entirely or keying it on the option value/version.

Cache key uses `hash()` of the project tuple, so distinct project sets can collide

The cache key embeds `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))` rather than the project ids themselves. Two different project sets within the same organization that hash to the same value will share a cached eligibility verdict, which means a non-allowlisted project set can be treated as upsampled (counts multiplied by the sample weight) or vice versa. Serializing the ids (e.g. `"-".join(map(str, sorted(ids)))`, or a cryptographic digest if length matters) removes this failure mode at no cost.

Docstring claims the allowlist is read fresh on every call, which the caller's cache contradicts

`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`'s docstring states: "This function reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time... This is intentional to ensure we always have the latest configuration state." Its only caller, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, caches the result for 60 seconds, so the system does not always see the latest configuration. The comment in the caller ("This is safe because allowlist changes are infrequent and eventual consistency is acceptable") asserts the opposite guarantee. A future maintainer reading either docstring will reason incorrectly about staleness; the two must be reconciled.

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is dead code and cannot invalidate in practice

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is not called from anywhere in this PR, and by construction it can only delete the single key for one exact (organization, project-id set) combination. Eligibility is cached per distinct project-id set, so a single allowlist option change would require enumerating every combination of project ids that has ever been queried. Shipping it gives the false impression that the cache is invalidated on configuration changes; either wire up a real invalidation (option-value-based cache key / option update hook) or drop the function.

`upsampled_count` has no fallback when `sample_weight` is missing/NULL

The new aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` with a comment asserting the schema guarantees `sample_weight` exists for all events in allowlisted projects. That guarantee does not hold for data stored before a project was allowlisted or before the SDK started sending `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` (the test factory change in this PR only sets `sample_rate` when that context is present). For such rows `sample_weight` is NULL/0, so `sum` silently drops them and a chart over a time range that spans the rollout collapses to zero or badly undercounts — with no error surfaced to the user. Wrapping the column, e.g. `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))`, makes unweighted events count as 1.

`upsampled_count` is registered as a public function, exposing it to arbitrary user queries

Unlike the neighbouring internal aggregates, the new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is not marked `private=True`, so any user can put `upsampled_count()` in a Discover/dashboard field or yAxis. This (a) lets users obtain sample-weight-scaled counts for projects that are not on the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`, bypassing the gating this PR builds, and (b) will fail at the Snuba layer (500 / SnubaError) for datasets or storages where the `sample_weight` column does not exist, since nothing validates dataset or project eligibility at resolution time. Mark it private, as this is an implementation detail of the server-side column rewrite.

`default_result_type="number"` conflicts with the integer result it replaces

`upsampled_count` is declared with `default_result_type="number"` even though the aggregate is wrapped in `toInt64` and it is substituted for `count()`, which declares `"integer"`. Because the rewrite aliases the result back to `count`, clients receive meta `fieldType`/`type` of `number` for a field they previously got `integer` for, which changes formatting/axis handling in the UI for the same logical series. Use `"integer"` for consistency.

Top-events path upsamples only the series, not the top-N selection or orderby

In the `top_events > 0` branch only `timeseries_columns`/`y_axes` are rewritten to `upsampled_count()`; `selected_columns=self.get_field_list(...)` and `orderby=self.get_orderby(request)` keep the raw `count()`. The top-N groups are therefore selected and ordered by un-upsampled counts while the plotted series are upsampled. When the per-event sample rates differ across groups/projects, the chosen top groups and their ordering do not match the magnitudes shown in the chart.

Accidental git submodule (gitlink) `sentry-repo` committed without a .gitmodules entry

This PR adds a gitlink entry `sentry-repo` pointing at `a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a` (the base commit of this very repository) with no corresponding `.gitmodules` mapping. Git will report "no submodule mapping found in .gitmodules for path 'sentry-repo'" and `git submodule update`/`clone --recurse-submodules` will fail, and the self-referential pointer serves no purpose. This looks like a local working-directory artifact and should be removed from the commit.

No test covers the public entry point, its cache, or the errors-dataset path

The unit tests only exercise the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) and the column transform. The public function `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` — which contains the new cache key construction, the `cache.get`/`cache.set` logic, and the combination of eligibility with the dataset check — is never called in any test, so the cache-hit path, cache-staleness behavior, and the empty-`project_ids` case are unverified. Separately, no test issues a request with `dataset=errors`, even though `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns `True` unconditionally for that dataset and `upsampled_count` was only registered in the Discover dataset's `function_converter`; if the errors dataset config does not inherit that function, the primary intended path raises an invalid-function error and nothing here would catch it.

Misleading comments on upsampled count assertions

In `test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` the assertions `assert data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10` / `== 10` are annotated "# First bucket has 1 event" / "# Second bucket has 1 event". The value 10 is the upsampled count derived from `client_sample_rate: 0.1`, not an event count; the comments make the expected values look like a bug to anyone reading the test. Reword to state that one stored event at a 0.1 sample rate is expected to be upsampled to 10.

Trailing whitespace and an over-length line will fail the repo's formatting checks

Several added lines contain trailing whitespace (e.g. the blank-but-indented lines inside the docstrings and between statements in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, and similar lines added in `organization_events_stats.py` around the `upsampling_enabled`/`final_columns` blocks), and the `cache_key = f"error_upsampling_eligible:..."` assignment exceeds the 100-character limit configured for black in `pyproject.toml`. The pre-commit/lint CI job will reject the branch until these are reformatted.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every denied Check now performs a full permission re-query against the database

The permission-cache read was removed from `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions`, and `Check` now only short-circuits on a cached *allow*. Any cached-but-denied result falls through to `getIdentityPermissions`, which executes `GetUserPermissions` (plus basic-role/team lookups on their own cache misses) against the DB. The new denial cache only suppresses repeats of the exact same (user, action, name, folder) tuple, so a workload that checks many distinct resource names the subject cannot access (per-object checks from the resource server, UI pre-flight checks) issues one permission query per check. `singleflight` only dedupes concurrent calls, not sequential ones, so this is a significant increase in DB load compared with the previous behaviour where the 30s permission cache absorbed denies as well.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same asymmetric permission-cache logic: Check immediately trusts cached allows but falls through to database queries for cached denials. Although it emphasizes database load rather than stale grants and unauthorized access, the underlying code issue matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
"Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" test is vacuous and its comment is wrong

The comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but the permission cache is seeded with `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`. A `false` value means the scope lookup in `checkPermission` fails, so the request would be denied even if the denial cache were never consulted (the fallback DB query uses the default `fakeStore` with no permissions and also denies). The assertion therefore passes regardless of whether the new `permDenialCache` short-circuit works; the value must be `true` for the test to actually prove the denial cache takes precedence. There is also no test covering the write side of the new behaviour (that a DB-confirmed deny stores an entry under `userPermDenialCacheKey`), so the whole denial-cache feature is effectively untested.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same mismatch: the comment claims cached permissions allow access, but dashboards:uid:dash1 is set to false, so checkPermission still denies that scope. Its additional testing concerns do not negate this direct match.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache can persist a deny caused by a stale folder tree, doubling the staleness window

After a DB re-query the result is cached as a denial for `shortCacheTTL` (30s). The re-query only refreshes the *permission* map; `checkInheritedPermissions`/`buildFolderTree` still use `folderCache` (also 30s), which is not refreshed. Concrete failure: a user with a grant on folder A creates subfolder B and a dashboard D inside B. `Check(dashboards:read, name=D, folder=B)` fails the direct `folders:uid:B` lookup and then walks `tree.Ancestors("B")`, which is empty because B is not in the cached folder tree, so the request is denied — and that denial is now written to `permDenialCache` with its own independent 30s TTL. If the deny happens just before the folder tree entry expires, the user keeps being denied for up to ~60s even though the refreshed tree would allow it. This is exactly the "creator cannot access the resource they just created" case the PR intends to fix. Consider also invalidating/refetching the folder tree before caching a denial, or not caching denials that depend on folder inheritance.

Permission-denial cache key omits identity type (and group/resource) that the decision depends on

`userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent)` is built in `Check` from the raw `checkReq.UserUID` returned by `types.ParseTypeID`, without the identity type. Different identity types share the same identifier space: `anonymous:0` and `render:0` both yield userUID "0", so a denial cached for the render service is returned for the anonymous user (and vice versa) for the same namespace/action/name/folder. The key also omits group and resource, while the decision does depend on them (`checkPermission` uses `mapper.translation(req.Group, req.Resource)` to derive the scope prefix and the `folderSupport` flag); any two group/resource pairs that map to the same action string would therefore share denial entries and produce false denials. Finally, because the raw subject identifier is used (numeric user ID for `user:1`, UID for `user:abc`), the same user gets separate denial entries depending on how the caller addressed them. Include the identity type, group and resource (or the resolved internal UID) in the key.

permissionCacheUsage metric is misreported in Check

`s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", ...)` at line 137 is reached whenever the cached permissions did not yield an allow — including the case where the permission cache *did* hit but the decision was deny. Conversely, a hit in the new `permDenialCache` (line 118) is reported as a `permissionCacheUsage` hit even though it is a different cache. The resulting hit-rate metric no longer measures permission-cache effectiveness and will look much worse than it is, making it useless for tuning TTLs; use a distinct label/metric for the denial cache and only count a permission-cache miss when the cache actually missed.

Disabling the in-proc client cache moves per-request cost onto the server path

In-proc mode now passes `&NoopCache{}` to `authzlib.NewClient`, so no Check/List response is cached on the client side any more. Every authorization decision now goes through the in-proc channel into `Service.Check`, which reads the permission map out of the byte cache via `cacheWrap` and JSON-unmarshals it on every call. For users/service accounts with large permission sets (thousands of scopes) this adds a JSON decode of the whole scope map to every API request, where previously identical checks were served from the 30s client cache. Worth measuring before merge, or caching the decoded map in memory instead of re-decoding bytes per request.

Denial cache has unbounded key cardinality in a shared in-memory cache

Denial entries are keyed per (namespace, subject, action, resource name, parent folder), so their cardinality grows with the number of distinct resources any subject is denied on. They are stored in the same unbounded `cache.NewLocalCache` instance as the identity/permission/folder caches (configured in-proc with `CleanupInterval: 10 * time.Minute`), so although entries expire after 30s they are only reclaimed every 10 minutes. A burst of denied checks across many resource names can therefore retain a large amount of memory in the Grafana process; consider a bounded cache or a shorter cleanup interval for this cache.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth `state` uses `pipeline.signature`, which is not a per-session nonce

`OAuthLoginView.dispatch` sends `state = pipeline.signature` to GitHub and then validates the callback with `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature` (line 412). `Pipeline.signature` is derived from the pipeline view definitions, not from the user's session, so it is the same constant for every user and every installation attempt of the provider — the new tests hardcode `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` and reuse it across different users and organizations, which demonstrates this. As a result the `state` check provides no CSRF/replay protection (any party can supply the correct value), contrary to what the PR description claims. The established pattern in `sentry/identity/oauth2.py` (`OAuth2LoginView`) is to generate `secrets.token_hex()`, `pipeline.bind_state("state", ...)` it, and compare the callback value against the bound state; this view should do the same.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same issue: OAuth state uses the static pipeline.signature rather than a fresh random value for each request, undermining CSRF protection.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unguarded `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` can raise KeyError/TypeError

The new user check indexes `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` directly. `GitHubIntegrationProvider.build_integration` only sets `metadata["sender"]` when `state.get("sender")` is present (line 376-377), so integrations created through the normal pipeline have no `sender` key at all (see `test_basic_flow`, which asserts the metadata dict without `sender`). This branch is reached whenever an `Integration` row exists but no `OrganizationIntegration` does (e.g. the org integration was removed while the Integration row survived, or legacy rows), and it will raise an unhandled `KeyError` (or `TypeError` if `sender` is stored in a different shape), producing a 500 instead of the intended failure page. Use `(integration.metadata.get("sender") or {}).get("login")` and fail closed.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unguarded access to integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] and the resulting KeyError when sender metadata was not set during integration creation.

false_positives.candidate:
Token exchange and user-info request can raise unhandled exceptions

`safe_urlopen(...)` on line 423 is outside the try/except, and `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` on line 434 is not wrapped at all. `sentry.identity.github.get_user_info` performs an HTTP request and calls `raise_for_status()`, so a revoked/invalid token, a GitHub outage, or any network error raises out of the pipeline view and yields a 500 error page rather than the user-facing `github-integration-failed.html` page this PR is designed to show. Both calls should be wrapped and converted into the `error(request, self.active_organization)` response (ideally with logging so these failures are observable).

GitHub user validation is skipped when no local Integration row exists

In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, if `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist` the pipeline continues immediately (`return pipeline.next_step()`) without comparing the OAuth-authenticated GitHub user to the owner/sender of the installation. `installation_id` is attacker-controllable (it is read straight from the query string at line 448, or from state bound from the query string in `OAuthLoginView`) and GitHub installation ids are small sequential integers. Whenever Sentry has no Integration row for a live GitHub installation (installation webhook never delivered/processed, row deleted while the GitHub-side installation remains, self-hosted installs), an attacker can submit someone else's installation id and `build_integration` will fetch it from the App API and attach it to the attacker's Sentry org, exposing the victim's repositories. The ownership check should be made against the installation data fetched from GitHub (e.g. `installation["account"]`), not only in the branch where a local Integration happens to exist.

test_installation_not_found no longer verifies the installation-not-found error

The assertion was changed from `b"The GitHub installation could not be found."` to the generic `b"Invalid installation request."`, which is the default `error_short` emitted by nearly every failure path in the new code (state mismatch, failed token exchange, missing `login`, user mismatch). In addition, the `state` value hardcoded here (`ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`) differs from the value every other test uses (`9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`) even though `pipeline.signature` does not depend on bound state, so this request almost certainly fails the new `state` check in `OAuthLoginView` and never reaches the installation lookup. The 404 stub installed by `responses.replace` is therefore dead, and the regression this test used to cover (GitHub returning 404 for `/app/installations/{id}` surfacing a specific message) is no longer tested.

No tests for the state-mismatch and failed-token-exchange failure modes

The PR description lists three new failure modes (GitHub user mismatch, `state` mismatch, and GitHub not returning an `access_token`), but only the user mismatch is covered by `test_github_user_mismatch`. There is no test asserting that a tampered/missing `state` or an access-token response without `access_token` (e.g. `error=bad_verification_code`, which GitHub returns with HTTP 200) renders the failure page, so regressions in those branches would go unnoticed. There is also no test for an existing `Integration` whose metadata lacks a `sender` key, which currently crashes (see the `metadata["sender"]` finding).

Hardcoded pipeline signature makes the setup tests brittle

`assert_setup_flow` asserts the exact redirect query string including `state=9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`, and five other tests hardcode the same md5 value as the `state` parameter. This value is an implementation detail of `Pipeline.signature` (a hash over the pipeline views): adding, removing or renaming a pipeline view will silently change it and break all of these tests with an opaque "Invalid installation request." failure rather than a clear assertion error. Reading the `state` out of the redirect `Location` (or binding a real nonce, as suggested elsewhere) would make the tests robust and self-explanatory.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup registers a non-existent alias, leaking 21 identity providers into the shared test realm

`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` (lines 381 and 425) uses the literal string "alias" instead of the alias of the provider just created (`idpRep.getAlias()`). Consequently the 20 providers `idp-alias-0..19` plus `idp-alias-20` are never deleted after the test, and the cleanup action itself targets a provider that does not exist (404 at teardown). Because `OrganizationCacheTest` uses the shared test realm across test methods, these leftover providers change the IDP counts other tests in this class rely on (e.g. `testCacheIDPForLogin` asserts exactly 5/5/10 login providers and `testCacheIDPByOrg` asserts 6/2/4), making results order-dependent and flaky. Note that the same mistake already exists at line 303 and is being copied here.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same incorrect cleanup alias: the literal "alias" is used instead of the created provider's alias, such as "idp-alias-" + i. The candidate's additional discussion of leaked providers describes consequences of that same bug.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation decision uses the org-aware wrapped model, so required invalidations can be skipped

In `update()` the "original" model passed to `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate()` comes from `getById(model.getInternalId())`, which returns the model wrapped by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel()`. That wrapper's `isEnabled()` returns `false` whenever the linked organization (or the realm's organization support) is disabled, even though the underlying IDP row is enabled. The login cache, however, is populated from the JPA query, which only filters on the IDP's own `enabled` flag and therefore *does* contain such IDPs. The result is an asymmetry: for an org-linked IDP whose organization is currently disabled, `getLoginPredicate().test(original)` is `false`, so an update that also makes the raw model non-eligible (e.g. setting `hideOnLogin=true`, `enabled=false`, or `broker_public=false`) takes the first early-return branch and no login cache is invalidated, while the cached id list still contains the provider. After the organization is re-enabled (organization updates do not invalidate the login keys), `getForLogin()` keeps returning that id from the cache, so a hidden or non-public (private) organization broker is still offered on the login page. Note that `create()` and `remove()` evaluate the predicate on raw models (`model`, `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)`), so only `update()` is inconsistent; the fix is to evaluate the predicate on the unwrapped model (e.g. `idpDelegate.getById(...)`).

One login cache entry per realm+fetch mode aggregates all organizations, causing cluster-wide invalidation churn

`getForLogin()` stores all results for a given realm and `FetchMode` in a single cache object keyed by `cacheKeyForLogin(realm, mode)`, using the organization id as the inner search key. Whenever a request asks for an organization that is not yet present in that object, line 236 calls `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)`, which drops the entry locally and broadcasts an invalidation to the whole cluster, then re-adds a merged copy. `OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean` calls `getForLogin(ALL, organization.getId())` on the login path, so in a realm with many organizations the first login for each new organization on each node wipes every other node's cached login IDP lists for that fetch mode, which must then be rebuilt from the database; the merged entry itself also grows with one id set per organization without any bound. Keying the cache per `(mode, organizationId)` (as `getByOrganization` does per organization) would avoid the shared-entry contention. Additionally, for `FetchMode.REALM_ONLY` the `organizationId` argument is documented as ignored, yet it is still used as the search key, so passing different organization ids creates redundant duplicate entries with identical content.

No coverage for the new create/remove login-cache invalidation

The new test only exercises the negative cases for the invalidation hooks added to `create()` and `remove()`: it creates an IDP with `hideOnLogin=true` and removes a disabled IDP, then asserts the login caches are still present. There is no case that creates a login-eligible IDP (enabled, not link-only, not hidden) or removes one and asserts that all three `cacheKeyForLogin(realm, mode)` entries are invalidated. Those are exactly the paths added by `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(model)` in `create()` and `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp)` in `remove()`, so a regression that drops either call (leaving stale login lists that hide a new broker or still advertise a deleted one) would not be caught.

Test asserts only on cache internals, never on what getForLogin returns

`testCacheIDPForLogin` discards the stream returned by `session.identityProviders().getForLogin(...)` and only inspects the sizes of the internal `IdentityProviderListQuery` entries. Nothing verifies that the cached code path returns the same providers as the uncached delegate path (for example that the aliases match, that disabled/hidden/non-public providers are excluded, or that the second, cache-hit call returns the same result as the first). A bug in the cache-hit branch (e.g. the `getById` loop returning wrapped models whose `isEnabled()` is false, or the fallback on a missing id) would pass this test unnoticed.

getLoginPredicate() silently gains an organization/BROKER_PUBLIC criterion that getLoginSearchOptions() does not have

`LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate()` now additionally rejects any IDP that is linked to an organization and does not have `BROKER_PUBLIC=true`. This criterion is not represented by any `LoginFilter` constant and is therefore absent from `getLoginSearchOptions()`, so the query-based and predicate-based helpers of the same enum no longer agree on what "available for login" means; the enum's javadoc ("contains all fields that are considered when deciding if a provider should be available for login") is now inaccurate. The change also affects every existing caller of `getLoginPredicate()` (e.g. `IdentityProviderBean.federatedProviderPredicate()`, which `OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean` builds on): non-public organization brokers that previously passed the predicate are now filtered out. If that behavior change is intended it should be documented; otherwise the extra condition belongs in the Infinispan invalidation logic rather than in the shared SPI predicate.

Cached getForLogin returns providers in non-deterministic order, unlike the delegate path

On a cache hit, `getForLogin()` returns `identityProviders.stream()` built from a `HashSet`, so the iteration order is arbitrary, whereas the fallback paths (lines 218 and 249) return the delegate's stream, which for `FetchMode.ALL` is realm-level providers followed by organization providers in query order. The order of providers returned by the same call therefore differs depending on whether the cache is warm or cold. Current login beans sort the result, but any consumer that relies on the stream order (or picks the first element) will behave non-deterministically; this should at least be documented in `IdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin`, which says nothing about ordering.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions has unreachable logic and silently neutralises the feature toggle

`enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` from both the `if enabled` branch and the fall-through, so the function is a constant `false` and the feature-flag lookup is completely dead. The negation is also inverted relative to the variable name (`enabled` is true when the flag is *off*), which makes the code read as a logic error rather than an intentional kill switch. Consequences: (a) the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle no longer has any effect on this code path, which is surprising for anyone later trying to re-enable the feature by flipping the flag; (b) static analysis/lint (ineffectual assignment, identical branch returns) is likely to flag it. If the intent is a hard disable, the function should simply `return false` with a comment explaining why, or the type case should return the error directly.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that enableSqlExpressions returns false on every path, unconditionally disabling SQL expressions and making the feature toggle ineffective. This is the same underlying issue as the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
User-facing error says "not implemented" while the sqlExpressions toggle is still registered and documented

Requests of `QueryTypeSQL` are now rejected with `sqlExpressions is not implemented`. The `sqlExpressions` feature toggle remains registered in featuremgmt and documented as an available (experimental) flag, so an operator who enables it, and users who already have saved SQL expression queries, will get an error that contradicts the documentation and gives no hint that the feature was deliberately removed/disabled for security reasons. Either the toggle/docs should be marked as unavailable, or the message should state that SQL expressions are currently disabled.

Feature gate only added to the new reader path; legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path relies solely on the stubbed DB

The explicit disable check was added only in `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` (pkg/expr/reader.go). The other entry point, `UnmarshalSQLCommand` -> `NewSQLCommand` (used by the classic/non-apiserver expression pipeline), has no toggle or disable check at all; it is only prevented from working because `sql.DB.RunCommands`/`QueryFramesInto` in the new `pkg/expr/sql/db.go` stub return `errors.New("not implemented")`. If `sql.DB` is ever re-implemented (which is the obvious next step for this package), that path silently becomes reachable again with no gate, re-opening the vulnerable surface. The gate should be applied at command construction/execution as well, not just in the query reader. Additionally, every such request now takes the `logger.Warn("invalid sql query", "sql", rawSQL, ...)` branch and surfaces an opaque `error reading SQL command` BadRequest, which both logs user-supplied query text on every attempt and gives no indication the feature is disabled.

No test asserts that SQL expressions are rejected

This change is a security fix that disables a code path, but no test is added or updated. There is nothing verifying that `ReadQuery` returns an error for `QueryTypeSQL` (with the toggle both on and off), nor that `NewSQLCommand`/`SQLCommand.Execute` fail safely against the new stub `sql.DB`. Without such a test, a future refactor (e.g. "fixing" the obviously odd `enableSqlExpressions` helper, or implementing `sql.DB`) can silently re-enable the vulnerable path with a green CI.

tablesFromAST indexes ast[0] without a length check

`tablesFromAST` does `flatten.Flatten(ast[0], ...)` immediately, so an empty JSON array (`[]`) returned from the serialization step causes an index-out-of-range panic. Today this is unreachable because `DB.RunCommands` is a stub that always errors, but the DuckDB-specific code in `TablesList` (the `SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')` command, the single-quote escaping) is left in place and will be the starting point if/when a real backend is wired up again. Either add a length guard, or remove this now-dead DuckDB-specific parser along with the dependency it was built for so it cannot be reactivated by accident.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write lock acquired without re-checking the cache (no double-checked locking)

After the fast path under `RLock` sees a nil cache, every goroutine falls through, takes the exclusive `Lock`, and unconditionally re-reads `assets-manifest.json` (or performs the CDN HTTP request) before setting the cache. There is no second check of `entryPointAssetsCache` after the write lock is acquired, so on a cold start with N concurrent requests the manifest is parsed N times, serialized one after another while holding the exclusive lock. Re-checking `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after `Lock()` makes the load happen exactly once and avoids the serialized duplicate I/O.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing cache re-check after acquiring the write lock, allowing concurrent goroutines that observed an empty cache to redundantly load and populate it.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is overwritten with nil when loading the manifest fails

`entryPointAssetsCache = result` runs unconditionally, including when `readWebAssetsFromFile`/`readWebAssetsFromCDN` returned `nil, err`. A transient failure therefore stores nil in the shared cache and the function returns a nil `*dtos.EntryPointAssets` together with the error; any caller that logs the error but still dereferences the returned pointer will panic. Guard the assignment with `if err == nil && result != nil` (and return the previous cached value on error) so a failed reload cannot poison the cache.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same unconditional cache assignment on fetch failure: a nil result overwrites a previously valid cache entry. The candidate's additional discussion of possible caller panics does not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
No test exercising concurrent GetWebAssets calls

The PR fixes a data race but adds no test that calls `GetWebAssets` from multiple goroutines, so the race fix is not covered and a future refactor (for example removing the lock or mutating the cached struct) could reintroduce the race without any CI signal. A small `t.Parallel`/`sync.WaitGroup` test run under `-race` would pin the behaviour.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Debug logging left in at Error level, dumping entire ID batches

Six new log calls use `r.log.Error(...)` for purely informational progress messages (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579), e.g. `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, ...)`. Consequences: (1) every cleanup cycle emits error-level log lines on a healthy system, which pollutes logs and will trigger error-rate alerting/monitoring; (2) the full `ids` slice is logged, so with a configured `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` (the test in this PR uses 32767) each iteration writes tens of thousands of IDs per log line, which can be megabytes of logs per cleanup run; (3) the `"err", err` field in the "to clean" messages is always nil at that point because the error path returned earlier, so it is misleading. These should be `Debug` level without the raw ID list (or removed).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying concern: informational or debugging messages are logged at Error level, polluting production error logs. Its additional concerns about ID dumps and nil error fields do not change the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup job interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute (looks like leftover debug change)

The background cleanup ticker was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (splitting the annotation cleanup query) and has broad consequences: every cleanup job (temp files, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history) now runs 10x more often, increasing database and I/O load on every Grafana instance. It also interacts badly with the 9-minute timeout in `clean()`: a cleanup pass that takes longer than one minute will be immediately followed by another pass, effectively making cleanup run continuously. Unless this is intentional and documented, it should be reverted to 10 minutes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the cleanup ticker interval reduction from 10 minutes to 1 minute and the resulting risk of increased database load from more frequent cleanup execution. The candidate adds details but describes the same underlying concern.

false_positives.candidate:
Quadratic string concatenation when inlining IDs for SQLite

In `deleteByIDs`, the SQLite inline-values path builds the ID list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside the loop. Each iteration reallocates and copies the whole accumulated string, giving O(n^2) copying. With the batch sizes this code path is specifically designed for (>999, and the new test uses 32767 IDs), this copies on the order of gigabytes per batch and allocates one string per ID, for every cleanup iteration. Use a `strings.Builder` (or `strconv.AppendInt` into a byte slice, as done in `getAccessControlFilter`) instead.

Bind-parameter path can exceed Postgres/MySQL parameter limits for large configured batch sizes

For non-SQLite databases `deleteByIDs` always builds `DELETE ... WHERE id IN (?,?,...)` with one placeholder per ID. Postgres and MySQL cap the number of bind parameters in a statement at 65535, so an operator who sets `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` above that will make annotation cleanup fail permanently with a driver error ("extended protocol limited to 65535 parameters" / "Prepared statement contains too many placeholders"). The previous implementation used a single parameterless DELETE with a subquery, so any batch size worked; this is therefore a regression. Also note the branch condition tests `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` instead of `len(ids)`, which couples the delete path to an assumption about how many IDs the caller fetched; checking `len(ids)` (and applying an inline/chunked strategy for all dialects above the limit) would be safer.

Test cleanup registered after data creation and assertions, leaking rows across subtests on failure

`createTestAnnotations` and the two `assertAnnotationCount`/`assertAnnotationTagCount` calls run before `t.Cleanup` is registered, and all subtests share the single `fakeSQL` database. If insertion or either initial assertion fails (they use `require`, so the subtest aborts immediately), the `DELETE FROM annotation` / `DELETE FROM annotation_tag` cleanup is never registered, leaving rows behind and causing every subsequent subtest to fail with confusing count mismatches instead of a single clear failure. Register the `t.Cleanup` before creating the test data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete puts the bare logger in the context instead of the enriched one

`ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` uses `d.Log` rather than the `log` built one line earlier with `name`, `kind` and `method` values. Downstream code that retrieves the logger via `klog.FromContext(ctx)` loses all of the request-specific context, unlike every other method in this file which stores `log`. Should be `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: klog.NewContext receives d.Log instead of the enriched log variable, so the name, kind, and method values are not propagated to the logging context.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records the object name in the metric's `kind` label, causing unbounded cardinality

`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. Each distinct resource name becomes a new Prometheus label value on the storage duration histogram, so the series count grows with the number of objects ever deleted. This is a metrics cardinality explosion that can blow up the registry and the scraping backend. It should be `options.Kind`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same metrics-recording inconsistency: Delete passes the object name instead of options.Kind. The candidate additionally explains the resulting label cardinality risk.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will be canceled when the request finishes

All four async legacy writes (`Create` line 51, `Delete` line 110, `Update` line 135, `DeleteCollection` line 163) build their context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming request context. In net/http (and therefore in the apiserver), the request context is canceled as soon as the handler returns, which happens immediately after the dual writer returns the unified-storage result. The spawned goroutine therefore usually starts or continues with an already-canceled context, so the legacy write is aborted (and silently only shows up as an error in the duration metric). Since the whole point of mode 3 is to keep legacy in sync as a safety net, legacy would systematically fail to be written. Use a detached context (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` as the parent, preserving the auth/user values) before applying the timeout.

Unrecovered panic in async legacy write will crash the whole process

The legacy writes are now executed in bare `go func()` goroutines (lines 50, 108, 134, 161) with no `defer recover()`. Previously these calls were synchronous and any panic inside the legacy store was caught by the apiserver's panic-recovery filter for that request. Now a panic in `d.Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection` (or in the validation callbacks it invokes) happens on a goroutine with no recovery and takes down the entire Grafana process. Wrap the goroutine body with a recover (e.g. `runtime.HandleCrash` semantics) or a helper that logs and swallows panics.

Storage failures in Create/Update are recorded as legacy-storage durations

In `Create` (line 45) and `Update` (line 129) the error path calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` even though the failure came from `d.Storage`. The success paths correctly call `recordStorageDuration`. As a result the legacy histogram is polluted with unified-storage failures and the storage error rate is under-reported, which makes the mode-3 dashboards/alerts misleading. Both should call `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

DeleteCollection records the legacy call duration into the storage metric

Inside the async goroutine of `DeleteCollection` the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration`. The legacy delete-collection latency/error rate is therefore never visible in the legacy metric and instead corrupts the storage metric (which was already recorded a few lines above for the same request), double-counting storage observations.

Legacy update now re-runs the caller's objInfo instead of applying the object already written to storage

The previous implementation fetched the current object, computed `updated`, and passed `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}` to the legacy store so that legacy received exactly the object persisted in unified storage. The new code hands the raw `objInfo` to `d.Legacy.Update`, so the legacy store re-evaluates the update/patch against *its own* copy of the object, including resource-version precondition checks. For PUT requests the resourceVersion in the request body comes from unified storage and will generally not match the legacy row, so the legacy update can fail with a conflict, and for PATCH/Apply the transformation is applied to a possibly divergent legacy object. Either way legacy silently drifts from unified storage, defeating the purpose of the mode-3 safety write. The failure is only visible as a metric label, since the error is not even logged.

The input object is shared with the async legacy write without a deep copy

`d.Legacy.Create(ctx, obj, ...)` is called from the goroutine with the same `obj` pointer that was just passed to `d.Storage.Create` and that the request handler still owns (admission/audit layers may read it, and generic registry code mutates object metadata in place such as resourceVersion/UID/name on name generation). Writing to that object from the legacy store concurrently with the handler's continued use is a data race that can also mean the legacy store persists metadata mutated by the unified store. Pass `obj.DeepCopyObject()` to the goroutine.

Destroy can tear down the stores while async legacy writes are still in flight

`Destroy()` immediately calls `d.Storage.Destroy()` and `d.Legacy.Destroy()`, but nothing tracks the goroutines spawned by Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection. On shutdown an in-flight legacy write can run against an already-destroyed store (closed DB handles/connection pools), producing errors or panics. A WaitGroup (or a shared lifecycle context) that Destroy waits on would make shutdown deterministic.

New mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy write

All of the new tests share a single `mock.Mock` between `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock`, so an expectation registered by `setupLegacyFn` is indistinguishable from the one registered by `setupStorageFn` (e.g. in `TestMode3_Update` both register `"Update"` with identical argument matchers). Combined with the fact that no test waits for (or asserts on) the goroutine that performs the legacy write, and no `AssertExpectations`/`AssertCalled` is used, the tests cannot show that the legacy store is written at all — which is the core behaviour this PR adds. They also cannot show that a legacy failure does not affect the response. Separate mocks per store (or distinct expectations) plus a synchronization point (channel/WaitGroup signalled from the legacy mock) are needed.

Unrelated, duplicated and unsorted go.work.sum entries

The added block contains `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` which is already present a few lines above, and inserts `github.com/grafana/grafana-azure-sdk-go/v2` out of sort order. These entries are unrelated to the dual-writer change and look like a hand-edited/stale generated file; they should be regenerated (`go work sync`) or dropped from this PR to avoid confusing future dependency updates.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing `key` prop on GrafanaRuleListItem inside rules.map()

In `FilterViewResults`, the `grafana` branch of `rules.map(...)` now renders `<GrafanaRuleListItem ... />` without a `key`, while the `datasource` and `default` branches still pass `key={key}`. The pre-computed `key` (from `getRuleKey`) is destructured but unused for Grafana rules.
